###### **EDITOR’S BIOGRAPHY** 

**Guillermo Ugarte** obtained in 1968 a degree in mining civil engineering at the University of Chile and in 1971 a D.I.C. and a Ph.D. from the Imperial College, University of London.  He then joined the Department of Mining Engineering at the University of Chile where he served as Head of the Hydrometallurgy Group.  He moved afterward to Minmetal Consultants as Head of the Mining and Metallurgical Division and later to the Chilean Copper Commission where he was appointed Technical Director.  In 1984, Dr. Ugarte joined CIMM as Head of the Extractive Metallurgy Division until 1993 when he moved to Davy International as Process Manager of the Santiago Office. At present he is Chief Engineer and Hydrometallurgical Consultant at AMEC.  He has been visiting professor to universities in Brazil, Colombia, Mexico and Argentina, and has given regular courses in hydrometallurgy at the University of Chile, University of Concepciуn and University of Santiago.  During 1991, he was Academic Visitor at Imperial College.  He has numerous publications in the field of Hydrometallurgy.  He has been Director and Vice-president of The Chilean Institute of Mining Engineers, and was a member of the Organizing Committees for Copper 87, Copper 91 and Co-Chairman of Copper 95.

###### **PREFACE** 

Copper 2013 International Conference is the 8<sup>th</sup> version of the most important global meeting that brings together leading scientists, researchers, academics, and executives from different companies and organizations devoted to the areas of economy, copper processing, metallurgical extraction techniques; environmental compatibility; copper applications, copper recovery, and waste management and recycling techniques. At the same time, the challenges faced by dif

ferent mining projects will be addressed. We appreciate the work and collaboration from colleagues coming from over 30 countries and representing more than 300 companies and institutions. Copper 2013 Conferences find their origin in the joint work conducted between the Chilean Institute of Mining Engineers (IIMCh) and the Metallurgical Society of the Canadian Institute of Mining, Metallurgy and Petroleum (METSOC). Since 2007, when the Copper Conference was held in Toronto, new co-organizer institutions have helped disseminate the results achieved by the Conferences while granting these a strong global character in terms of convening power, submittal of papers, and the generation of collaborative knowledge. We deeply appreciate the disinterested contribution from GDMB of Germany, MMIJ of Japan, and TMS and SME from USA. This time, the current global situation is not only a scenario where competitive prices are being realized but also where strong and serious uncertainties are being handled in connection with the global economy; energy and key resources prices. Globally, ore grades have declined to historically low levels and, therefore, the recycling and recovery of what used to be waste material, nowadays represent great opportunities for the overall development of new projects. Water uses in production processes and the solutions applied no doubt represent a source of knowledge for the community gathered at this venue. Likewise, new long-term and mid-term forecasts to be made in the future will certainly set their focus on eventual challenges and on mining and metallurgical development opportunities in the decades ahead. The total of 330 papers submitted in response to the original call will present the main changes to take place in metallurgical processes, as well as the state-of-the-art techniques responsible for providing effective solutions to new challenges posed by metallurgical processes. The widespread interest generated by innovations, particularly in the area of pyrometallurgy will undoubtedly occupy a special place in the course of the Conference, thanks to the research and development of technological solutions conducted in countries like China, for example. _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ The 2013 Conference has issued 7 volumes of Proceedings containing all the papers and management initiatives presented in each of the 10 symposiums hosted by the Conference. ###### **FOREWORD** 

The response to the Hydrometallurgy Symposium of Copper 2013 has been most gratifying. Near 50 papers were submitted for inclusion in the Symposium program. The international nature of the Symposium is attested to by the fact that the 41 selected papers are drawn from 13 countries, including Australia, Canada, Chile, China, Finland, Germany, Italy, Japan, Mexico, South Africa, Spain, Ukraine and United States. 

The Symposium program encompasses six sessions: three on Leaching and three on Solvent Extraction.  The sessions cover a range of topics within the hydrometallurgy of copper: new projects, leaching of ores and concentrates, hydrometallurgical process innovation, modeling, simulation, improving of leaching and solvent extraction technologies and precious metals recovery. 

Solvent extraction for copper recovery is the subject of several papers which deal with modern solvent extraction equipment, global survey of copper solvent extraction operations and practices, new extractants and the effect of impurities on the reagent stability. 

It is hoped that the Hydrometallurgy Symposium volume will provide not only a record of a meeting but also a basis for further excellent work in copper hydrometallurgy.

Design and Management of Copper Heap Leach Pads|……………515| V 3 ###### **TECHNOLOGY LEVERAGING OPPORTUNITIES FOR IMPROVING THE ECONOMICS OF LOW GRADE COPPER DEPOSITS** C.A. du Plessis, and C.B.Ward, and J. Cucuzza AMIRA International _Level 2, 271 William Street, Melbourne, VIC 3000, Australia chris.duplessis@amirainternational.com_ ###### **ABSTRACT** The exploration pursuit of high grade deposits also results in an increasing inventory of known deposits of sub-economic grades. Importantly, economic viability is dependent upon the available processing options and economic parameters imposed by the use of such methods. Current processing options are limited to either concentrate production or leaching and have not fundamentally changed for several decades. The exponential increase in comminution power, per unit of contained copper, generally precludes economic concentrate production from ore with grades below 0.5% Cu. In some instances, low grade ore is economically treatable via heap leaching methods, where the mining costs are carried by higher grade ore. Heap leaching economics are, however, challenged by the presence of high acid consuming gangue minerals, poor hydraulic control of heap leach solutions, and copper mineralization occurring as refractory primary sulfide. Technical and economic viability of in-situ leaching is limited to a very small number of high grade oxide copper deposits in highly fractured and relatively porous deposits. A number of significant technology advances in nonmineral industries may provide opportunities for economic step-changes to copper project developments. Such technologies range from rock fracturing and solution containment technology developed in the petroleum industry, to drug delivery methodologies developed in the pharmaceutical industry. This article expands on a number of these technology concepts that may have a significant impact on low grade copper economics. _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 4 ###### **INTRODUCTION** Exploration programs continue to target high grade (>1%) copper deposits with significant expenditure on this endeavor. Using the conventional processing paradigm, copper ore grades of <0.8% and <0.5% for Greenfield and Brownfield applications respectively, are generally uneconomic. The vast majority of discovered copper resources, however, fall within this low grade category. Although exploration will continue to target high grade discoveries, it strategically important for the copper industry to also invest in improving the economics of lower grade ore processing though improved technology. AMIRA International, an independent association of minerals companies that develops and brokers collaborative research projects, has developed number

of related technology project concepts with the objective of improving the economics of low grade ore processing.  The motivation for this program is based on: (1) the large, and growing, inventory of low grade copper resources that fall below the cutoff grade for conventional concentrate production; (2) the relatively poor metal recovery from heap leaching (the processing method most often considered for low grade resources), particularly for primary sulfide minerals such as chalcopyrite; and (3) the economic impact successful technology development would have on low grade copper resources. 

Falling industry head grade trends require a deliberate industry response to sustain future economic margins. The operating costs for most conventional processing methods increase exponentially with a reduction in grade (Figure 1), with the highest proportion of operating costs incurred through mining and milling unit operations. 



Figure 1– Typical open pit operating costs as a function of ore grade 

Although heap and dump leaching technologies are applied to low grade ores, 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

5 

recoveries are generally poor, variable and unpredictable.  Importantly, the current methods available for low grade processing are ineffective for recovery of primary copper sulfide ores, most notably chalcopyrite, the predominant form of copper mineralization.  It is therefore clear that improved economics should look beyond heap leaching, in addition to addressing the key hurdles of heap leaching. 

###### **PROJECT CONCEPTS IN THE LOW GRADE COPPER PROGRAM** 

The projects that comprise the AMIRA Low Grade Copper program have been tailored to significantly change the economics of low grade deposits.  The projects range from those with immediate process design and operational improvement applications (heap leaching hydraulics and gas dispersion), to those with the potential to significantly change the economic processing paradigm for low grade deposits (in-situ fracture stimulation and leaching, as well as micro-capsule leaching).  The overall objective, of all the projects within the program, is to increase resource-to-reserve conversion of low grade ore deposits.  Although each project has its own specific objective, there is considerable synergy between the various projects. While the program has an initial copper focus, the projects have significant application potential to other commodities including nickel, uranium and gold.  Each project is briefly described, as well as application area synergy and relationship between these technology concepts. 

###### **Heap Leach Scale-up for Liquid and Gas Dispersion** 

The aim of the project is to develop a robust heap leaching scale-up methodology, where laboratory-determinable parameters reliably translate into full-scale heap performance.  The scale-up methodology will focus specifically on liquid and gas distribution, as these factors are most critical to improved heap leaching

performance. Sub-optimal heap leaching performance can often be attributed to inadequate determination and understanding of the fundamental parameters governing solution percolation.  This leads to over-reliance on generic rules-of-thumb, empirical testing methods and extrapolation of design parameters from one project to another. Optimal scale-up design can be informed through geomechanical testing procedures to determine permeability and percolation characteristics relevant to  liquid and gas dispersion combined with appropriate and validated predictive models. The purpose of this project is to provide robust and operationally validated methods for process optimization and design. 

###### **Continuous Saturated Coarse Particle (Vat) Leaching** 

In many instances heap leaching is not an appropriate or viable treatment option for low grade ore, even when optimized for hydraulic and gas dispersion properties. Heap leaching is not effective for applications with inherent unfavourable hydraulic properties, where copper occurs mainly as chalcopyrite, or where extended heap leach times lead to high acid consumption. An important reason for low rates and recoveries in heap leaching is because solution access to most of the target mineral surfaces is via 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

6 

capillary diffusion rather than bulk solution flow. This results in solution chemistry gradient effects that preclude effective chalcopyrite leaching.  Diffusion-related limitations can be overcome by using a saturated continuous leaching reactor in which coarse particles are minimally and intermittently mobilized (not agitated) to alter the pore space arrangement. This strategy eliminates the occurrence of stagnant pore spaces (and thus diffusion-controlled solution gradient effects) and facilitates high solution throughputs, improving control of the leach solution chemistry and increased metal recovery.  The aim of the project is to develop a viable alternative option for low grade ore, based on high rate leaching kinetics (~two orders of magnitude greater than for heap leaching) in continuous coarse particle (3 – 6 mm) saturated leach reactors (new generation, vat-style reactors).  Reactor development for this project will draw upon technology advances in dredging, slurry conveying and stirring, as well as thickener technologies. 

This project will also investigate methods for high rate oxidant regeneration, by both biohydrometallurgical and conventional chemical methods. Oxidant regeneration, is important because of the requirement for oxidants in sulfide mineral leaching and because oxidant regeneration cannot occur within saturated leach reactor. Oxidant regeneration also has relevance and application to the In-Situ Fracture Stimulation and Leaching project, where external oxidant re-generation will be required. 

###### **In-Situ Fracture Stimulation and Leaching** 

Heap leaching and coarse particle continuous vat leaching, circumvent the

high energy cost associated with milling, thereby reducing operating costs. However, neither of these methods circumvent mining costs, which along with milling are typically the main operating costs.  For this reason, heap leaching and saturated coarse particle leaching, is most applicable to Brownfield low grade scenarios where the ore has already been mined (and mining costs have been expensed) as part of a higher grade mining operation.  Many low grade deposits, however, do not have a high-grade component. Such deposits can only be made economically viable if both the mining and milling costs are circumvented.  In-situ leaching provides a potential option to achieve this objective. The aim of this project is therefore, to enable viable in-situ fracture stimulation and leaching (ISFS&L) technology for suitable hard rock sulfides mineral deposits.  In addition to circumventing mining and milling costs, the in-situ leaching also offers the potential to overcome the capital costs of pre-stripping and significantly reduce aboveground processing plant costs. 

In recent years there have been significant technology developments in nonmineral industries that may be deployed, with suitable adaptation, for in-situ fracturing and leaching. Hydraulic fracture stimulation techniques have been developed to a high level of sophistication and maturity in the oil and gas industries. Similar fracture stimulation techniques are also used for hard rock fracturing in the mining industry as pre-treatment for block caving. The maturity of these methods provides the basis for adapting the technology for mineral in-situ leaching processes. The project is designed to 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

7 

overcome the main hurdles to effective deployment of in-situ fracturing and leaching, which include: 

Solution containment and hydraulic management to prevent groundwater contamination. 

- Ore permeability and the extent to which existing or induced fractures can effectively access and intercept target minerals - particularly relevant in the context of hard rock mineralization. 

- The ability to leach target minerals for economically effective metal recovery. 

The process, to be developed in the project, is referred to as In-Situ Fracture Stimulation and Leaching (ISFS&L) to emphasize the importance of fracture stimulation to access hard rock sulfides, as opposed to In-Situ Leaching (ISL) of existing porous/fractured material.  Low grade copper sulfide deposits at <500 m depths are suggested for initial development of the technology. The target application would be geological formations in which sulfide minerals are present as late stage veins or in stratabound ore. 

###### **Micro-Capsule Leaching** 

Economically viable hydrometallurgical metal recovery from low grade ore is dependent upon two criteria: (1) effective recovery and (2) affordability.  An important constraint for low grade ore processing is that high potency (effective) leaching reag

ents are often consumed by gangue mineral interaction, thereby precluding their use.  This, in turn, results in the use of low potency leaching reagents and reactor methods, with poor metal extraction outcomes, particularly from low grade chalcopyrite ores.  In this project, micro-capsule technology is proposed as a means to overcome this constraint by facilitating selective interaction of lixiviants with valuable target minerals.  Microcapsule technology, as conceptually illustrated in Figure 2, can be used to create optimal leaching conditions locally by encapsulating and presenting leaching agents selectively and directly to target minerals, with minimal gangue mineral interaction. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

8 



Figure 2– Diagrammatic representation of a micro-leaching capsule 

Conventional mineral processing already makes use of selective chemical interaction with sulfide minerals over gangue minerals, in the form of collectors.  The most widely used example is the use of xanthate chemicals that selectively interact with sulfide minerals to render them hydrophobic, enabling effective mineral flotation.  The proposed concept is that similar selectivity can be achieved through functionalising the outside of the micro-capsule wall with collector-like functional groups so that they selectively bind to valuable sulfide minerals. Once delivered to the target sulfide mineral surface, the capsule discharges its lixiviant cargo in close proximity to the target mineral site. The cargo in the capsule can be tailored to initiate a leaching reaction, prevent passivation or disrupt already-formed passivation layers, deliver oxidants or provide local pH modification at target mineral surfaces. The micro-capsule cargos can be designed either to improve conventional leaching methods (such as heap leaching) and chemistry or to facilitate leaching using unconventional solution chemistry conditions (e.g. in non-acidic bulk solutions).  Micro-capsules may also be used to enhance coarse particle saturated leaching kinetics, or for effective metal recovery from in-situ leaching scenarios.

These tests were performed as suites involving all six composites – first were incremental rougher tests (flotation kinetics), then multi-stage cleaner tests which included the addition of an oxide scavenger flotation stage, following the sulphide rougher stage. The starting point was the generic copper porphyry flotation flowsheet. The objective of the rougher stage was to maximize the recovery of the copper sulphide minerals while remaining as selective as possible against pyrite and non-sulphide gangue. This left the scavenger stage to be defined purely as an oxide scavenger without fear of depressing remaining copper sulphide minerals by the sulphidization conditioning. It was also pre-determined that the oxide scavenger concentrate would be kept separate as a potential leach feed rather than combined with the rougher concentrate for cleaning. This was due to the high collector dosages applied in the oxide scavenger which would be counter to pyrite rejection during the cleaning of the rougher concentrate. Each suite of tests had a specific purpose. The rougher incremental tests aimed at establishing an initial flotation response for each composite and identify the rougher flotation time ensuring recovery of the copper sulphides. The first suite of cleaner tests built on the knowledge from the rougher tests and added a rougher concentrate regrind along with multistage cleaning to assess the upgradability of each composite. Also, preliminary conditions were applied for the oxide scavenger stage. The second suite of cleaner tests aimed at refining the conditions for the sulphide and oxide flotation stages as well as producing samples for leaching tests. A final third suite of cleaner tests was performed for the troublesome East Arguelles and West Oxide Sulphide composites to evaluate the potential impact of Unimax SD-300 for pyrite depression. 14 As such, only two tests were required for the well behaved Porphyry Sulphide composite to yield the desirable outcom

e while three tests were performed for the other composites with the exception of the most challenging East Arguelles and West Oxide Sulphide composites which needed four tests in total. The rougher kinetic tests (F1 - F6) were initially planned to be executed at natural or weak alkaline pH to investigate the pyrite rejection with a relatively lower lime consumption, so 400 g/t lime, 15 g/t XD5002 (copper collector) and 5 g/t diesel (molybdenum collector) were added into the primary grind for Porphyry Sulphide, Skarn Sulphide, Hornfels Sulphide and East Arguelles composites while the lime and XD5002 dosages increased to 1000 g/t and 30 g/t respectively for West Oxide Sulphide and Skarn Oxide composites consider

ing their specific mineralogical composition. The float times for each sulphide rougher concentrate were 1, 2, 3, 3, 3 minutes respectively. 

The pulp pH in the rougher kinetics tests was maintained between 8.5 – 10.0 and the total lime consumption ranged from 400 to 1750 g/t for the six composites. It was observed that the mill discharge pH for the West Oxide Sulphide composite was only 5.5 when an addition of as much as 1000 g/t lime in the primary grind was made and the pulp pH only increased to 6.5 with a further addition of 750 g/t lime in 1<sup>st</sup> rougher stage.  Such a pH response suggested that the West Oxide Sulphide composite was highly reactive (presence of soluble sulphate salts) and, as the increased pH did not result in improved pyrite rejection, flotation at natural pH was subsequently used.  The observed behavior of the West Oxide Sulphide composite may be related to the high proportion of copper as copper sulphate present. 

One of the diluents in the sulphide rougher concentrate was pyrite. The pyrite content and distribution in each product in the metallurgical balance was calculated assuming the sulphide 

15 

components in all six composites were only chalcopyrite, molybdenite, and pyrite.  However, negative pyrite assays and/or distributions being more than 100% were obtained for most composites and this suggested that the sulphide mineralogy was more complex than assumed. As the results of the QEMSCAN became available and confirmed the suspicions about the complexity of the copper mineralogy, the estimation of pyrite content was discontinued for all but the Porphyry Sulphide composite.  Despites this set-back, the severity of the dilution of a flotation concentrate by pyrite could be qualitatively assessed by how much the sulphur assay exceeded the copper assay. 

The sulphide copper recoveries of six composite samples ranged from ~31.0% to 96.1% to the rougher concentrate while the copper grade varied from 2.28% to 10.0% Cu. The copper recoveries in the sulphide rougher stage  are greater than the distribution ratio of sulphide copper in QEMSCAN examination for composite samples of Skarn Oxide, East Arguelles, Hornfels Sulphide and West Oxide Sulphide, indicating other copper associated minerals were also recovered in the sulphide rougher flotation circuit. 

Molybdenum recoveries were poor, ranging from 20.4% to 75.4% in sulphide rougher stages, and they were usually 20 percent less than copper recoveries under the same flotation conditions except for East Arguelles which yielded a 44.6% Mo recovery for a 31.0% Cu recovery. The head grade of molybdenum is low (around 20 ppm for these six composites), and up to nearly 40% as soluble molybdenum oxide.  The combination of both factors results in poor molybdenum recoveries. 

An oxide scavenger flotation stage was implemented via a sulphidization conditioning (NaHS) followed by  Potassium Amyl Xanthate (PAX) addition once the pulp potential bounced back to around -50

mV. NaSH was added to a target pulp potential (EMF) from -150 to -100 mV for PorSul, SkarnSul, SkarnOx, Hornfelsul and East Arguelles. The pulp pH for WestOxSul was 6.3 in oxide scavenger stage, so the pulp potential for the sulphidization conditioning was increased from -100 to -30 mV with the purpose of achieving a similar pulp oxidation-reduction state as obtained at pH 9.5-10 for the other samples. In addition, the pulp potential was allowed to rebound to a value between 0 and 100 mV prior to addition of the PAX and flotation. The copper recoveries from the oxide scavenger stage varied from 0.1% from Porphyry (essentially no oxide copper) to 46.3% from East Arguelles while the molybdenum recoveries ranged from 0.5% to 8.3%. The shape of grade and recovery curves for Porphyry, Skarn Oxide and Hornsfels Sulfide are smooth. The grade of copper and molybdenum continuously drop while their recoveries increase with time. ###### **CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS** 

The Escalones deposit in Chile contains a significant resource of copper, gold, silver and molybdenum. The processing of the Escalones ore has been studied using a combination of sulfide flotation followed by direct tails leaching or flotation and leaching of an oxide concentrate (obtained from the sulfide float tails).  A series of six composite samples were prepared. The Porphyry, Hornfels Sulfide, Skarn Sulfide and Skarn Oxide samples all produced good quality cleaner flotation concentrates in batch and locked cycle flotation testing.  The leaching of either the flotation tailings or an oxide scavenger concentrate produced a significant overall increase in copper recovery.  The overall copper recovery for these samples ranged from 79.3 to 94.7%.  The West Oxide-Sulfide and East Arguelles samples were too oxidized to generate high quality copper sulphide concentrates. Nevertheless, a low grade concentrate was obtained and an oxide scavenger concentrate for leaching.  The overall recovery of copper was 74.9 and 65.8% for East Arguelles and West Oxide-Sulfide composites respectively. 

Gold and silver were successfully floated with the copper sulphides.  Molybdenum was also floated.  Further work on copper-molybdenum flotation separation is required.

Cobre Las Cruces (CLC) project, property of First Quantum Minerals, LTD, is located approximately 20 km NNW of Seville in Andalucнa in southern Spain, and consists of an open pit mine and a hydrometallurgical plant to produce copper cathodes. 

The project has been designed for a nominal copper capacity of 72,00

0 t/y copper cathodes, grade A LME.  During the fifteen (15) year lifetime of the project, approx. 16,8 million tonnes of dry ore will be processed, with a total content above one million tonnes of copper metal, and for a capital cost of € 500 million. 

The geological resources are located at a depth of 150 meters. Two main ore types are exploited: a massive sulphide ore mainly comprised of pyrite, and a semimassive ore. The mineralogy is mainly pyrite 65-75% w/w, digenite and chalcocite, and also minor amounts of covellite, chalcopyrite, galena, and blende. The ore is crushed, milled, and then atmospherically leached and the obtained pregnant solution is treated by solvent extraction and electrowinning to render cathodic copper. 

The main challenge of the project is in the atmospheric leaching at 90 ºC and using ferric sulphate for the oxidation of copper. The ferric sulphate will be obtained from leaching of pyrite and oxidized with oxygen, this process has been selected after studies with Outotec and is licensed by such a company, an innovative approach to what is currently being used in this industry. The target is to have above 92% copper extraction in leaching reactors and certain proportion of the pyrite is expected to be leached to maintain concentration of iron in the solution. 

Crushing and milling capacities will be designed to handle up to 1.3 million tonnes of dry ore per year. An availability factor is applied to reach an “instantaneous” flowrate. This “availability” will reflect the actual operating hours of the plant sections and equipment items.  To this instantaneous flowrate is then added a design factor and the equipment selected will be the next largest size available from the equipment provider. 

In EW mass balance it has been applied a specific design factor to maintain maximum acceptable current density of 325 A/m<sup>2</sup> . 

The infrastructure required to support the operation will include an adjacent oxygen plant built and operated by a recognized oxygen production company (outside the project scope), a steam plant, ancillary facilities, and all required administration buildings. 

Environmental protection is first priority for CLC. This project demands full protection of the underlying aquifer whose water is to be diverted around the pit by extraction and reinjection wells. To improve water consumption the plant will use almost entirely treated sewage water from a nearby facility. 

All rain water, mine water and contact water runoff will be collected and treated if necessary before use in the plant or release. 

The plant employs approximately 250 staff and operators.

There is a liquid loop which leaches copper from the ore, delivers it to the next process stage which the joins with the fresh ore to leach more copper. The liquid loaded with leached copper is known as pregnant liquid solution (PLS). The liquid with low copper content _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 30 which joins the fresh ore is known as raffinate. Leaching

is not copper selective and therefore PLS bears other metals than copper. Copper in leaching pregnant solution is transferred selectively to an organic liquid loop which subsequently delivers it to a third final aqueous loop in electrowinning (EW). The organic loop is a process that prevents impurities passing from the leaching aqueous loop to the EW one. The organic that transfers copper from PLS is known as loaded organic and once the copper has been delivered to EW loop is named as unloaded organic. Copper in the EW solution, named as electrolyte, is deposited as metal copper of 99.999% purity by means of an electrical current. The copper-bearing electrolyte from the previous stage is called rich electrolyte and the one leaving EW to be charged with fresh copper is called lean electrolyte. Since PLS temperature decreases as it leaves the reactors, it becomes supersaturated in gypsum, leading to scaling problems in pipelines and SX plant. ###### <u>Solvent Extraction</u> 

PLS from leaching mainly contains copper and iron. The aim of SX stage is to selectively extract copper from PLS. This is carried out mixing the two phases: the aqueous phase (PLS) with an organic phase bearing a chemical reagent (aldoxime in kerosene as diluent) which bonds copper. The efficiency of this reaction greatly depends on PLS pH value. In the extraction stage, organic and PLS flows are mixed in counter-current flows. There are two counter current extraction circuits: a primary circuit for the primary PLS coming from the PLS pond and a secondary circuit for the secondary PLS mainly composed of the belt filters washing outlet stream. The organic loop is common for both circuits. 

The loaded organic is sent to a loaded organic tank and to a washing stage to remove aqueous traces trapped during the extraction due to inefficiencies. This washed organic is then mixed with the electrolyte in order to strip the copper and send it to the EW loop. 

Primary PLS is heated at 38 ºC previously to being fed to SX to prevent calcium precipitation. Secondary PLS is cooled at 33 ºC. 

Copper is stripped from loaded organic in the stripping stages, from where it is pumped to the tank farm and EW area. 

In SX there is crud generation as a consequence of solids entrainment in the aqueous organic interface. Cruds are periodically removed and treated. A view of SX circuit is shown below.

###### **CONCLUSIONS** 

Cobre las Cruces plant ramp up after the start-up did not reach design specifications. Basic points concerned plant capacity limitation, leaching recovery and some operation parameters which were beneath standard. 

When design production rates were achieved, cathode quality was affected as a consequence of combined effects regarding process operation, layout and anodes. These weak points had not been noticed until standard production rates settled 

Different actions and modifications were carried out aiming at all the points above. In summary, the issues can be grouped as: 

- Related to plant capacity: 

   - Cooling towers outlet modification to allow higher PLS flows 

   - An increase in grinding product size to prevent tailings filters from getting blocked 

   - A decrease of TS to prevent pipeline blockages by scaling and SX solids overload. Aforementioned action being the placement of a pinned bed clarifier. 

   - Tailings thickening and filtration stabilization by adding surge capacity 

   - Reactor materials substituted for agitators and transference boxes lining 

- Related to leaching recovery: 

   - Residence time increase 

   - Acid control loop implemented 

   - Operational density better control 

   - Iron recirculation 

   - Oxygen diffusion enhancement 

- Related to cathode quality: 

   - TSS filtration in electrolyte 

   - Progressive replacement of anodes 

   - Proper reagents 

All these issues led to a stable design production of 6.000 t cathodes/month since April 2012 as well as achieving leaching recoveries over design (91.7%) since September 2012, with an average value of 92.8%. These data give evidence that copper production through hydrometallurgical processing out of secondary copper ores can be carried out with high efficiency as well as low environmental impact through an atmospheric ferric leaching process.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

This paper gives a description of the current operation of the CuproChlor® process at Minera Michilla which has been successfully implemented since 2001 to date for leaching secondary copper sulfide ore. 

The technology incorporates as many other copper hydrometallurgical plants, a process of agglomerate and acid curing but adding an additional additive that is calcium chloride, CaCl2. This allows produces an agglomerated with better physical properties that achieves a heap with better permeability properties which allows improving the copper recovery in the leaching process. 

An important feature of this technology is a stage of resting after the acid curing stage before start the irrigation. The leaching period is around 120-130 days total with an effective irrigation time from 80-90 days, obtaining a copper recovery of secondary sulfide minerals, in the order of 90% for copper grade between 1-3%. Tests for ore with primary copper sulfides are in development. 

Industrial results demonstrate that the CuproChlor ® process is very efficient for the extraction of copper from sulfide and mixed, minerals being very competitive technology in the world mining market.

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Minera Michilla is a company held by Chilean capitals, whose main shareholder is Antofagasta Minerals, and is located at the North of Chile, in the second region, 110 km to the north of  Antofagasta city, very close (10 km) to the Pacific coast. 

The CuproChlor® process belonging to Minera Michilla SA is a hydrometallurgical technology applied since 2001 to leach the secondary copper sulfides by means of a high chloride content solution. The process is similar to a conventional process since it consists of a crushing plant, followed by an agglomerate stage, ore stockpiling, and agglomerate rest stage, and leaching by means of traditional irrigation. The difference lies in the fact that water, sulfuric acid, and calcium chloride are added in the agglomerate stage. The addition of calcium chloride along with sulfuric acid produces calcium sulfate, gypsum, and releases chloride ions, that is, the chemical composition of the agglomerate solution changes from a sulfate to a chloride medium. When forming in this stage, gypsum allows to form solid bridges in the agglomerate ore. The foregoing results in an improved stability of the agglomerate ore, reason why a better hydrodynamic property of the ore bed is obtained, such as porosity, liquid and gaseous permeability, hydraulic conductivity, which are related to the equilibrium and kinetics of the oxygen transference from the gaseous phase to the liquid phase. 

The addition of calcium chloride in the agglomeration stage improves the physical properties of t

he agglomerate material, but at the same time has chemical and physical effects on the system. Passing from a sulfate system to a strong chloride means allows to improve the kinetics of some reactions in the presence of a cuprous ion.  But, it also permits to modifying the morphology of the product  layer of the sulfide reaction, in this special case, the sulfur  produced by the coveline reaction, a sulfur porous layer is then obtained allowing the reaction to continue. 

It should be clarified that Minera Michilla, for over 20 years, uses sea water in its leaching plants, then, adding a reagent in  agglomeration providing chloride to the solutions was not a problem, since the design and construction of its LX, SX, and EW considered, from the beginning, a high level of chloride in the leaching solutions,  45 to 50 gpl, approximately. 

The purpose of this work is showing this technology high competitive potential to leach secondary copper sulfides currently applied by Minera Michilla SA in its industrial operation for 12 years. Results will be shown from the initial stage, at pilot plant column level, followed by semi-industrial tests of 1000 t each, to then show the results obtained so far at industrial scale.

###### **INVESTIGATION OF TENNANTITE/TETRAHEDRITE TREATMENT PROCESS BY ALKALINE LEACHING AND PRECIPITATION** 

Atsushi Shibayama, Batnasan Altansukh and Kazutoshi Haga _Akita University, Graduate School of Engineering and Resource Science 1-1, Tegata gakuen machi, Akita, Japan sibayama@gipc.akita-u.ac.jp_ 

###### **ABSTRACT** 

A process for removal of arsenic (As) and antimony (Sb) from a copper ore containing tennantite (Cu12As4S13) and tetrahedrite (Cu12Sb4S13 **)** in NaHS-NaOH media was discussed in this study. The main objective of the study was to investigate the effects of temperature, time, NaHS concentration, pulp density, and sulfur addition on the removal process of arsenic and antimony from the tennantite/tetrahedrite in alkaline media. The main results showed that both arsenic and antimony contents in the sample were reduced from 4-5 mass% to < 0.5 mass% at optimum alkaline leaching condition determined. In the precipitation step the vast majority of the arsenic (> 99%) and antimony (> 90 %) was recovered from the leachate by the addition of 0.2 M elemental sulfide which can form precipitate as Na3AsS4 and Na3SbS4.

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Enargite (Cu3AsS4), tennantite (Cu12As4S13) and tetrahedrite (Cu12Sb4S13) are the main minerals with high As/Sb contents that associate with copper sulfides [covellite (CuS), chalcocite (Cu2S), chalcopyrite (CuFeS2) and bornite (Cu5FeS4)] and are normally recovered by flotation. Copper ores containing these minerals are offered as copper resource to smelters for copper recovery. However the high content of As/Sb effectively reduces value of copper resource due to environmental implications of toxic As/Sb. As demand for copper continues to grow, a need to source copper from all resources including those that contain high As/Sb also becomes necessary. Reviews on copper resources containing these minerals with high As/Sb are covered widely in literatures by many researchers [1-8]. 

For feed to smelters, first, the copper ores/concentrates containing enargite, tennantite and tetrahedrite were separated by flotation to obtain a clean concentrate with As/Sb content <0.5 wt% and a dirty reject mainly containing these minerals by employing slurry potential and pH control with depressants and activators can be achieved [9-13]. In the second case involving leaching, the transformation of enargite, tennantite and tetrahedrite to CuO or Cu2S by selectively dissolving As/Sb into solution with sodium hypochlorite (NaClO) or sodium sulfide (Na2S) in alkaline solutions in the presense of NaOH gives very promising results [1-5, 14-18]. 

Other hydrometallurgical treatment options through chloride and sulfates leaching, or in ammonical solutions and at elevated temperatures and pressures are reported elsewhere [2, 6, 19, 20]. 

In recent studies, Tongamp et al.,[21-23] have introduced sodium hydrosulfide (NaHS) as a leaching

media for the conversion of enargite (Cu3AsS4) to Cu2S in NaHS–NaOH solution, showing near complete removal of As (> 99 %) in enargite within 4–6 h and at very high pulp density of 1000 g/L. In this paper we discuss our work on As/Sb removal and control of the solid residues before their final disposal by advanced processes which include alkaline leaching with NaHS-NaOH solution as medium for selective removal of As/Sb in the tennantite and tetrahedrite minerals and precipitation of As/Sb dissolved in solution. Our main target is to reduce the content of As/Sb in the tennantite and tetrahedrite to < 0.5 mass% by leaching and prercipitation process. ###### **EXPERIMENTAL SECTION** ###### **Materials and Methods** A copper ore containing tennantite/tetrahedrite minerals obtained from Teine Mine in Japan was used as a starting material in this study. Mineral constituents of the sample as detected by XRD measurement shown in Fig. 1, where main dominant phase was the tennantite/tetrahedrite ((Cu,Fe)12(As,Sb)4S13) and SiO2. The XRD measurements for phase constituents of the samples were taken using Rigaku, RINT–2200 / PC system with a Cu Kα irradiation source (λ = 1.5405 Е) at 40 kV and 50 mA. Figure 2 - Schematic illustration of the As and Sb removal process from tennantite/tetrahedrite in an alkaline media ###### Alkaline leaching All leaching experiments were conducted in a 200 mL Teflon beaker enclosed with a thermometer and gas exhaust pipe for preventing the evaporation of the solution. The beaker was placed in a water bath on a hot plate with magnetic stirrer. The slurry with a density ranging from 100 g/L to 1000 g/L and varying concentrations of NaHS (100-250 g/L) and NaOH (50-100 g/L) were used to prepare a solution containing > 30 g/L As and Sb, respectively. The slurry temperature was varied from 30 °C to 95 °C to analyze the effect of the temperature on the leaching. A solid feed containing As/Sb was added to the slurry after experimental temperature reached at 90 °C and the slurry was stirred continuously with a magnetic stirrer at 500-750 rpm keeping the temperature. The leaching time was varied from 10 min to 6 h and after that both solution and solid samples were separated by filtration. The _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 59 filtrate and the residue obtained by filtration were analyzed ICP-AES/OES and XRD for their chemical and mineralogical compositions. ###### As/Sb precipitation In this experiment, the leachate obtained from tennantite/tetrahedrite in alkaline media was used. The As and Sb concentration in the leachate was higher than 30 g/L respectively. After conditioning the leachate at 90 °C during 1 h, elemental sulfur with weight ration of As/Sb between S:(As+Sb) = 1:0 and 1:0.35 was added to the solution and continued the heating at 90 °C for another 1 h. When heating stopped, the solution was transferred to a 200 ml glass beaker placed in ice and allowed to cool the solution quickly to 30 °C with moderate stirring (300-500 rpm). The precipitate was formed very fast in the solution with addition of sulfur when temperature reached up to 30 °C. After 1-10 h, the precipitate formed were filtered and dried at 70 °C overnight and the filtrate was analyzed for As and Sb content. ###### **RESULTS AND DISCUSSION** ###### **Leaching mechanism of tennantite/tetrahedrite in alkaline condition** Leaching mechanism of Cu as formed Cu2S from tetrahedrite/tennantite (Cu12Sb4S13/Cu12As4S13) in a NaHS-NaOH solution media can be represented by Reactions 1-2 as shown below. Dissociation of NaHS as a leaching medium can be shown by Reaction 3, and HS– ions further dissociated into S2– and H2O in the presence of OH– (NaOH) to provide S2– ions which promote the dissolution of As and Sb from the minerals (Reaction 4). Cu12As4S13 + 9NaSH + 3NaOH → 6Cu2S + 4Na3AsS4 + 6H2O (1) Cu12Sb4S13 + 9NaSH + 3NaOH → 6Cu2S + 4Na3SbS4 + 6H2O (2) NaHS → Na+ + HS– (3) HS– + OH– `⇌` S2– + H2O (4) The stoichiometric requirements according to Reactions (1) and (2) allowed to quantify t

he amount of substances in the solution as stated that 1 mol of arsenic (As) and antimony (Sb) would requires 2.25 moles of sulfur (S/As=2.25 (9/4)) for dissolution of As and Sb from tennantite and tetrahedrite mineral. On the other hand, maintaining the high pH of the solution (pH > 12.5) prevents the sulfur hydrolysis from the S2– to HS– , which sustain the high concentration of S2– ions to dissolve As and Sb from the minerals. _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 60 ###### Effect of temperature on the alkaline leaching Leaching behaviour of metals (As, Sb, Cu and Fe) from –75+38 µm fraction of tennantite/tetrahedrite at different temperatures ranging from 30 **°** C to 95 **°** C is shown in Figure 2. The leaching solution which consists of 200 g/L (2.7M) NaHS and 100 g/L (2.5 M) NaOH was added to the slurry with the density of 100 g/L and fixed the leaching time at 6 hs. The results showed that the leaching rate of both As and Sb was increased up to 70 and 74 % while the temperature increased until 90 ºC, but the leaching rate was kept when the temperature increased further. At 90 ºC, leaching rate of As and Sb was reached 70% and 74%, respectively, while their contents in the solid residues reduced to < 0.2 mass%. However, the contents of As and Sb in the solids remain above 0.5 mass%, which should be reduced to < 0.5 mass%. The process consists of 2 major steps: alkaline leaching and precipitation. The main results obtained in the process can be summarized as follows: 1. As and Sb as impurities in the copper ore containing tennantite/tetrahedrite were selectively dissolved in NaHS-NaOH media at determined optimum condition. After the alkaline leaching, content of As and Sb in the sample was decreased up to 0.05 mass% for As and 0.11 mass% for Sb. XRD analysis revealed that the tennantite/tetrahedrite was converted completely to Cu2S. 2. Dissolved As and Sb in alkaline media could be recovered by precipitation with addition of elementary sulfide. It was revealed from XRD patterns that the main constituents of the precipitates are Na3AsS4 and Na3SbS4. ###### **ACKNOWLEDGEMENT** This research work was supported by JSPS KAKENHI (Grant-in-Aid for JSPS Fellow 22 `･` 00084 and Scientific Research (C) 21560845). ###### **AMMONIA HEAP LEACHING OF CHALCOPYRITE IN LOW GRADE ORES – A FRESH PERSPECTIVE?** 

###### **Jochen Petersen, Caroline Muzawazi,  James Mwase**

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Ammonia leaching of copper minerals has been explored many times and for many materials in the past 60 years. Although it has been shown to be an effective leach environment also for copper sulphide dissolution, its commercial application has remained niche. Heap leaching appears to be the most sensible option for economic Cu recovery from low-grade ores, but in terms of a sulphate leach system (with or without bacterial assistance) it has been successful only for secondary sulfide minerals, whereas chalcopyrite remains elusive. Some sucess had been achieved with thermophilic heap bioleaching, but this process is slow and difficult to control. 

Ammonia heap leaching of chalcopyrite has barely been explored, although it would appear attractive. Reasons probably relate to high reagent loss due to evaporation, difficulty with the recovery of ammonia from waste solutions, and economic sulphate recovery, but there is remarkably little discussion of this in the literature. 

Column leach studies of a PGM ore in which chalcopyrite is the main Cu bearing mineral has indicated the potential to recover at least 90-95% Cu from coated concentrates and >85% directly from coarse ore within much shorter time periods compared to thermophile bio-leach

ing. The conentrate data is discussed in more detail – it suggests that NH3 leaching of Cu is first order in NH3 and has an acivation energy of 36 kJ/mol and that the maximum rate of leaching in both systems is determined by the gas-liquid mass transfer from air into the heap solution. While the bioleach rate rapidly declines, it stays more or less constant throughout the ammonia leach, thus enabling much faster overall extraction rates. 

NH3 losses to the atmosphere were monitored and were found to be significant and acceptable only at ambient temperatures. Given still reasonable extraction rates at ambient, chalcopyrite ammonia heap leaching remains a strong contender in this area of research. However other aspects of a potential flowsheet, esepcially metal and ammonia recovery and sulphate removal, require further careful investigation.

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Recovery of metal commodities form low-grade ores is a challenge of increasing importance as world-wide demand continues to be high, while ore grades are declining, and energy costs and environmental controls are increasing. In terms of copper, heap leaching has become well established as a technology to achieve reasonable extractions from crushed ore, requiring considerably less energy to prepare than concentrates. The chemistry involved in these systems is largely acid sulphate, which is straightforward for copper oxides. It works reasonably well in combination with the ferric/ferrous redox couple for secondary sulphide minerals, which can be supported by micro-organisms native to the ore or deliberately introduced. For chalcopyrite this system has proved not feasible, except at elevated temperatures in the presence of certain thermophile organisms (Dew et al., 2011). Maintaining suitable conditions in a heap environment is possible, but is technically challenging and difficult to control, which is why thermophile heap bioleaching has not moved beyond demonstration scale to date. 

In terms of alternative approaches, only acidic chloride heap leaching has drawn some significant attention, both for secondary sulphides and chalcopyrite (Nicol et al., 2011). The attractiveness of chloride media lies in that they can stabilise the Cu<sup>2+</sup> /Cu<sup>+</sup> redox couple, which is more effective as an oxidant, and can also rapidly be re-oxidised by oxygen. Some uncertainty remains in terms of handling large solution inventories of acid chloride media and suitable materials of construction and to what extent the aggressive chloride environment attacks the rock matrix, leading to significant gangue mineral dissolution. 

Ammonia leaching allows selective extraction of base metals such as Cu, Ni, Co and Zn by forming stable metal-ammine complexes in a mildly alkaline environment, whilst being inert to iron and acid consuming gangue (Gupta and Mukherjee, 1990). Like chloride it can easily stabilise the Cu<sup>2+</sup> /Cu<sup>+</sup>

redox couple, thus making it potentially attractive as an alternative lixviant for copper sulphides, while avoiding some key drawbacks of chlorides.  The leaching of base metals in mildly alkaline ammonia solution is a well-established technique and finds application in the Caron (Canterford, 1975) and Sherritt Gordon (Forward, 1953) processes for the extraction of copper, nickel and cobalt operated under high temperatures and pressure and/or after pre-treatment of the ore, although this is energy intensive and uneconomical for low-grade ores. 

Several researchers have investigated the ammoniacal leaching process of copper sulphide dissolution, under different experimental conditions (Bell et al., 1995; Warren and Wadsworth, 1978; Beckstead and Miller 1977; Reilly and Scott, 1977; Peters, 1976). The process has been proved to work, though ‘passivation’ of chalcopyrite by a ferric iron oxide residue was claimed to be a limitation. The overall reaction proposed by Beckstead & Miller (1977) for chalcopyrite dissolution in ammoniacal solutions is:

Although the patent literature abounds with processes in the context of ammonia leaching, most of these are focused on the treatment of Ni and/or Co containing ores and concentrates. The patent by Duyvestein et al. (1993) describes a process for the partial leaching of cuprous sulphides from a mixed cuprous/cupric sulphide material in an ammonia liquor. An earlier process by Satchell (1979) for Phelps Dodge envisages NH3 leaching of copper oxides and sulphides in (NH4)2CO3 with oxygen. Dixon et al. (1975) describe a similar process using ammonium chloride or nitrate. Industrial application of this was attempted at the Anaconda Arbiter process (Kuhn et al., 1977), which did not achieve production capacity to various technical problems and was discontinued after a mere 3 years of operation. 

Literature on heap leaching with ammonia is very scant, with Dutrizac (1981) being the only definite reference which has shown success with column leaching of a chalcopyrite ore for over 3 months. Chuanhui et al. (2000) also studied the possibility of using ammonium salts on copper sulphides in a heap leaching environment for 7 days in a column and obtained 30% copper extraction from copper oxide ore. Heap leaching using ammonia is covered in the patent by Welham et al. (2009), although focused not on any specific minerals. The core of the patent revolves around the agglomeration of ores with curing agents, in the case of copper sulphides these being common oxidising agents, such as hypochlorite, nitrates or hydrogen peroxide. Metaleach, as subsidiary of Alexander Mining plc, have explored ammoniacal heap leaching from copper carbonate materials, but no applications of this technique to sulphide materials have been reported. 

Althou

gh not explicitly stated in the literature, a potential drawback of using ammonia in a heap leach operation is that it is too volatile, causing significant loss of reagent to the atmosphere if not controlled. Other reported issues with ammoniacal leaching refer more to the downstream processing of PLS, especially NH3 loss through solvent extraction and the difficulty to either recover NH3 by evaporation and re-adsorption, or removal of impurities and sulphate from the barren leach solution before recycle. 

In a recent study Mwase et al. (2012) developed a two-stage process for the heap leaching of a PGM bearing ore. The first stage involved the thermophilic heap bioleaching of base metal sulphides (essentially phyrrotite, pentlandite and chalcopyrite) with which the PGMs are associated, but which remain largely undissolved. These are dissolved with cyanide in a second heap leach stage. In the context of this work, ammonia leaching was attempted as an alternative to the bioleaching stage, given it might avoid the need for heap neutralisation prior to the cyanidation stage. These two studies allow direct comparison between ammonia leaching and thermophilic bioleaching of copper from the same chalcopyrite containing material in a heap leaching context.

###### **Experimental procedure** 

All tests were conducted in PVC leach columns, 0.5 m in height and 0.1 m in diameter, fitted with a thermocouple, temperature controller and heating mantle, The concentrate was prepared using the GEOCOAT<sup>TM</sup> method (Johansson et al. 1999) of coating concentrate onto support rock and the agglomerate packed into columns (approximately 4kg of agglomerated material per charge). The whole ore material was agglomerated with distilled water and charged directly into the columns. 

Solut

ion was supplied via a feed pipe supplied by a peristaltic pump at flowrate of    1 L/d (5 L/m<sup>2</sup> /h, a typical value for operating heaps). Aeration at 130 mL/min was via a rotameter through a gas inlet at the base of the column and outlet with liquid trap near the top. Exhaust air from the column was directed to wash bottles in which any volatilised NH3 was scrubbed out. Effluent solution was collected at the bottom of the column through an air lock to avoid loss of aeration through the outlet. The pregnant leach solution (PLS) was collected at the bottom of the column into a reservoir and recycled as feed for three days. After three days, the PLS was removed and fresh feed solution placed into the reservoir. The pH and redox values were monitored. The PLS was analysed for Cu, Ni and Fe using AAS. pH and redox potential were measured using a Metrohm, 713 pH and 827 redox meter respectively The NH3 losses in the wash bottles were measured a spectrophotometric test with ammonium test kits obtained from Merck.

Estimated column kLa values were calculated at ambient temperature, 40°C and 65°C, and obtained as 0.013 s<sup>-1</sup> , 0.017 s<sup>-1</sup> and 0.023 s<sup>-1</sup> , respectively.  This increase with temperature is offset by a concomitant decrease of oxygen solubility in aqueous solution (from about 8 to 5 ppm) and hence the net rate of oxygen mass transfer is barely affected by a change in temperature. This would explain the fact that although ammonia and bio-leach were run at different temperatures, the maximum mass transfer rates are similar. However, in the present case the rate of oxygen consumption cannot be tallied with the rate of leaching as Ni and Fe sulphides are being oxidised at the same time. Nonetheless the maximum uptake rate is indicative of the mass transfer limitation which applies in any heap context, regardless of the reaction chemistry. 

Ammonia losses in the off-gas from the coated concentrate columns were measured by measuring the total NH3 lost from the reactor and recovered in the wash bottles. The total NH3 lost in 4 days ranged from 6 to 16%. NH3 losses were observed to increase marginally as temperature increased and noticeably as NH3 concentration increased. NH3 losses may contribute to a drop in pH due to the release of protons from dissociating ammonium ions. Evaporation of NH3 th

erefore, contributes not only to loss of reagent, but may also shift the system outside the pH window in which the Cu-ammine complexes remain in solution. It must be borne in mind in this context that the columns operated at an aeration rate substantially higher than what is

Also, in taller columns or heaps the passing air is likely to become saturated near the base and then not evaporate any more as it travels to the surface, thus reducing the net loss. Nonetheless, these results do indicate that NH3 evaporation could potentially be problematic in heaps, supporting the notion that they should be operated at as low a temperature as possible. 

###### **CONCLUSİONS** 

This study has shown that ammoniacal Cu extraction from an ore which contains the metal as chalcopyrite in very low concentrations is feasible in principle and appears to perform signficantly better than a comparable thermophile bioleach, reaching Cu extraction in excess of 90% at a more or less constant rate. While temperature enhances the rate of leaching, reasonable rates are still possible at ambient temperature for a heap reactor environment. A low temperature environment is favourable to contain evaporative losses of ammonia, and while a slight elevation in temperature would accelerate the rate of Cu leaching, oxygen gas-liquid mass transfer limitations are unlikely to enhance this effect by much. This limitation will represent the ‘speed limit’ to heap leaching in any context where oxygen is the terminal oxidant. 

Thus, while ammoniacal leach processes for Cu concentrates have remained a niche application, in the context of heaps they may very well represent a feasible option. This would thus be a motivation to renew efforts to tackle challenges relating to downstream processing of a Cu-ammine PLS, such as the extraction and recovery of metal values and removal of sulphates to regenerate the NH3 liquor.

###### **OPERATIONAL RESULTS** 

In actual operation, we are able to maintain the copper leaching rate between 90 and 95%, which is equivalent to the experiments. By employing the ferric leaching process, copper content in lead sulfate is decreased from 6.0-8.5% to 0.7-0.9%. As a result, the following effects are achieved. 

- 1) It become possible to recover copper (5 t/month), lead (14-15 t/month) and tin (3-4 t/month) from the Cu-scum that has been stagnating in HMC. 

- 2) The amount of Cu-scum is decreased, and the workload of skimming scum, etc. are reduced. 

- 3) In the Harris furnace, there has been less failure caused by contact between solid Cu-scum and the agitator during melting of crude metal from the electric furnace. 

###### **CONCLUSION** 

Ferric leaching process was employed to recover copper from lead sulfate, which is generated in the sulfuric acid leaching process of converter dust in the copper smelter. Consequently, copper content in lead sulfate was decreased from 6.0-8.5% to 0.7-0.9%. As a result, the amount of generated Cu-scum was decreased, recovery rates of lead and tin were improved, and the operation became more stable. Next, by employing the sulfurization process to recover the copper leached-out in the ferric leaching process, it became possible to recover copper as CuS with copper content in the 36-44% range and return it to the copper smelter as raw material.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Copper production through traditional technologies requires some pyrometallurgical steps and a heavy recycling loop of materials. The SO2 scrubbing and its conversion to H2SO4 is complex and requires feeding a dilute gas stream. 

Some extensive tests and a pilot campaign for the direct conversion of copper matte/white metal to cathode were run through the ECUPREX® process, a hydrometallurgical process based on a fluoborate electrolyte. 

The experience made in recent years using the same electrolyte in a successful demonstration plant campaign for the production of lead from concentrate allowed us to test equipment, to solve technical problems and to design the industrial cell which can also be applied to copper. 

In this paper we will show the results achieved during this test campaign.

92 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Conventional pyrometallurgical smelting and refining continues to be the main method for production of refined copper from primary sulphides despite the potential drawbacks and limitations in to implementation. The development of new smelters is characterized by high investment cost and high environmental and work place concerns. 

Economies of scale typically mean that small scale smelting plants are not a viable way to produce copper when traditional pyro-technology is applied. Conversely, moving to larger scale plants requires a suitable amount of concentrate which introduces some critical economic and organizational considerations: 

- <u>Transportation: only a few mines in the world are large enough to support a single</u> large smelter. Large scale toll smelters typically require the output of several different mines that can be far away from the smelter and sometimes with poor connection routes. Transportation costs are very expensive and can represent a significant the cost for the concentrate and its processing. 

- <u>Environment: analyzing the cost we can say that the main business of a smelter is</u> not the copper smelting but the control of emissions. This problem is always more and more important because the smelters are often close to population centres. In some instances, although the smelter was originally built away from a town, over time the spread of population closed these distances. 

- <u>Process: receiving concentrates with different compositions, the process has to be</u> highly flexible. Any incremental addition of equipment to handle this problem is an increase of costs and process complexity. Most of the time impurities also lead to high TC/RC’s. 

A lot of research efforts have been spent in the last year trying to find an hydrometallurgical r

oute for treating copper sulphide concentrates, but none of them gave results good enough to design an industrial plant. However promising, most of these processes are far from being competitive with the conventional pyrometallurgical processes based copper smelting and refining. 

One possible alternative could be considering the intermediate white metal, copper matte or blister as a final product (1) or as an intermediate to be electrochemically refined (2). The mini smelters joined with an electrochemical refining unit could be a powerful answer to the above mentioned problems. 

The direct electrorefining of matte was studied as a possible alternative to the copper converting step. This concept was developed around the end of 19<sup>th</sup> century and, despite the theoretical advantage of this application, no industrial scale plants were designed and built, even though an analogous process on nickel matte was operated successfully for many years. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

93 

The direct electrorefining of copper matte is a story of failures (2). Two pilot plants were operated in Germany at Stolberg in 1885 and at Eislenben on 1906 but they were shut down without being scaled-up to industrial size. Some other studies were performed with chalcopyrite anodes but the results were the same. 

Nevertheless, this concept is particularly attractive because the separation of the converting from the smelting process can induce some interesting potential advantages such as: 

- the smelter can work in “smelting only” mode, i.e. de-coupling of the main unit operations 

- coordination and complexity of product transfers can be reduced, decreasing or eliminating idle time and delays 

- revert recycling inefficiencies can be eliminated too 

- smelting cost can be improved 

   - the furnace can be operated at almost the full capacity because the recycle streams, which are heavy and part of the conventional processing route, are minimized 

   - the smelting furnace is the only source of SO2 improving the H2SO4 unit production performances 

- the labour requirement is greatly decreased. 

In addition, when the produced matte is high grade, i.e. a “white metal” (Cu 70 – 78 %), it means that not only is converting avoided, but we have some other interesting improvements: 

- no anode furnace is required 

- no anode casting is required 

- no recycling of anodes is required 

One of the important advantages, as already anticipated, is that SO2 production is concentrated in one step, the smelting furnace, with a more constant and higher SO2 concentration in the gas phase fed to the sulphuric acid plant, making acid production easier and more efficient.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Electro-assisted reduction is an effective pretreatment to render chalcopyrite less refractory towards oxidative leaching. In this p

rocess, chalcopyrite is selectively converted to chalcocite or copper metal in an electrolytic cell under ambient conditions, while ferrous ion is leached into solution. It has the additional advantage of being selective for copper and some silver phases, and therefore, can be used on complex sulfide concentrates. However, the reaction velocity is still subject to passivation, especially at elevated solid to liquid ratios. In the present work, the influence of solution composition, temperature, cathode/particle contact and electrode materials were tested and are discussed, in reference to the proposed reaction mechanism. Electro-assisted reduction and, subsequent oxidative leaching tests for copper show that, once the solution formulation was optimized, the cathode/particle contact time and electrode materials were found to be the most significant variables, while the temperature was deemed unimportant. Although this last finding is counterintuitive, it is consistent with the dominant mechanism. 

Keywords: Chalcopyrite, Leaching, Electro-assisted Reduction

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Direct chalcopyrite oxidation has shown to be difficult due to passivation, the nature of which is still under discussion. Reductive pretreatments, that transform the chalcopyrite to less refractory phases, have been less studied because it usually implies the use of a large excess of reducing agent [1]. A number of years ago, Biegler and Constable reported the electrolytic reduction of chalcopyrite in acidic slurries or in a packed bed through contact with a copper, lead, mercury or graphite cathode in an electrolytic cell [2-4]. Recently, Lapidus and Doyle [5] and Fuentes-Aceituno et al. [6] reexamined this method, employing an electro-assisted reduction at ambient temperature. These authors suggest that the active reducing agent is monatomic hydrogen, H  , formed on the cathode surface, as an intermediate species in the hydrogen evolution reaction. The chalcopyrite is transformed when it contacts the cathode, according to the following reactions: 





Where, H  (surf) represents the monatomic hydrogen produced on the cathode. The reduction of chalcopyrite to chalcocite, Equation (1), was identified as being the rate limiting step. Both of these processes occur within the mineral particle. This implies that, while the ferrous ion associated with the chalcopyrite leaves the particle, the copper phases (Cu2S and Cu<sup>0</sup> ) remain and are carried as a solid into a subsequent oxidation stage, allowing an effective separation. The H2S is converted to sulfur at the anode, supplying the necessary electrons and H<sup>+</sup> ions for the reduction. 



Studies on several concentrates show that other sulfide phases, such as sphalerite and pyrite, are basically untouched by the pretreatment. Precious metals remain in the solid and may be recovered in a subsequent process. 

High conversions and acceptable current

However, with more solids, the presence of elevated quantities of both H2S and ferrous ion enhances the formation of ferrous sulfide (FeS) or pyrrhotite, which passivates the reaction surface. To lessen the problem, di- or triethanolamine (DEA or TEA) was added to capture the H2S produced, facilitating its transport and oxidation at the anode [7]. These additives accelerate the reaction, resulting in the production of more metallic copper in less time. However, the detrimental effects of H2S on the reaction kinetics as well as on the operation of process persisted. Further research on the anode material found that a lead-silver alloy, commonly used in zinc refining, promoted sulfide oxidation to sulfur, decreasing its accumulation in the bulk solution and lessening the passivating effect [8]. _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 105 In the present work, a mechanism is proposed for the electro-assisted reduction of chalcopyrite, which is consistent with the above results. The mechanism of passivation at high solid to liquid ratios was explained and solutions to minimize it were suggested. A sequential experimental technique, electro-assisted reduction followed by oxidation, was used to clarify the phases formed in the first stage. The transformation of chalcopyrite to chalcocite was identified as the rate limiting step, after which metallic copper was formed. The sulfide sequestering agent, triethanolamine (TEA), was effective in catalyzing this second reaction to form metallic copper within the mineral particle. Temperature elevation was found to decrease the formation of metallic copper since the amount of available monatomic hydrogen was diminished. On the other hand, the competition between the reduction of chalcopyrite and the generation of hydrogen gas favored the former when the recombination reaction was slowed by a lower current density. The results obtained in this rese

arch contribute to the economic viability of this alternative process which is especially interesting for mixed sulfide concentrates.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

The methods of hydrometallurgical extraction enable nowadays about 20% of the total primary copper production, which equals about 2.5 mil

###### **INTRODUCTION AND PROBLEM STATEMENT** 

Nowadays approximately 2.5 million tonnes of metallic copper per year is produced by hydrometallurgical extraction methods. It makes up about 20% of total primary copper. The essential hydrometallurgical technique currently used in mining is heap leaching [1, p 301]. 

It is known that copper extraction rate increases and the process efficiency improves with decreasing ore piece. However, crushing below 1 cm does not further improve copper extraction while crushing below 0.5 cm, on the contrary, leads to the decrease of heap permeability and therefore reduction of the process efficiency. [1, p. 299]. The major reason for the poor permeability caused by the presence of fine particles is that they clog the natural flow channels and form impermeable layers (lenses) within the heap that limit the percolation of leaching solution. Consequently, this leads to poor solution distribution and low metal recovery [2]. 

At present, agglomeration of the crushed minerals is used as a pre-treatment option for heap leaching operations. It is required for ores that contain excessive amount of clay or an excessive quantity of fines generated during mining and crushing. A mineral feed crushed to a nominal size below 19 mm is agglomerated with strong sulphuric acid and placed on the leach heap. Although agglomeration is considered as possible insurance for good recovery in heap leach technology an improper agglomeration could be one of the major causes for reduced recovery and higher costs associated with heap leach operations [3]. 

Another way to minimise the impact of the fines on the heap leaching efficiency is to separate them from the course fraction and treat them separately. It was proposed [4] to leach the fines with a particle size below 0.21 millimetres with a ferric sulphate lixiviant at atmospheric pressure and a temperature of between 50 and 80 C. The major drawback of this technique is that it cannot be used for sorption of metals from pulps and requires a system for the liquid/solid separation, which in turn leads to loss of some copper w

ith solids, and therefore, results in a relatively low recovery rate. An alternative method [5] based on ion exchange technology has been developed by InnovEco Australia. The laboratory tests and mini pilot plant trials have demonstrated that the copper extraction rate from fine solids may exceed 95%. The proposed method could be a cost effective way to process fines, low grade ores, tailings and cut-offs. This paper presents results of testing the proposed technique in several applications that might solve existing problems in copper heap leaching. _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 115 ###### **LABORATORY TEST RESULTS** The laboratory tests are conducted to study the chemistry of the leaching and sorption processes and obtain preliminary information about the ore characteristics, resin selectivity and process parameters. The separated fractions were weighed and their percentage in the total weight was calculated. The results are provided in Table 1. It was found that approximately a half of the provided sample is a fine fraction which passes through the 425 micron screen. The laboratory tests and mini pilot plant trials were conducted with different copper ore materials that varied in copper content and particle size. The tests demonstrated the possibility to use the ion exchange technology for effective copper recovery from fine fractions of the copper ore. The copper extraction rate from solids was achieved at the level of 94-98%. The copper extraction from liquid exceeds 97%/ The product of this process was generated in the form of a concentrated copper sulphate solution.  The copper content in the product could exceed 40 g/l with the impurities level below 1 g/l. The product can be used in electro winning process to produce cathode copper. As an alternative, dry copper sulphate could be produced. 

The proposed process could be a cost effective way to process fines, low grade ores, tailings and cut-offs. It could solve some existing problems in copper mining, in particular, it enables the processing of fine fractions of ore. The process is easily scalable and can be adapted for various copper plant productivity.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Mining companies with hydrometallurgical processes have the intrinsic need to bleed a percentage of their rich electrolyte to keep the concentration of impurities at a certain level (such as chloride and ferric / ferrous ions). As this stream has a high concentration of copper, acid, and pollutants, the destination used for this solution is commonly the raffinate pond. It is well known by Fick’s Law that this procedure impacts negatively on the leaching recovery as copper contribution to the raffinate increases the cationic load and therefore decreases the diffusional flux. In recent research, copper from electrowinning bleed was recovered using emew® technology before sending it to the raffinate. Two leaching

columns – with raffinate fed with both emew®-treated and untreated bleed – were set to determine whether this copper depletion has an appreciable impact on the leaching recovery. The results showed a difference of 8.9% of copper recovery in favor of the emew® treated stream. The following publication details the procedure, results, and discussions of this interesting breakthrough.
