###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Ore leaching is not a selective process, and resulting pregnant leach solution (PLS) may often include different species besides the desired metal. In copper recovery, the solvent extraction process (SX) generates a clean and highly concentrated copper stream; however, it is inevitable for some pollutants to be dragged into the electrowinning process (EW). Due to the constant recirculation, some pollutants like Fe<sup>+2</sup> , Fe<sup>+3</sup> and Cl<sup>-</sup> ions, increase their concentration inside the EW tank house causing current efficiency loss or poor deposit quality. To maintain an acceptable level of impurities, a determined volume of rich electrolyte is bled and replaced with process water. This purge or bleed stream is commonly sent to the raffinate pond, which is finally used for heap leaching. As the bleed stream has an important copper content – above 35 grams per liter – the impact of its discharge to raffinate compromises global recovery by an unwanted recirculating copper overload. Moreover, when the heap leaching cycle is over, the remaining moisture within it – typically 5% to 8% – is removed along with the ore, causing tons of copper to be lost every year. 

The emew<sup>®</sup> technology can work under extreme operating conditions producing high-quality copper from highly contaminated solutions. Furthermore, it was not only the most appropriate tool to conduct the following experiment but the only available technology capable of doing so. 

To begin with, a 40 gpl of synthetic copper sulfate solution was depleted with a lab scale emew<sup>®</sup> cell, obtaining a high-quality copper cathode and a 5 gpl of Cu and a +270 gpl of H2SO4 spent solution. Then, two leaching columns were mounted on a wooden rack to study the leaching behavior using different irrigation solutions: 

- Synthetic raffinate mixed with a synthetic bleed solution 

- Synthetic raffinate mixed with an emew<sup>®</sup> -treated synthetic bleed solution

From day 5 to 13, a slight difference in favor of raffinate with untreated purge can be seen and from the fourteenth day on, the curves began to constantly diverge until the end of the experiment reaching an 8.9% in favor of leaching using raffinate mixed with emew® –treated bleed solution. Results show a substantial improvement when the ore is irrigated with a lower concentrated copper solution. One explanation to this phenomenon is the renowned first Fick’s Law. It relates the diffusive flux to the concentration field, the diffusion coefficient and the particle radio. It says that the flux goes from regions of high concentration to regions of low concentration with a magnitude proportional to the concentration gradient. In connection with this experiment, lower copper concentration in the aqueous media will produce a dCAdifference, accelerating the leaching process. Based on this, the divergence seen in the curves is explained due to the difference in concentrations of the irrigation solutions. As shown in Table 4, raffinate mixed with treated purge has a lower copper concentration which results in a larger _dCA_ gradient. Diffusional flux is favored by this phenomenon and therefore the copper recovery from the ore is increased to the aforementioned percentage. It is well known that leaching has two controlling processes. At the beginning the leach rate is very fast due to the presence of copper on the particle surface, where the leaching solution instantly dissolves the copper. As time passes and the amount of copper on the surface decreases, the leaching solution must diffuse into the particle to contact more copper. Since this is a more complex process than the initial chemical reaction, the leaching rate slows down. Chemical reaction in copper leac

hing happens rapidly – almost instantaneously – leaving diffusion as the prime cause of the downfall. This can be better illustrated by analyzing the slopes of each curve in Figure 2, where each of them represents the leach rate. It is also important to mention the free acid generation (via electrowinning). Even though pH difference between solutions is relatively small and at those low values the leaching efficiency does not have substantial variations, it is well known that a higher concentration of acid allows better diffusion into the particle. What is also noteworthy is the money savings due to the constant acidulation through this exercise. Raffinate pond must be constantly fed with free acid in order to keep pH down to a level where leaching _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 128 is efficient, and in this context, emew® allows an important saving by a continuous acid mass discharge equivalent to 1.54 times the mass of plated copper. 100

A. Aracena, I. Dнaz and H. Olivares

###### **ABSTRACT** 

In this work, a preliminary study of the effect of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) in a chalcopyrite mineral containing 15 g of Cu, in a temperature range between 20 and 50ºC; and it suggests possible reaction mechanisms. The experimental work was carried out in an acrylic column equipped with a feed tank, a coil surrounding the column that carries a high temperature solution, thermocouples and container to collect the percolated solution. Samples were taken every once in a while to be analysed for Cu and Fe. In addition, solid residues were collected to be analysed by DRX. The results without H2O2 showed that when leaching with Fe2(SO4)3 + NaCl, a leached copper mass of 0.2 g was obtained in 25 days, while pre-treating the material with NaCl increased the amount of Cu in solution to 0.6 g in a period of 11 days. The results with H2O2 showed that when using the Fe2(SO4)3 + NaCl + H2O2 solution (30% v/v) through pulse leaching, 0.85 g of copper was recovered after 17 days. This was due to the action of the hydrogen peroxide reaction. When the mineral was pre-treated with NaCl, the mineral dissolution velocity was increased, resulting in a recovery of 0.65 g of Cu in 5 days. Finally, when increasing the solution temperature up to 50º C, copper recoveries of 0.9 g were obtained in only 3 days of leaching. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

132 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Currently, chalcopyrite (CuFeS2) is the major copper mineral component. Copper is extracted from chalcopyrite by smelting or hydrometallurgical techniques. Smelting is the method that is most commonly used, however it causes environmental problems due to SO2 emissions to the atmosphere. Therefore, hydrometallurgical techniques can be used to treat low-grade minerals without any environmental problems. 

In the case of chalcopyrite, extensive leaching studies have been carried out using a variety of oxidants such as ferric chlori

de and ferric sulphate, but chalcopyrite is a mineral that has high level of resistance against the attack of these strong oxidants. This happens because the chalcopyrite surface becomes passive due to the formation of sulphides in the form of crystals and irregular globular masses [1]. 

Based on the former, this work’s main aim is to study the variables that influence the increase of the CuFeS2 dissolution such as the use of solid NaCl in a mineral pretreatment, hydrogen peroxide in pulse leaching and an increase in the temperature of the leaching solution. 

###### **EXPERIMENTAL WORK** 

The experimental work was carried out in 20-cm diameter acrylic columns equipped with a feed tank, a coil surrounding the column transporting a high temperature solution, thermocouples and a container that collected the percolated solution. 

The chalcopyrite mineral samples were obtained from Andina Division (CODELCO-Chile) that were comminuted and classified by sieving into size fractions coarse; -12700+6350 μm (-1/2+1/4 inch) and fines; -150 μm. The samples chemical analysis showed that they contained 0.64% total Cu and 0.06% acid soluble Cu. A mineralogical analysis indicated that Cu in the sample was mainly of chalcopyrite. Samples were pre-treated with agglomeration – curing, consisting on the bonding of fine particles to coarse particles in a 90:10 ratio (coarse:fine particles) with technical grade (94% purity) sulphuric acid (H2SO4) and distilled water. The H2SO4 and H2O rate (in %v/v) used were 25:50. Curing times were 3 days. In addition, agglomeration was achieved with solid sodium chloride (NaCl) at a rate of 71.4 kg NaCl/ton of mineral. 

There were two types of leachant solutions: 1 g/L Fe<sup>3+</sup> and 1 g/L Fe<sup>3+</sup> + 0.3 M NaCl. The ferric was originated from Fe2(SO4)3. The solutions had a pH=2 value adjusted with analytic grade (~98% purity) sulphuric acid (H2SO4) drops. Leaching times varied depending on the experiment. In some experiments, a new leaching method called “pulse leaching” was used. It consisted on adding different volumes (mL/day) of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) on the surface of the bed through graduated pipettes. 

Then, the samples obtained (PLS) were collected, filtered and sent to Atomic Absorption Spectroscopy to be analysed for Cu and Fe.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Global practice in copper solvent extraction is reviewed, based on individual plant operating data for 2012. Trends in feed and electrolyte compositions and flow rates, and extractant and diluent selection, together with their impact on copper recovery and reagent utilisation, are reviewed.  Optimisation of copper transfer and copper production by changing circuit configurations with changing feed composition during the life of mine is discussed. Emerging trends in equipment design are assessed. The rapid adoption and expansion of this technology in the African Copper Belt is also addressed, along with the unique challenges pertaining to operating conditions in this region. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

138 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Continuing from similar surveys carried out in 1997, 1999, 2003, and 2007 [1-4], global operating practice in copper solvent extraction (SX) in 2012 is reviewed. Contributing operations include established sites from the USA (10), Chile (11), Peru (1) and Mexico (1), as well as newer operations from Africa (4). Trends in operating conditions and performance, as well as equipment design and process technology choices are analysed. The significant expansion in production in the African Copper Belt is also discussed.  The detailed survey results are provided on the CD-ROM of the proceedings. 

In contrast to past experience, there is an increasing reluctance of many operations to participate in this survey, indicating a more competitive commercial operating environment: a more sophisticated understanding of this technology is evolving, such that optimisation of process conditions may add competitive advantage. Several new operations currently commissioning or ramping up to full production in Africa and Europe declined to participate since their operations are not yet at stable performance. It is also notable that more than 100 copper SX plants exist today in China [5]. Although most of these are smaller than 1,000 t/a Cu and none of the Chinese operations participated in this survey, they represent a growing and important influencer in this industry, particularly through the explosion of Chinese-owned operations outside China, notably in Africa. Most Australian operations have closed in recent years. 

There are currently some 75 operations worldwide with cathode production above 10,000 t/a. The top ten producers account for approximately 45% of the total SX copper production, which is in the order of 4 million t/a. The largest of the plants that participated in the survey is Morenci, AZ (245 kt Cu in 2012), while the smallest is Pinto Valley, AZ (2.77 kt). It is significant that 72% of the operations produced below their nameplate capacities in 2012 (Figure 1). In Chile and southwestern USA, this is largely d

ue to declining ore grades, while in Africa this reflects recently commissioned operations that are still ramping up. A notable performance is that of Tenke Fungurume (Democratic Republic of Congo, DRC), which produced 37% above design capacity. 

###### **TRENDS IN OPERATING CONDITIONS AND PROCESS PERFORMANCE** 

Distinct characteristics emerge when one examines copper SX on a regional basis. 

North America is the most mature region, with mostly low grade, mixed oxide/secondary sulfide ores. The pregnant leach solutions (PLS) are typified by low Cu, low Fe, high Mn, and a wide range of pH values. The circuits are mostly configured in series-parallel to allow for increased PLS throughput. At a number of sites the high PLS flowrates give extraction organic-to-aqueous (O:A) ratios well below 1:1, which results in raffinate stages being operated in aqueous phase continuity. Emphasis on organic recovery is therefore important ( _e.g_ ., increased retention time in the raffinate pond; use of equipment such as Pace Setters, Jameson cells, and pond skimmers).

Figure 1 – Comparison of nameplate production capacity with 2012 production 

In South America the operations process mostly medium-grade ‘oxide’ and secondary sulfide deposits and are primarily located in the Atacama Desert. The circuits are usually configured in series, _i.e_ ., 2E+2S and 2E+1S. Leaching of the predominant mineral in the region, atacamite (Cu2Cl(OH)3), results in elevated levels (1 to 30 g/L) of chloride in the PLS. Wash stages are common to control chloride transfer to the electrolyte. Several operations have experienced nitration issues associated with high levels of nitrates dissolved in the PLS. 

In Central Africa, ore copper grades are significantly higher than in other parts of the world, ranging from 2.5 to 5%. The minerals are predominantly malachite and heterogenite, which are processed by grinding and agitated leaching rather than by heap leaching. Most SX circuits are series with either two or three extraction stages combined with two strip stages. In many of the operations, cobalt is produced as a by-product. 

###### **PLS Composition** 

The nature of the PLS varies considerably (0.23 to 43 g/L Cu), depending largely on geographic location (Table 1). Chilean operations (mainly heap, dump, and run-ofmine leaching) frequently have elevated levels of Fe in the PLS due to secondary sulfides (as well as chloride, nitrate, and elements such as W and Re); the African agitated leach operations contain Co in the PLS and much higher levels of total suspended solids (TSS) which exacerbate crud formation. Average Mn levels are similar across the globe, but the ratio of Fe:Mn is usually lowest in African plants and highest in North American plants.

High overall recoveries from high PLS tenors are also often facilitated by use of a split circuit or processing through a second SX circuit. Complete stripping of the loaded organic phase is never achieved because of the chelating nature of copper extractants. The acidity of the spent electrolyte is the main parameter influencing the extent of stripping that is possible (Figure 3), however stripping also depends on the specific extractant chemistry (ketoxime and/or modified _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 142 aldoxime), circuit staging, and other operating conditions. Operating at higher spent electrolyte acidity permits a lower Cu concentration on the stripped organic phase and increases the electrolyte conductivity (lowers the electrowinning energy requirements), however, strong sulfuric acid also hydrolytically degrades the extractant and can result in increased extractant consumption. The highest spent electrolyte acidity recorded in this survey is 202 g/L H2SO4 at Quebrada Blanca (Chile). A compromise of operating conditions to minimise operating costs, while maintaining product quality, is always necessary. ###### **Organic Losses and Reagent Consumptions** 

Organic losses to the raffinate vary between 7 and 125 mg/L, while those to the advance electrolyte are given as 1 to 250 mg/L. It would, however, generally be expected that entrainment losses to the electrolyte would be lower than those to the raffinate because of the higher acidity of the electrolyte and greater density difference compared to the organic phase. Extractant consumptions (Table 3) vary widely across the plants surveyed, from 1.7 to 8.7 kg/t cathode Cu, with a strong dependence on extractant concentration and solids’ content of the PLS. A high TSS content in the PLS generally correlates with high organic losses to the raffinate, although there are notable exceptions to this (Figure 4). Figure 5 indicates little apparent relationship between organic entrainment losses to the raffinate and advance electrolyte and overall extractant consumption: this is likely due to difference in efficiencies of organic reclamation from ponds and crud. This unexpected observation also highlights probable errors in reporting of entrainment figures: accurate direct measurements of entrainment losses are difficult to achieve due to the inherent inaccuracies of sampling a highly variable and nonhomogeneous fluid, and analysis methods remain less than ideal [8,9]. The most reliable indication of control of organic losses is generally the extractant consumption, as measured by the volume of extractant added to the organic phase over a given period. High extractant consumptions can also be due to other factors, such as high rates of degradation (such as by nitration at Lomas Bayas, Chile [10]) or high temperatures. 

Diluent loss occurs primarily through evaporation, with secondary sources of loss by organic entrainment and crud. Diluent consumption therefore varies widely (Table 4), depending on ambient temperature and relative humidity, and on whether the settlers are open, have covers, or have building roofs.  The low consumptions measured on the African plants are influenced by the much lower proportion of diluent in the organic phase due to the high extractant concentrations employed (Table 3).

###### **TRENDS IN EQUIPMENT DESIGN** 

###### **Staging** 

Most older plants in North and South America have two extraction stages and a single strip stage. With declining PLS grade, many of these circuits have converted their original series configuration to include several stages in which a parallel PLS stream is introduced, thereby allowing copper production to be maintained from an increased total PLS flow. In the recently commissioned African plants, the higher tenors of the agitation leach cir

cuits (>30 g/L Cu) require a greater number of stages to maintain extraction efficiency. The viscosities of modern extractants permit a maximum extractant concentration of ~35 vol.% to be employed, so high net copper transfer is maintained by use of higher O:A flowrate ratios and increasing the number of stages. Kamoto Copper (DRC), for example, commissioned in late 2012, has three trains of three extraction and two strip stages, which is typical for new plant designs in this part of the world. 

In Chile, where the PLS typically contains high chloride (and sometimes nitrate) from leaching of minerals from the Atacama Desert, one wash stage is usual. Wash stages are not commonly found in the African or North American circuit designs, although Sierrita and several of the Morenci plants do include a wash stage for limiting iron transfer to the electrolyte by aqueous-in-organic entrainment. 

###### **Mixers and Settlers** 

With respect to mixer design, the newer plants use cylindrical mixing boxes with a primary and secondary mixer in each stage. Mixer residence times of 3 min are 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

145 

typically employed. There is a wide range in the style of impellers used: those surveyed range from 9 to 83 m<sup>3</sup> in volume and from 7.5 to 134 kW in power. Outotec’s Spirok and DOP mixer designs have received some application in copper, including at Kokkola (Finland), Casserones, Radomiro Tomić, Zaldivar, Franke (Chile), Milpillas (Mexico), Sepon (Laos), Cobre Las Cruces (Spain), and Chambishi (Zambia). Tenova Bateman Technologies recently presented a new impeller design, claimed to improve mass transfer and reduce entrainment losses [11]. Both extraction and strip circuits almost universally run organic-continuous, although older plants, pushing for production targets at high PLS flowrates and low tenors, increasingly run aqueous continuity in their extraction stages and accept the higher organic losses that this will inevitably introduce. 

Modern settlers are designed with settling duties of 3 to 5 m<sup>3</sup> /m<sup>2</sup> /h.  There is considerable variation in the design of settlers from dimensions to the number of picket fences and additional settler furniture. Most settlers are 1 m deep, while length ranges from 12 to 34.5 m, and width ranges from 3.7 to 30 m. Organic depth averages 0.27 m in both extraction and strip stages, with a range of 0.1 to 0.5 m. New plants are increasingly employing stainless steel as the material of construction––although considerably more expensive than the alternatives, it offers valuable resistance to fire initiation and propagation. Increasing use of reverse flow settlers is evident, such as recently installed at Milpillas and Kamoto Copper. Coalescence in settlers is usually facilitated by the installation of one to three picket fences. Some plants use hydrophobic coalescing packs. Quebrada Blanca has modified their settler internals using PIP technology, developed

by Igor Polski, in the feed distribution, the picket fences, and in the settler overflow. These modifications allow a reduction of 70% in aqueous entrainment [12]. 

###### **Ancillary Equipment** 

Crud is usually removed by pumps and treated by centrifuge to recover the organic component. Most operations treat the recovered organic with clays, zeolites, or diatomaceous earths before returning it to the SX circuit. Organic recovery from aqueous streams is facilitated by the use of aftersettlers, flotation columns, carbon columns, and directly from the surfaces of aqueous tanks and ponds. The use of coalescence packs in loaded organic tanks assists with removal of entrained PLS ahead of the strip circuit. 

###### **Modern Plant Design Trends** 

Where capital constraints permit, new or refurbished SX circuits are more frequently designed upfront for multiple pipe configurations, thereby allowing processing flexibility and for combinations of series and parallel staging to be readily implemented over the lifetime of plant, as the nature of the ore body, PLS, or economic conditions change. Where footprint and topography permit, processing of the PLS through three or four parallel trains, spaced some distance apart from each other, is the preferred approach to minimising the risk of fire spreading through all parts of a circuit as well as mitigating the business interruption loss that occurs following a fire event [13]. This approach is well exemplified by the Spence (Chile) design and layout. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

146 

Optimisation of new and existing mixers and settlers is increasingly facilitated by computer-aided modelling and computational fluid dynamic simulations. This is seldom carried out for specific plant designs because of cost, but engineering companies and research consortia are sponsoring interesting work in this area, the results of which should manifest in the designs of the future [8,14,15]. Contacting equipment other than mixer settlers is unlikely ever to be used in the copper industry, mainly due to the small number of stages that are required for extraction and stripping and the relatively slow extraction kinetics of oxime extractants. 

Fire-fighting systems are receiving increasing attention in recent designs [16]. One of the more significant developments is high pressure water fog systems (installed at Sepon and Cobre Las Cruces). Traditionally, fluoroprotein (FP) and aqueous filmforming foam (AFFF) systems have typically been employed, but these are difficult to test once installed since they affect the phase disengagement properties of the organic phase (FP more than AFFF) and it can take some time for the situation to restore itself. Water fog does not have this problem. Although the capital cost for water fog is greater than that of foam systems, the life-cycle cost is estimated to be cheaper. However, a new patented, proprietary formulation foaming agent, recently tested, apparently washed

out of the organic phase within two plant cycles and showed excellent characteristics. This is combined with a unique foam make up and delivery system that is reported to reduce the installed cost to 25% of a conventional foam system. It is currently being designed for three large African plants. ###### **COMMISSIONING OPERATIONS AND PROJECTS** In Europe, two interesting flowsheets are under commissioning and ramp-up. Cobre Las Cruces (Spain) (72 kt Cu/a commissioned in 2008), treats a copper concentrate by agitated ferric leaching at 90o C, which produces an SX feed containing ~10 g/L Cu and 50 g/L Fe. This high iron content in the PLS gives rise to some challenges in achieving selectivity of copper transfer to the advance electrolyte [17]. Assarel Medet (Bulgaria) is a 2,000 t/a Cu plant designed by Outotec, which is ramping up from commissioning in 2009. This operation faces challenges of -20o C temperatures and ambient wind speeds of 25 m/s. This plant is the first to combine both straight- and reverse-flow mixer settlers, and has very compact settlers with stage efficiencies of 95% and settling rates double the industry standard at 8.8 to 9.7 m3 /m2 /h [18]. Most large, new copper projects under design, construction, or commissioning today are in the African Copper Belt (Table 5). The combined cathode capacity coming on line is likely to ensure that this region overtakes Chile as the primary producer of SX copper within the next decade. Most operations are agitated atmospheric or pressure leaching operations, which produce PLS tenors above 30 g/L Cu and contain relatively high TSS, although heap leaching accounts for a small proportion of the intended production. Traditional operations in the southwestern USA and Chile typically treat low tenor solutions from heap leaching, which have low solids’ content and operate essentially trouble-free. In contrast, operations in Africa treat very high tenor liquors from agitation and pressure leaching, with high solids’ contents, and in far more difficult operating environments. ###### **ABSTRACT** 

Outotec  has  decades of experience in  developing  a  wide  range  of  solvent extraction  technologies and  now introduces the new VSF<sup>®</sup> X Plant. The standardized and modularized Outotec VSF<sup>®</sup> X Plant provides a novel way to design, manufacture, transport, install, operate and maintain a solvent extraction plant more efficiently than in the past with highly sustainable and safe methods. Modularization is based on the use of prefabricated transportable ISO freight container sized settler modules, which can be easily assembled on-site. VSF<sup>®</sup> X mixer-settlers enables considerably shorter lead times for projects, easy capacity expansion possibilities and decreased downtime for settler maintenance. This paper presents a comparison of capital expenditures and project lead time between a conventional and a modular type VSF<sup>®</sup> X solvent extraction settler and also evaluates the trends and demands for the future.

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Mining is a very capital intensive field of industry and recently capital expenditures (CAPEX) for new projects have climbed even higher. CAPEX are escalating mainly because of declining ore grades which makes extraction processes more complicated and creates a need for even larger plants. Plant lifecycles tend to be shorter

and plants have to be located in remote locations. Outotec has responded to this challenge by developing various cutting edge equipment and solutions which aims towards lowering capital expenditures of new mining projects and meet other challenges industry faces. One new solution is the modular VSF<sup>®</sup> X Plant, which is designed to offer lower risks and costs for Greenfield and Brownfield mining projects using Outotec’s proven VSF solvent extraction (SX) technology. 

In solvent extraction process, the incoming in pregnant leach solution (PLS) is concentrated and purified and metal-ions are transferred into an electrolyte solution. A pure electrolyte is then used in electrowinning (EW) to produce chemically and physically high-quality products. Solvent extraction is a suitable hydrometallurgical process for producing various non-ferrous metals and minerals, such as copper, nickel, cobalt, zinc and uranium. Outotec is a well-known technology provider in the field of solvent extraction possessing a proven track record. Various plants worldwide operate using Outotec’s VSF<sup>®</sup> SX-technology, which offers a cost effective, reliable and sustainable solvent extraction process solution. 

Despite the recent development and innovations, for the last 30 years the technical solutions in building solvent extraction plants have stayed more or less unchangeable. Outotec’s new VSF<sup>®</sup> X Plant has a positive impact on engineering, manufacturing, construction as well as installation, operation and maintenance of an SXplant by offering high level of modularity and scalability. 

The aim of this paper is to compare the CAPEX of conventional and modular solvent extraction plants. The results are obtained by comparing Outotec’s in-house budgetary capital cost estimates for two types of solutions. Additionally, project lead time of two technologies are evaluated and compared.

###### **BACKGROUND** 

This section presents the main technical features of conventional and modular types of SX-technologies. 

###### **Conventional Mixer-Settlers** 

A typical solvent extraction process is conducted in mixer-settlers. In a SX plant, normally 2-3 mixers are used to mix organic and aqueous phases in order to create a dispersion which enables the extraction and stripping reactions. The two phases of dispersion are separated by gravity in the following settler. One plant can include various mixer-settler stages depending on the used process design. [1] 

Settlers are typically square pools, which vary in length and can be built from various materials. A concrete settler with steel structures and fiber reinforced plastic (FRP) lining is widely used technical solution and it presents a conventional settler solution for this paper. The size of the settler may vary widely depending on the chosen process parameters. [1] The ratio of the settler’s length and width is called the aspect ratio and it is depen

dent on the flow rate of the settler. For example in copper solvent extraction processes, the flow rate is relatively high and the aspect ratio (L/W) sets below 1:1, in other words in many cases copper SX-settlers tend to resemble a square. [2] 

Conventional settlers have been built with various different methods. The most common arrangement is a settler built on ground. The on-ground-structure has lower investment costs but it can cause soil contamination, which requires special groundwork after plant shutdown. The other option is an elevated settler, either on fill, or on steel and/or a concrete structure. Elevated settlers have various advantages, for example, leakage detection and maintenance is easier and there is no need for deep trenches. Disadvantages of elevated settlers include a high cost of support structures. [3] In this study, the conventional settler is assumed to be an on-ground-settler. 

The construction of a conventional on-ground-settler requires large excavation works in order to place mixers and settlers at right elevation. Even though the FRP lining and roof elements and other FRP components are usually pre-fabricated on some level, a large amount of installation work is still required on-site. Typical construction phases are (in order of execution) excavation, foundation, erection of steel structures, concrete work, lamination of FRP linings and components (e.g. launders, flanges etc.) and the installation of settler roof modules. Due to a large amount of lamination work, the construction phase is vulnerable to external factors such as weather since lamination requires very specific temperature and humidity limits.

###### <u>Procurement & Manufacturing</u> 

The materials used in settler modules are mainly carbon steel and FRP which are procured through a predefined and audited supply chain. Manufacturing is performed by a reliable supplier in a factory environment using standardized working methods, which enable high quality and a precise on-time delivery. Manufacturing can be started promptly after receiving a purchase order. The finished modules can be transported to the project site easily,

where they can be stored until the installation starts. 

###### <u>Installation</u> 

The installation of the VSF<sup>®</sup> X settler starts from building the concrete foundation slab and pillars, on which the settler modules are installed. Due to the elevated construction, the need for large excavation works is reduced. Installation of the modules is designed to be simple and quick requiring fewer site personnel. The remaining on-site lamination work is minimized since all lamination joints are predefined and the lamination work procedures are standardized. Additionally, work ergonomics and safety are significantly improved due to the standardized working procedures and the reduced number of installation personnel allowing easier collaboration and supervision on-site.

###### <u>Operation & Maintenance</u> 

The maintenance of the VSF<sup>®</sup> X settler can be performed without shutting down the process by by-passing a one whole settler or a settler module. Special attention has been drawn to settler crud removal. The elevated structure makes leak detection possible before any serious problems occur, therefore enabling preventative maintenance. The settler structure is completely enclosed so it emits less volatile organic compounds and other emissions in the atmosphere. Additionally, the enclosed design offers higher operator safety. 

###### <u>Disposal</u> 

The settler modules have residual value since the settlers can be dismantled and moved to another location, offering a sustainable solution since modules can be re-used after plant shutdown. The majority of the materials used are recyclable, which further simplify the end-of-life procedures. 

###### **METHODOLOGY** 

This section introduces the methods used to evaluate the CAPEX of two types of settler technologies. In general CAPEX refers to the total installed costs of a certain construction project. A major part of CAPEX usually consists of direct costs, indirect costs and project contingency. When estimating CAPEX, it is important to identify the project development stage and project scope, which directly affects the accuracy of the estimation. 

A typical mixer-settler plant size with a processing capacity of 2450 m<sup>3</sup> dispersion flow per hour was chosen for this study. The example project would be an EPC (engineering, procurement and construction) delivery of this kind of settler including engineering, procurement, construction and installation of the settler. The project would take place in an environment where weather and high humidity would create challenges for lamination work, but overall, the environment does not pose great risks for project implementation. Project development stage is a feasibility study or basic engineering, which means that CAPEX -estimate is budgetary. 

The Data for the CAPEX of a conventional settler was obtained through a capital cost estimate made in a recent basic engineering projec

t in 2011. The data was updated to follow the current industry trends and costs. The general accuracy of CAPEX meets ±15% of final project costs before contingency.

Respectively, the data for VSF<sup>®</sup> X settler was achieved from an extended basic engineering project. The level of accuracy is believed to be of sufficient since most of the components are manufactured in a factory environment and their costs were based on quotations made by Outotec’s suppliers. Other necessary estimates were made by Outotec personnel according to industry standards. The level of accuracy meets ±15% of final project costs. 

###### <u>Direct Costs</u> 

For investment projects, direct costs form the major portion of CAPEX. The following direct costs were included in the cost calculations of the conventional settler: engineering, excavation, foundations, concrete work with materials, prefabricated FRP modules (manufacturing and material), steel structures and installation work. The manufacturing of FRP modules and structures for the conventional settler is performed in low-cost-countries. 

Respectively, the following necessary costs were taken into account in cost calculations of modular settlers: engineering, manufacturing of prefabricated settler modules including materials, excavation, foundations, concrete work including material and installation. The manufacturing of the settler modules is performed in Western countries. 

###### <u>Indirect Costs</u> 

In general, indirect costs include items such as supportive labor, other work, material or costs which are not directly related to project e.g. transportation, construction equipment, utilities, insurances etc. The following indirect costs were included in both cost estimations: crane rental for site work, inventory carrying cost for site storage and settler installation material. 

Transportation, travelling, food supply, accommodation, office, admin, clothing costs, general overhead costs and other indirect costs were left outside the scope of this study since they do not vary significantly between different technologies. However, the transportation costs of the VSF<sup>®</sup> X settler modules would be relatively low since they are designed to be fully transportable by the ISO -container standard. Automation, instrumentation and piping were also left outside the scope of the study since they would create similar costs in both situations. 

Since construction projects tend to last several months, the site inventory binds a noteworthy amount of capital. In this study, the bound capital was taken into account by calculating general inventory carrying cost of the settler equipment for settler installation time. Inventory carrying cost is used to take into account capital costs, inventory service costs, storage space costs and inventory risk costs. The VSF<sup>®</sup> X settler modules consist of transportable and storable ISO standard containers so the

y were assumed to have better storability compared to conventional FRP settler elements which are relatively fragile.

Consequently, 25% inventory carrying cost was used for VSF<sup>®</sup> X and 30% for conventional settlers. 

###### <u>Project Contingency</u> 

Project contingency includes allowances used to cover unforeseen or unknown events which may occur during the project design and implementation. In this study project contingency was evaluated by a traditional percentage method. Different contingency percentages were used for two types of technologies. As it has been discussed in this paper, the new VSF<sup>®</sup> X settler technology carries significantly lower construction risks due to high level of prefabrication and the contingency percentage was chosen to be as low as 5%. Conventional settler technology has proven to have relative low design risks but a high amount of site lamination incurs noteworthy construction risks. Consequently, total contingency percentage for conventional technology was chosen to be 7%. 

###### <u>Work Breakdown Structure (WBS)</u> 

For CAPEX and project schedule evaluation, the project was broken down into four separate work packages: engineering, equipment manufacturing, construction and installation. Each of these individual packages consisted of different sub-phases so that a sufficient level of detail in cost estimation could be achieved. The engineering package included basic engineering, equipment engineering and plant design sub-phases. The equipment package consisted of settler elements manufacturing and procurement of necessary raw materials. 

The construction phase included concrete and foundation works. Conventional design incurs more construction work since the settler structure is mainly built from concrete. The modular VSF<sup>®</sup> X settler is installed on concrete pillars to obtain elevated structure, so the construction phase mainly consists of building up pillars. The installation phase contains all equipment installations.

Costs are not just decreased but the whole cost structure of the project is changed since more components are prefabricated. This decreases the need for site installation, which poses greatest risks and typically it creates the highest costs and possible cost overruns for projects. Factory manufacturing allows a high level of cost control due to a stable working environment and it assures high quality of modules so that the need for repairs is lower. Major savings in project lead time can be achieved through the use of modular settler design. Time saving begins at the initial engineering phase. The use of predefined and scalable modules allows the fast design of the settlers without shortcuts in process design. The manufacturing of the settler modules can be started instantly when the basic engineering is done, no complicated procurement or competitive tendering is needed since the suppliers and the whole supply chain are known and possess a proven trackrecord. In most cases the settler modules stay unchangeable from project to project, which allows continuous improvement of known manufacturing processes. The construction work of the new VSF® X settler is simpler and less time is consumed prior to equipment installation. Of course earthworks for each different project are relatively unique, but elevated settler construction and standard pillar structure is suitable for most projects. VSF® X settler uses less on-site construction material which enables achieving cost and time savings and offers a more eco-friendly solution. The main cost and time savings of the new modular settler solution comes from installation work. It was estimated in this study that installation man-hours will decrease by 77%. Project risks, including safety, schedule and cost risks, will be decreased significantly due to less complicated site work. Installation of settler modules requires less labor which will have further positive impact on the indirect project costs such as travel, accommodation and food expenses. It should be noted that this study was based on the availa

ble data from a previous successful basic engineering project of conventional settler design and from pilot project of the new modular settler. This data might contain certain shortcomings but still it is based on reliable estimates conducted by industry experts. In order to achieve even more reliable results, data should be measured from implementation projects. Despite these facts this study proves the high potential of the modular solvent extraction plants in implementing fast track projects in a sustainable manner.

###### **CONCLUSION** 

Outotec has designed a novel way to manufacture, install and operate a solvent extraction plant, which is based on fully modular and scalable mixer-settler design. The objective of this paper was to compare the CAPEX of two alternative solvent extraction settler solutions, the conventional settler and the new Outotec VSF<sup>®</sup> X modular settler. This study was conducted evaluating the existing data from previous basic design project and estimating costs of the new settler design by analyzing existing manufacturing data achieved from a pilot/proto project. The accuracy of these estimates was ±15% of final project price, which can be seen to meet sufficient confidence level for this comparison. 

The study shows that through modular design 24% savings in project CAPEX can be achieved. Cost structure of a solvent extraction plant can also be radically changed by shifting emphasis more to prefabrication lowering the portion of uncertain site work. Additionally, a reduction of 25% in project lead time could be possible using modular design. All major steps of the project including engineering, procurement, manufacturing, construction and installation can be shortened by using the predefined modular and scalable VSF<sup>®</sup> X mixer-settler plant. 

As a conclusion it can be stated that the Outotec VSF<sup>®</sup> X mixer-settler plant offers more sustainable solution for solvent extraction processing that brings major cost savings in project implementation through the use of highly productized modules. Additionally the possibility to dismantle and reuse the equipment after the productive life of the project adds an important level of sustainability.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Efficient solvent extraction (SX) performance is crucial to cost effective separation of metals in an increasingly broad range of mineral processing operations.  The challenges involved in improving solvent extraction equipment and operations include development of the principles behind sustaining or increasing throughput whilst reducing entrainment, optimising mass transfer and separations, reducing costs and improving operational stability.  With the financial help of numerous industrial sponsors, CSIRO has been undertaking research targeting SX operation over the past decade, in particular via the AMIRA P706 (2004-2006) and MERIWA projects M401 (2007-2010) and M418 (2010-2013).  A multiple-pronged research approach has been adopted, including a combination of SX chemistry and kinetics, small scale physical modelling, development of a variety of measurement tools and probes for mixer-settler characterisation, and development and ongoing refinement of computational fluid dynamics (CFD) models, including extension to three phase (air, aqueous, organic) models of bench and full scale contactors.  Recent developments have included successful site-based investigations of liquid flow patterns in operating commercial settlers, providing a deeper fundamental understanding of SX processes which have translated into tangible outcomes for operating plants. ###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Liquid-liquid separation or solvent extraction (SX) is an important step in hydrometallurgical processes which facilitates selective separation of one or more metal ions of interest, e.g. copper, from an aqueous solution containing various other metal ions.  Efficient SX performance is crucial to an increasingly broad range of mineral processing operations.  The challenge is to understand how to increase throughput, reduce entrainment, optimise performance, reduce costs and improve operational stability.  Reductions in capital and operating costs, and improved efficiencies can be achieved in SX plants by: 

- Optimising the use of current equipment (usually mixer-settlers) through improvements in operation and design, 

- Where appropriate, introduction of newer technology such as pulsed columns, and 

- Better management of reagents, especially with respect to phase separation and organic degradation and loss. 

With the financial help of numerous industrial sponsors, CSIRO has been undertaking research targeting efficient SX operation over the past decade, via the AMIRA P706 (2004-2006) and MERIWA proj

ects M401 (2007-2010) and M418 (20102013).  The following presents a brief chronological outline of research areas and developments throughout the three projects, and outlines planned future research directions which are expected to continue to deliver industry benefits. 

###### **RESEARCH PROGRESSION** 

###### **The Beginning: AMIRA P706 (2004-2006)** 

The AMIRA P706 project set the initial direction of this research with the philosophy encapsulated in the three dot points above, and aimed to develop a fundamental understanding of the parameters that control the performance of SX equipment and reagents.  To this end, it reviewed the theory, design, modelling and application of mixer-settlers and pulsed columns, along with the current state of modelling SX reactors.  Dispersion and coalescence were discussed with respect to droplet size distribution and reactor design and operation.  Reagent degradation and phase separation issues in a variety of SX systems were also reviewed, with degradation mechanisms for hydroxyoximes (e.g. LIX<sup>®</sup> 84-I, Acorga<sup>®</sup> M5640) and phosphinic acids (e.g. Cyanex<sup>®</sup> 272) amongst others considered.  The impact of cruds and impurities, and the effectiveness of organic remediation on phase separation were described.  Multiple studies in these various areas were undertaken, including work into the chemical stability of reagents under sponsors’ selected operating conditions.  An example of such a study using Acorga M5640 is disclosed at this conference [1].  Other work focussed on both mixer-settler and pulsed column operation, including comparison of the two.  Besides

###### i) <u>Fundamental Science and Entrainment</u> 

Work in this area included a comprehensive review of solvent extraction principles and various techniques for mass transfer and kinetic measurements.  Based on this, a CSIRO Lewis cell with improved features was developed and validated (Figure 3), offering a useful tool for kinetic measurements for various solvent extraction systems with minimum ambiguity.  Mass transfer and kinetic measurements for a copper system were made using a LIX984N / ShellSol D70 reagent system [3], enabling their incorporation into the computational fluid dynamics (CFD) modelling package. 

In addition, a review of entrainment in solvent extraction was undertaken, focussing on entrainment factors, methods for sampling and entrainment measurements, with major entrainment streams and issues in sampling and entrainment measurements identified for further research and development.  A comprehensive review of new solvent extraction equipment (e.g. the VSF mixer-settler, the Koch-Glisch inline mixer-settler and centrifugal contactors) was also undertaken.

Work in this area targeted the development and testing of both design and operating improvements for solvent extraction equipment, primarily mixer settlers with limited work on pulsed columns.  It involved the development of laboratory and pilot testing capability, including the investigation and improvement in a number of diagnostic tools, which were used in site-based activities.

Numerous probes were evaluated for flow pattern measurement, including the UVP system which was developed and proven on laboratory, pilot and full scale settlers as being robust and appropriate for measurement of velocities in commercial SX systems. ###### **The (Near) Present: MERIWA Project M418 (2010-2013)** 

The overriding goal of the MERIWA M418 (or ‘SXT2’) project, which concluded in August 2013, was to assist operations achieve improved performance of their solvent extraction operations, with a focus on improved performance by the reduction of entrainment.  The research effort was undertaken through four themes of work being i) ‘Operational impact’, ii) ‘CFD modelling’, iii) ‘Physical modelling and measurement’, and iv) ‘Mass transfer and entrainment’.  As per the previous projects, the objectives were tuned to provide a mix of fundamental development and operatorrelevant outcomes.  These proposed foci included: 

- Improvement of the CFD modelling code and provision of expert computational modelling support to the SXT2 research team and its sponsors, including use of the CFD modelling to predict flow patterns in existing laboratory, pilot and full scale settlers and extend its use to modelling improvements (with physical modelling / measurement validation) to full scale development of plant modifications. 

- Development of improved fundamental and comparative capabilities for mass transfer determination in SX processes to allow all sponsors to determine fundamental characteristics of their processes, e.g. impact of various modifiers. 

- Development of best practice for sampling and determination of entrainment, organic in aqueous and aqueous in organic – leading to possible development of on-line determination capabilities. 

- Extension of physical modelling capability to allow increasingly sophisticated changes and improvements in the engineering or operation of mixers and settlers. 

- Develop additional or improved probes for determination of critical characteristics of model, pilot and full scale performance including but not limited to phase velocities, droplet sizes, dispersion band and interface levels. 

- Undertake several site based studies to characterise, diagnose and then make recommendations for potential improvements in operating sponsors’ plants. 

- To transfer the core understanding of the fundamental and modelling work within SXT2 onto the selected operations in a manner that allow appropriate adaptation and plant performance improvements, 

   - Work with operators and engineering companies to prioritise and test new design concepts in mixing, droplet formation, feed distribution, coalescence and settling in computational and physical models prior to demonstration / testing on operating plants. 

   - Identify with operators further opportunities for site-specific design, modelling and testing of new components prior to installation.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

SNF FloMin, Inc. has introduced a complete line of extractants for various metals recovery.  Among them are the CuPRO MEX™ Brand of copper extractants that are based on the well- known 2-hydroxy 5-nonylsalicylaldoxime and 2-hydroxy

acetophenoneoxime.  This paper presents the laboratory and pilot plant trial results for SNF FloMin’s CuPRO MEX™ 3302 reagent, the equivalent to the well-known ACORGA® M5640 extractant, and the composition of these reagents are described. Some examples of SNF FloMin’s _CuPRO-Sim™ Advanced_ solvent extraction simulator are presented.

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Copper solvent extraction reagents have been provided predominately by two suppliers for many years – BASF (formerly Cognis Corporation) [1] and Cytec [2].  Both suppliers have been present under different corporate names, but the core people and the reagents and technology provided by both have been relatively constant over many years. There have been several attempts by other suppliers to enter this market, most notably Shell International Chemicals [3]   from the UK in the 1970’s and 1980’s and by AlliedSignal [4]  (Inspec) in the 1990’s.  Both of these businesses, including their products and/or plants, were eventually purchased by Henkel (a predecessor to Cognis/BASF). More recently, Star Orechem Industries Ltd. in India made an effort to enter this important market.  After some limited success, mainly in Africa, this company and its products and plant were purchased by Cytec, leaving still only the two major suppliers to provide the global supply of critical solvent extraction reagents for copper recovery. 

These other suppliers failed largely due to their lack of long-term commitment to the mining sector in their business portfolio.  Now, SNF FloMin, Inc. has made the strategic decision to provide copper solvent extraction reagents as a part of its extensive portfolio of mining related chemicals and services.  SNF FloMin, Inc. is the PERFORMANCE MINING REAGENTS Company with a large global presence and a firm commitment to the long term growth of its various portfolios, and it is now the second largest flotation chemical company in the world. The purpose of this paper is to demonstrate the efficacy and commercial success of the latest solvent extraction products being offered by SNF FloMin, Inc. and its various global subsidiaries. 

To date, laboratory and pilot plant studies have been carried out at SNF FloMin’s metallurgical/analytical laboratory in Chile and at Anglo American Chile’s El Soldado, Mantoverde, and Mantos Blancos mines.  Plant scale industrial trials are being carried out at the El Soldado Division since August, 2012; at the Mantos Blancos Division since April, 2013; and at the Mantoverde Division since June, 2013. 

This paper presents the testing methods and the chemical, physical and metallurgical comparisons of SNF FloMin’s CuPRO MEX™ 3302 to the ACORGA® M5640 extractant in numerous experiments, both bench scale and continuous pilot plant scale.  Data mainly for the Mantoverde and Mantos Blancos Divisions of Anglo American Chile are presented, and these results include: chemical and physical characterizations,

copper extraction and strip points, kinetics, net transfer, recovery, Cu/Fe selectivity, re-extraction data, and both extraction and stripping isotherms. Physical properties include: phase separation in each phase continuity, density, viscosity, surface tension, and interfacial tension.  The pilot plant results were completed in sideby-side mini-pilot plants, calibrated for precise comparison of different reagents or

**ACORGA® M 5640** [5]: is a mixture of 2-hydroxy-5-nonylsalicylaldoxime (~ 48 wt.%) and TXIB (2,2,4-Trimethylpentanediol diisobutyrate, ~ 25-30 wt.%) in a low to medium aromatic hydrocarbon solvent.

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Nitration is a phenomenon that acquired interest in the copper mining industry in the late 90’s as a result of the events that affected the Lomas Bayas SX plant in northern Chile. In this period, the first measurements of nitrates in PLS evidenced concentrations between 30 and 40 gpl. Due to the lack of knowledge about the nitration phenomenon, follow-ups were made neither on the development of nitrate concentration in PLS nor on the electrolyte.  As a result of this uncommon phenomenon, the organic inventory started to show the first deficiencies: a reduction in the transfer of Copper along with a loss of the physical characteristics, resulting in higher levels of entrainment and a reduction in the quality of cathodes. 

Upon the emergence of the phenomenon, some steps were taken in order to reduce the negative effect of nitration. These measures consisted in reducing the acidity in the leaching circuit (higher pH in PLS), controlling the nitrate in PLS with heap wash, reducing the streams, modifying the SX configuration by adding an additional wash stage, controlling the redox potentials, and even changing the extractant reagent from LIX 622 (alcohol modified Aldoxime) to LIX 84I (Ketoxime and Nonylphenol, residual raw material from the manufacturing process). 

On the basis of this experience, different projects that may have had the presence of nitrate in their PLS chose the reagent LIX 84I, sacrificing copper transfer and selectivity regarding Iron. At present, of the seven projects with possible presence of nitrates, four of them only have evidenced nitrate contents in their PLS. At present for this four two of them are using the extractant ACORGA NR® of Cytec Industries Inc. (modified aldoxime with protection against nitration), one is using a mix of both extractants and one is using LIX 84I. 

This paper presen

ts the theoretical explanation of the nitration phenomenon and the experience in SX plants regarding the resistance to nitration of the formulations of extractants currently used in the market. _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 195 ###### **BACKGROUND INFORMATION** ###### **What is Nitration?** Nitration is a chemical reaction by substitution produced between the Oxime and the nitronium ion that is present in the PLS solutions or electrolyte. This reaction produces a pseudo stabilization of the organic-metallic complex (Copper) thus avoiding the stripping reaction (removal of the Cu ion) in the electrolyte solution, resulting in a circulating load that prevents the normal transfer of copper. The formation of the nitronium ion is based on the following: NO3 - + H2SO4  HNO3 + HSO4 - (1)
HNO3 + H2SO4  NO2 + + H2O + HSO4 - (2)
The mechanism proposed for the nitration reaction of the oxime is: OH

The nitration reaction will directly depend on the nitrate concentration present in the aqueous solutions of the plant and the level of acidity, but it is also affected by the variables of temperature, redox potential, interfacial tension and the reactivity shown by the aqueous and organic phases (2). Depending on each of them, the nitration conditions will be more or less aggressive. _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 196 The nitration of the oxime may cause different problems in the normal operation of the SX plant. The most important of such problems are the following: - Loss of capacity in the copper transfer. - Increased phase separation times. - Reduced interfacial tension. - Increased entrainments. - Increased consumption of extractant. - Increased hydrolytic degradation rate. Operations with the presence of nitrate ion under the conditions mentioned above should establish a routine control to prevent or reduce the probabilities of oxime nitration. They are: - Determination of residual copper: A non-nitrated organic must be completely unloaded in the standard laboratory conditions. The copper detected after the unloading is known as residual copper and is directly proportional to the amount of nitrated oxime. - Analytical measurement of the content of the nitrated products (gas chromatography). Cytec, in turn, has developed different processes to evaluate the level of aggressiveness of the solutions with nitrate levels both in the PLS and in the electrolyte (TAP Test), standard tests for the evaluation of the response of reagents against nitration (Accelerated nitration test) has also developed the formulation of an extractant th

at shows a better resistance against the nitration phenomena while maintaining the metallurgic advantages of the modified aldoximes (greater transfer of copper and Cu:Fe selectivity). The different developments and studies carried out with the tools mentioned above and applied on real cases of the Chilean copper industry that have presented nitration phenomena are shown below. ###### **RESULTS AND DISCUSSION** ###### **TAP TEST** Regarding the criticality of facing a nitration condition, having a procedure which allows the determination of the magnitude of the nitration risk becomes a priority. With this consideration Cytec developed a methodology at the laboratory level, which provides a relative indication of the nitration risk of any projected SX plant which facilitates the assessment of the potential solutions for controlling the risk. Cytec chose Tert-Amyl Phenol (TAP) as the compound replacing the real oximes. This compound is clearly more reactive with the nitronium agent than the real oxime, as the benzene contains only half of the OH-activator and its solubility in the aqueous _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 197 solution is much higher due to the fact that its alkyl chain is much shorter. Depending on how aggressive are the nitration conditions in the aqueous solution, the Tert-Amyl Phenol dissolved in an appropriate solvent is partially or completely nitrated as 2-nitro-4tertamyl phenol. The TAP test procedure is generally 0,2mM in heptane, which is agitated in the 1:1 v/v ratio with the studied aqueous phase at 40°C. After 3 hours of reaction, the aqueous phase is separated and the organic phase is analyzed through gas chromatography. The nitration potential is expressed as the area percentage of 4-nitrophenol tertamyl in comparison with the total area detected (Tert-Amyl Phenol area + 4- nitro-phenol tertamyl area). ###### **CONCLUSIONS** 

From the studies presented above, the following conclusions can be made: 

- The TAP Test is a useful tool that provides us with the level of aggressiveness in both the extraction and stripping stages in the presence of nitrates in aqueous solutions. 

- Under aggressive conditions of nitration the extractant ACORGA® NR20 shows a greater resistance than LIX 84I, or any commercial copper extractants against nitration phenomena. 

- The extractant ACORGA® NR20 maintains the traditional metallurgic advantages of the modified aldoxime, obtaining better results for the transfer of copper and Cu:Fe selectivity than the extractants based on Ketoxime. 

- In the second nitration phenomenon (Capacho Viejo Mining) that affected the copper industry in Chile (with greater much aggressiveness in comparison with the occurred in Lomas Bayas), the extractant ACORGA®NR20 presented high resistance to nitration phenomena.

At present the large-scale mining of Chile presents significant challenges, since over time CuT grade in oxidized ores have been declining and production programs continue to be demanding.  This forces the current operations of solvent extraction to innovate in a new way to make more efficient the current facilities.  As an alternative, this new condition requires to analyze the way of supplementing low grade with greater flows of processing and define which is the best configuration for the particular conditions of each operation. 

Given this situation, Codelco Chile, Gabriela Mistral Division, is studying the transformation of their solvent extraction plant, in order to process a higher volume of PLS to lower copper concentrations. 

This study shows the alternatives configurations evaluated to meet productions levels settled until the year 2024.

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

The solvent extraction plant concentrates and selectively transfers the copper contained in the solutions coming from the leach toward the electrolyte that caters to the electrowinning plant. 

The selective transfer mechanism is fulfilled through liquid-liquid ion-exchange (SX). This physical-chemical process develops in machines called mixers-decanters and used as a transfer vehicle a fluid called the organic phase. 

General characteristics of the SX Gabriela Mistral Division plant are as follows: 

• Its main facilities include two independent circuits of mixers backstreaming decanters provided by Bateman, known as trains A and B, which each consists of  5 stages:  a section of washing organic solution (W), two extraction sections (stages E1 and E2) and two re-extraction sections (stages S2 and S1).  See configuration in figure 1. 

• Each train has its own organic pond (LOT) from which it is fed adequate organic flow to the plant. 

- Both trains work independently and are the same in design and operation. 

Each train operates at a flow rate of 1.650 m³/h of organic and fed at a rate of 1.650 m3/h of leaching from PLS and a flow rate of 700 m³/h poor electrolyte from electrowinning, resulting the mixture 1.650 m³/h of refining and 700 m3/h of rich electrolyte.

###### **CONCLUSIONS.** 

This study reveals the need of a configuration change in the SX plant, to meet the production program established in the PND 2013 to 2024. 

All the simulated configuration alternatives are able to reach the 2013 PND.  The three best alternatives from the point of view of the transfer of copper were: E1//E2+S1+S2, E1+E2//E3+S1 y E1+E3//E2+S1. In addition, the three selected alternatives can be optimized concerning the status of the current operation (base case) through °/v extractant, acid increasing in EP, E.A.E. and workflow in EP. 

The alternatives proposed must have a greater flow of PLS; there is the possibility of ILS modules skip to SX. 

For the conditions simulated in the base case projected in PND 2013 to 2024, the current configuration only reaches the target of production in the year 2021. 

Interferences associated with configuration E1//E2+S1+S2 are minimal; manufacturing time would be about 1.5 months and 4 days mounting; these would be associated to the team work and injected resources to perform  faster assembly 

According to the F.O.D.A analysis and study of interferences, the easiest alternative to implement is the E1 //E2+S1+S2 configuration. With an economic return, for the case of the current operational conditions, of 545.471 KUS$ and 935.157 KUS$, for the case of the optimized condition; this is between the years 2013 to 2024. 

After developing the studio considering the aspects of economic, administrative and processes, the recommendation is to change current configuration to the configuration E1//E2+S1+S2. This will allow to DGM: 

- Reach a production over the PND 2013. 

- Increase the profits of the Corporation. 

- Innovate with respect to industry worldwide 

- Lower cost investment and time to implement 

- Flexible operation. 

- Easy return to the present settings.

###### **EFFECT OF TEMPERATURE AND AIR SPARGING ON SELECTED CHEMICAL AND PHYSICAL PROPERTIES OF THE ACORGA M5640 / SHELLSOL 2046 ORGANIC SYSTEM** 

K.R. Barnard, P. Miovs

ki and J. Li _CSIRO Process Science and Engineering / CSIRO Minerals Down Under National Research Flagship PO Box 7229, Karawara, WA 6152, Australia. keith.barnard@csiro.au_ 

###### **ABSTRACT** 

As part of the AMIRA P706 solvent extraction project which preceded the MERIWA SXT projects, the effect of temperature (40, 55  C) and intermittent air sparging on organic solutions of 25% v/v Acorga M5640 / Shellsol 2046 under copper strip conditions was assessed.  Stoichiometric decomposition of aldoxime extractant to aldehyde was observed in all systems.  Whilst increased operating temperatures hastened the rate of degradation, regular air sparging, which provided the possibility of oxidative degradation of aldoxime, was actually found to inhibit oxime degradation.  The impact of the degradation conditions on crud formation, formation of water soluble organic species, and the interfacial tension, phase disengagement time, copper extraction kinetics and copper over iron selectivity of the resulting organic solutions is presented. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

220 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

As a process used in the concentration and purification of metal ions of interest, solvent extraction (SX) relies on the mixing and subsequent rapid and efficient separation of immiscible aqueous and organic solutions.  In SX, the organic solutions are continually recycled, allowing organic degradation products to accrue to an equilibrium level in the organic phase.  Organic contaminants such as degradation products have the potential to adversely impact the SX process in various ways, including decreased metal selectivity, poorer metal transfer kinetics, increased phase disengagement time, accelerated reagent degradation, increased entrainment levels, and emulsion and/or crud formation.  As these can all affect the cost/efficiency of an SX operation, minimising _in situ_ degradation of organic reagents is desirable.  Chemical stability was one of the foci of work performed in the AMIRA P706 project Improving Solvent Extraction Technology, which subsequently evolved into the MERIWA Solvent Extraction Technology projects which have been undertaken over the last six years at CSIRO in Australia.  A summary of outcomes from these projects is provided elsewhere in these proceedings [1]. 

Copper SX utilises hydroxyoxime extractants such as 5-nonylsalicylaldoxime (aldoxime, Figure 1) which is present in the commercial reagent Acorga M5640.  Copper complexation by this extractant results in a square planar complex with a 1:2 copper:aldoxime stoichiometric ratio.  Due to its viscous nature, the aldoxime is shipped in a diluted form and is present at about 50% concentration in Acorga M5640.  A diluent such as Shellsol 2046 is used to further dilute the extractant to a suitable concentration for use in an operating SX circuit. 

Hydroxyoxime reagents have been used commercially for over 40 years to extract copper from acidic sulphate solutions.  Conseque

ntly, work regarding degradation of these reagents has focussed on these conditions.  Acid-catalysed hydrolysis of the oxime group is the most common degradation pathway, generating the corresponding aldehyde or ketone species (Figure 1).  Increasing either acid concentration or temperature increases the rate of hydrolysis [2,3].  Some organic additives including alcohols and phenols can increase the rate of hydrolysis by acting as phase transfer reagents, allowing acid-containing aqueous solutions to infiltrate the organic phase more readily [4-6].  The aldehyde hydrolysis product, being a large, relatively non-polar organic molecule, accrues in the organic phase.  This and the corresponding ketone species increase the organic viscosity and density and may also act as weak phase modifiers [6]. 

Hydroxyoximes are also known to degrade via oxidation e.g. by high oxidation state manganese species in acidic conditions, which has been linked to poor circuit performance e.g. [7-10].  Adverse effects include a reduction in reaction kinetics and extractant capacity, a decrease in interfacial tension, increases in phase disengagement times, increased entrainment losses and increased crud production.  For acidic sulphatebased systems, clay treatment can be employed to help alleviate these problems, e.g. [8,11-14].  Under laboratory-based acidic oxidising conditions using permanganate, 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

221 

identified products include aldehyde/ketone, 5-nonyl salicylic acid (carboxylic acid), shorter chained aldoximes and possibly aliphatic alcohols [10,15,16].  The aldehyde and ketone products form much more readily under oxidising conditions [10,15].  As phenols can act as antioxidants, some polymerisation of these phenolic-based organic species may also occur. 

The paraffinic and naphthenic components of Shellsol 2046 are unreactive and require relatively severe conditions to undergo chemical reaction, predominantly via free radical addition [17].  The aromatic components of diluents are more susceptible to chemical attack.  Contact of aromatic-containing diluent with concentrated sulphuric acid (e.g. during addition of concentrated sulphuric acid to a circuit) can produce sulphonated aromatic species [17].  Oxidation of Shellsol 2046 by KMnO4 in 150 g/L H2SO4 has been observed to result in a darkening of the organic solution and the generation of insoluble crud [15].  Oxidation however did not adversely affect phase disengagement of the filtered organic solution, and resulted in an increase in interfacial tension.  Organicsoluble aromatic oxidation products included naphthoquinones, naphthalenecarboxaldehydes, binaphthalenes, indenones and hydroxybiphenyl species. Detection of aliphatic degradation products was not attempted. 

Although permanganate degradation has been shown to be detrimental to hydroxyoxime, it may not necessarily be a common SX degradation pathway.  An alternate and potentially very common oxidativ

e route is via gaseous oxygen. The following work therefore aimed to assess the effects of temperature and air sparging as a possible route for oxidation on selected physical and chemical properties of 25% v/v Acorga M5640 in Shellsol 2046 when continually mixed under aqueous strip conditions. Properties examined for the organic solutions degraded under the different experimental conditions included phase disengagement time (PDT), interfacial tension (IFT), dissolved organic in aqueous levels, metal loading capacity, loading kinetics and metal selectivity. Changes in chemical composition (aldoxime, aldehyde) were also determined. OH

###### **Phase Disengagement Tests and Interfacial Tension Measurements** 

Phase disengagement time (PDT) tests were performed under strip conditions using fresh aqueous strip solution and the four degraded organic solutions.  The organic solutions were each pre-washed by shaking with fresh aqueous strip solution (A:O 1:20). PDT tests were also performed using fresh, organic solution which had been pre-washed with fresh aqueous strip solution (A:O 1:1, mix 15 min at 750 rpm) to replicate the A:O ratio experienced by each of the degraded organics during the 43 day trial.  All resulting aqueous pre-wash solutions were discarded.  The temperatures of the organic and fresh aqueous strip solutions were maintained at 22.5  0.5  C.  PDT was monitored after aqueous continuous (A/C) and organic continuous (O/C) mixing.  The procedure employed was comparable to that described previously [18], except that solutions were mixed for two minutes at 1200 rpm and the impeller was located 8 mm from the base of the box.  Solutions were not centrifuged prior to each analysis.  IFT measurements on pre-equilibrated and centrifuged samples were performed as described elsewhere [18]. 

###### **Total Organic Carbon Analyses** 

Dissolved organic in aqueous analyses were performed using a Dohrmann DC190 total organic carbon (TOC) instrument in which samples are pyrolised and the evolved carbon dioxide is measured by infra-red spectroscopy.  Aqueous samples taken from the reaction mixture were centrifuged and filtered (0.4  m Gelman filter discs with a Supor<sup></sup> membrane) prior to TOC analysis. 

###### **Extraction Kinetics, Metal Selectivity and Metal Loading Tests** 

Extraction kinetics, metal loading and metal selectivity tests were performed using procedures adapted from the reagent manufacturer’s notes [19].  All organic solutions were completely stripped (600 g/L sulphuric acid) and diluted to a predegradation concentration of 10% v/v Acorga M5640 by addition of 150 mL of Shellsol 2046 to 100 mL sample. 

For the extraction kinetics tests, organic (250 mL) and synthetic aqueous feed solution (250 mL) were separately adjusted to 23  C.  The organic was then placed in a stainless steel mixing box (9 cm Ч 9 cm base, 15 cm height).  A 6-vaned teflon impeller (40 mm diame

ter) was located just beneath the top of the organic solution.  Mixing was commenced at 1600 rpm and aqueous solution (250 mL) quickly added.  Samples (approximately 40 mL) were taken from the mixing emulsion after 15 seconds, 30 seconds, two minutes and fifteen minutes, after which mixing was ceased.  For each sample, the organic and aqueous phases were separated as soon as possible.  The aqueous and organic phases were filtered using 0.45  m Supor membrane filters and Whatman 1PS filter papers, respectively.  The organic samples were stripped (600 g/L sulphuric acid, A:O 2:1) and the resulting aqueous strip solution filtered (0.45  m Supor filter). All aqueous samples were analysed by inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy (ICP-AES) for Cu and Fe content.
