As all aqueous samples were centrifuged and filtered prior to TOC analysis, the results are only indicative of the generation of more aqueous-soluble organic species, not organic entrainment levels. ###### **Organic Composition** HPLC-determined aldoxime and aldehyde levels in each organic solution taken during the trial are shown in Figure 2, with the initial and final levels summarised in Table 1. For the HPLC results, the average 95% confidence intervals for aldoxime and aldehyde analyses were found to be 2.3 and 2.6%, respectively. The aldoxime contents determined by HPLC and by maximum copper loading were comparable for each sample. In all four stability tests, conversion of aldoxime to aldehyde was found within experimental error to be stoichiometric. Increasing the operating temperature resulted in a greater degree of aldoxime decomposition to aldehyde, an expected outcome. Unexpectedly, it was also found that intermittent purging of the organic solutions with air conferred a beneficial effect via the suppression of this reaction. This result also indicates that oxidative degradation of aldoxime is not readily achieved using gaseous oxygen under the selected conditions. The reason why which aldoxime hydrolysis is inhibited by air sparging is of interest. Given the constant mixing protocol used in these experiments, any benefit associated with the possible removal of residual entrained aqueous acid by the purging process would be short-lived. Conversely, the results are consistent with the benefit which co

uld be derived if the purging process permanently removed a species that either promoted oxime hydrolysis directly or which facilitated increased aqueous acid uptake/retention in the organic phase during mixing (e.g. enabled production of smaller droplets resulting in increased interfacial area) which in turn promoted hydrolysis.  Such a species could have been present initially, in which case the initial purge(s) may have 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

226 

removed it.  Alternatively, degradation of an organic reagent in the system (possibly but not necessarily aldoxime) could be generating small quantities of an undetected product that facilitates the same effect, in which case regular purging would be necessary to minimise its impact.  Assuming this impurity possibility is correct, in either case the mechanism of removal via air sparging could be chemical (e.g. oxidation of the component rendering it less active) or physical (e.g. evaporation of the offending species).  Given the potential to decrease reagent consumption, further investigation to confirm and establish how widespread this effect is (i.e. determine that it is not purely associated with a particular batch of reagent used in this trial) and, if common, to elucidate its mechanism of action is of interest.  This could be achieved via comparing purging with air against an inert gas such as nitrogen in parallel systems, as well as comparing the results from sparging just initially against sparging on an ongoing basis. 

The rate constants associated with hydrolysis of aldoxime to aldehyde were determined by the method of integration assuming a first order rate of reaction, with the gradient forced through the origin.  Larger rate constants were obtained with operation at higher temperatures (Table 1).  From these, aldoxime half lives under the conditions used were calculated to be approximately 11-15 weeks at 55  C and 40-63 weeks at 40  C. Other work has been performed on the stability of aromatic aldoxime extractants when mixed continuously under typical copper strip conditions (45  C, 180 g/L sulphuric acid, 30 g/L copper; [20]).  In that case, half lives of 16 and 31 weeks were calculated for the nonyl and dodecyl aldoximes, respectively.  The Acorga M5640 used here contains nonyl aldoxime.  Extrapolation of the current results suggest an oxime half life of 25-38 weeks at 45  C in the absence/presence of added air, respectively.  As differences in operating parameters such as mixing intensity can affect reagent stability, detailed comparison of the current results to those of the earlier work is not necessarily valid.  However, it has previously been noted that the presence of the diester modifier in Acorga M5640 (2,2,4trimethyl-1,3-pentanediol diisobutyrate, or TXIB) inhibits oxime hydrolysis [5]. 

The approximate activation energy (Ea) for the hydrolysis reaction, determined using the calculated rate constants and an Arrhenius plot, were calculated to be

84 kJ/mol and 77 kJ/mol with/without air sparging, respectively. Given that only two different temperatures were trialled in the present work, it needs to be stressed that these calculated values are only approximate. ###### **SUMMARY AND CONCLUSION** 

The present work was performed to assess the effect of temperature (40, 55  C) and air sparging on the physical and chemical properties of organic solutions of 25% v/v Acorga M5640 in Shel

lsol 2046 when mixed under synthetic strip conditions. Hydrolysis of aldoxime to aldehyde was found within experimental error to be stoichiometric in all systems.  Increasing the operating temperature resulted in a greater degree of aldoxime decomposition to aldehyde, increased quantities of water soluble organic species, with some crud formation observed at the higher operating temperatures. Substitution of aldoxime for aldehyde had no appreciable effect on adverse interfacial tension, phase disengagement time or copper extraction kinetics.  A slight deterioration in Cu/Fe selectivity appears to be attributable to the loss of aldoxime, an outcome which could be rectified by addition of fresh reagent. 

Although intermittent air sparging provided the possibility of oxidative degradation of aldoxime, it was found to play a beneficial role in the present system. Relative to the non-sparged systems at the same operating temperature, it resulted in reduced rates of aldoxime hydrolysis and reduced the generation of crud and water soluble organic species.  No adverse effect on interfacial tension, aqueous continuous phase disengagement time or copper extraction kinetics was noted.  Based on the current results, further research to more fully investigate the merits of air sparging is warranted. Such an investigation should aim to confirm and establish how widespread this effect is

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Developed in Excel a mathematical model has been produced that predicts the thermal behavior presented by Solvent Extraction process (SX) and the transfer of heat generated in their flows, mainly in the rich electrolyte and raffinate, when there are changes temperatures in PLS (pregnant leach solution) due to reactions caused by bacteria within the stockpile, as in the case of bioleaching, or by environmental conditions to which this is located. The model was developed for a particular plant that used bacterial leaching and this consist in to enter flow data, physical properties and inlet temperatures, to a sequence of equations based primarily in energy balances performed at different stages of the SX process. Keeping constant the inlet temperature of the lean electrolyte, were used historical temperatures of the PLS recorded by the plant to perform sensitization of the thermal impact generated en SX. Rich electrolyte temperatures and raffinate, delivered by the model showed an average deviation of 0.63 ° C, compared to the actual values.

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Currently, the politics of mining companies are increasingly focused on incorporating renewable energy and energy efficiency measures into their production processes to reduce their impact on the environment and contribute to sustainable development. In turn, evidence of depletion of oxidized minerals have forced companies to obtain copper from low grade ores by bioleaching, because it is feasible for these new conditions. However, the bacterial leaching implies the obtaining of a higher temperature PLS due to the oxidation reactions generated by bacteria, affecting directly the thermal conditions of the processes that occur. This work aims to encourage the use of renewable energy through a mathematical tool that quantifies the energy demand of companies when facing PLS variable thermal conditions, either by environmental conditions or by the exothermic reactions inside the stockepile leach, as indicated above. The mathematical model was created for a SX plant particularly who used bacterial leaching in order to meet fuel demand, which involved heating the rich electrolyte before entering to the process of Electrowinning (EW). In this way, you can optimize the temperature variability presented by the PLS because the model serves as input for incorporation and the correct sizing of renewable energy plants to meet the energy needs of the company. From not knowing the variation that presents fuel demand over time, the incorporating plant could be oversized. ###### **PREDICTION OF PHASE SEPARATION TIME IN COPPER SOLVENT EXTRACTION USING NEURAL NETWORKS** 

S. Jara, P. Navarro and F. Cubillos _Universidad de Santiago de Chile Departamento de Ingenierнa Metalъrgica Departamento de Ingenierнa Quнmica Av. Libertador Bernardo O´Higgins # 3363 Estaciуn Central, Santiago, Chile sebastian.jaram@usach.cl_ 

###### **ABSTRACT** 

A study of the effect of four variables on the time required to separate organic and solution phases for a copper solvent extraction process is presented. The study was conducted in a cylindrical glass container of one liter volume which is used as a mixersettler reactor. The variables under study are the copper concentration in a leach solution, concentration of the extractant in the organic phase, the stirring time and agitation speed. A set of experiments were carried out consisting in changing these variables and determining the time elapsed until phase separation occurs. The variables with a larger effect on the phase separation time resulted to be the extractant reagent and stirring speed. A feed forward neural network was trained and validated using experimental data to capture the static mapping between the phase separation time and the variables mentioned above. The FFNN was able to predict the phase separation time with less than 2% error. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

246 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Chile has become a major copper cathode producer via hydrometallurgical processes, relegating the production of electrorefined and fire refined cathodes to a secondary place. The advent of the solvent extraction process (SX) in conjunction with electrowinning (EW) starts in 1994. Before 1993, production did not exceed 160,000 tons per year by this process, situation that increased exponentially with time, exceeding in less than five years one million tons annually “Ocaranza [1]”. 

Copper hydrometallurgy has grown exponentially due to the invention of hidroximes organic extractants around (1960), which over the years has evolved in selectivity and physical properties for the different conditions that present processing plants of copper ore by leaching stages, solvent extraction and electrowinning “Castillo, Biela and Navarro [2]”. 

In the copper extraction process, the most common way of mixing the aqueous and organ

ic phase, to carry out the transfer reaction, is to disperse one phase into the other by mechanical agitation, In order enhance, to make the process to be useful it is necessary that the dispersion must have a temporary nature “Hartland and Jeelanni [3], Nadiv and Semiat [4]”. 

Organic droplet size affects the mass transfer and the speed at which the phases are separated. Smaller drop sizes increase the surface area available for the reaction between chelating and copper (Cu<sup>+2</sup> ) and therefore improve mass transfer. On the other hand, very small droplet size increases the time required for separating both phases affecting performance and the formation of a stable dispersion (emulsion) “Kordosky, Virnig and Boley [5]”. 

The main problems associated with the presence of organic in the rich electrolyte and raffine solutions are: 

- Impact on the cathodic quality, (burned cathodes in critical cases). 

- Environmental pollution and fire hazards in the electrowinning stage produced by high volatility at operating temperatures. 

- Significant impacts on operating costs due to organic phase loss, additional labor required for circuit cleaning, deterioration of cells used as coatings pitch, higher requirements of cobalt and other additives required because of the increasing of anodic corrosion. 

- Clogging of the leach distribution systems.

The main problems associated with the increase of the organic in aqueous entrainments can be summarized as: 

- Contamination of the electrolyte with chloride, manganese, nitrate, aluminum, silica, iron, iodine, solids and others. 

- Major anodic corrosion. 

- Major cathodic pollution. 

- Major environmental contamination in the electrowinning stage. 

- Major electrolyte losses on stripping stage because entrainments which increases requirement for purging. 

- Loss of copper, H2SO4, cobalt and additives from the electrolyte. 

A phenomenological modeling of the effects under study is complex. An attractive tool for addressing this kind of problem is to use neural networks which have the ability to learn nonlinear multidimensional mappings in a simple and efficient manner “Flуrez and Fernбndez [6]”. 

Neural networks allows the development of a mathematical model consisting of a number of procedural elements organized in levels. They can learn to distinguish patterns by examples and training, without a priori modeling and the need to specify probability density functions. The basic structure of a feed forward neural network is shown in Figure 1 “Flуrez and Fernбndez [6]”.

###### **CONCENTRATED ACID ADDITION INTO WASH STAGES – CASE STUDY AT FREEPORT-MCMORAN COPPER & GOLD MORENCI OPERATIONS** 

Jacklyn Steeples _FREEPORT-MCMORAN COPPER & GOLD 8500 N. Freeport-McMoRan Rd Safford, AZ 85540 jacklyn_steeples@fmi.com_ 

###### **ABSTRACT** 

A series of tests was conducted at the Freeport-McMoRan Copper & Gold Morenci Stargo Solvent Extraction facility to determine if adding concentrated sulfuric acid to a wash stage was an effective alternative to adding Lean Electrolyte (LE).  Tests were conducted with the objective of increasing operational flexibility within the production plant as well as decreasing the amount of LE bleed required.  Four different tests were performed over ten weeks.  It was determined that concentrated sulfuric acid was an acceptable solution that can be added without negatively affecting the performance of the wash stage. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

254 

###### **BACKGROUND** 

Iron transfer into the electrolyte via the solvent extraction (SX) process can negatively affect the downstream electrowinning (EW) process.  Iron is transferred into the electrolyte in two ways. 

1. Physically, by entrainment of pregnant leach solution (PLS) into the loaded organic phase (LO),[1] due to imperfect separation of the organic and aqueous solutions, and its subsequent de-entrainment to the electrolyte in the strip circuit. 

2. Chemically, by the attachment of Fe<sup>+3</sup> onto the extractant component of the organic from the (PLS), followed by the stripping of the Fe<sup>+3</sup> from the extractant into the electrolyte. 

Chemical iron transfer is a competing reaction with copper transfer in SX plants, as shown by the chemical reactions below. 



where RH represents the uncomplexed oxime extractant. 

There are two mechanisms of iron scrubbing in a wash stage. 

1. Chemical transfer of copper in exchange for iron on the organic, also called crowding[2] 

2. Stripping of iron from the organic usi

ng the acid in the wash solution 

In addition to chemical removal, iron is also removed by physical washing out of aqueous droplets entrained in the LO.  While there are two mechanisms of iron removal, this trial focused on the scrubbing portion. 

Performance of the wash stage, commonly called scrubbing efficiency or wash efficiency, is determined by taking the ratio of iron removed from the loaded organic, now designated as washed loaded organic (WLO), to the original amount of iron in the loaded organic.  This is shown by equation 3. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

255 



Other key process indicators (KPIs) to monitor the effectiveness of a wash stage include the difference in copper concentrations between LO and WLO and other impurity concentrations, such as manganese and chloride, in the wash solution.  The former is important to monitor to ensure that copper is not being stripped off the organic in the wash stage.  Acid concentration in the wash solution is a main factor influencing the amount of copper stripped off the LO.  Monitoring this value is important in evaluating overall wash stage efficiency.  The latter is important to ensure that physical entrainment from the wash stage does not increase the concentration of impurities in the electrolyte. Monitoring the impurity levels allows for adjustment of the bleed and fresh water flows into the wash stage and regulation of the process. 

In SX plants with wash stages, the wash stages generally follow the final stage of organic copper loading, where the organic is considered loaded organic (LO).  At the Stargo SX plant, the wash stage follows the E1 stage, as shown in Figure 1.  Wash stages provide an opportunity to reduce the amount of chemical iron that is transferred to the organic in the extraction process by contacting the LO with an aqueous wash solution that is mid-strength in acid and may also contain copper.  In many plants, wash solution is created by adding lean electrolyte (LE) and fresh water into the wash stage primary mix box[3].  The majority of wash solution is recycled and only a small amount of fresh water and LE are added.  Testing of acid in the wash stage was conducted as an opportunity to increase operational flexibility.  Continuing to optimize plant performance and increase operational flexibility were the justifications behind the test work.

Analyzing the two primary KPIs for the wash stage demonstrated that performance was not affected by switching from LE bleed to concentrated sulfuric acid. ###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Hydrometallurgical processes are economically feasible due to their low treatment costs, but they are not devoid from intrinsic production problems. One of these problems is in the size reduction stage, where a large amount of fines are created. These fines contain an important amount of valuable material and depending on their amount, there could be future permeability problems in the leaching pads. One of the solutions used is the application of a pre-treatment to the material before leaching, which is called agglomeration – curing process. 

The agglomeration – curing process consists on the bonding of fine particles to coarse particles by treating the mineral with sulphuric acid (H2SO4). When the mineral is wetted with an appropriate amount of liquid, the superficial tension required is reached to allow bonding the fine to the coarse particles when they collide due to the surface tension and the inter-particle chemical bonds. In addition, when the material is cured, the minerals sulphation and the gangue material dehydration occur, hence improving the mineral’s mechanical characteristics and the gen

eral hydraulic behaviour of the porous bed, stabilizing the silica generated by the decomposition of the gangue’s silicates. Therefore, this work is focused in increasing Cu recovery from a mixed ore, through artificial sulphuric acid and raffinate mixtures applying agglomerate – curing pre-treatments varying the sulphuric acid rate, curing time, particle size and different oxidants (Fe3+ and H2O2). ###### **EXPERIMENTAL WORK** The experimental work was done in a pilot scale agglomeration drum. The coarse and fine mineral was fed into the tank together with the raffinate and sulphuric acid. Agitation was started without reaching the critical velocity. The samples used were 400 g samples. 10% were fines (-150 μm) and 90% was coarse material. The coarse material was classified in several size fractions -12800+9525 μm, -9525+4000 μm, -4000+2000 μm and -2000+150 μm, which corresponded to an average particle size of 11163, 6762, 3000 and 1075 μm, respectively. The H2SO4 and raffinate (% v/v) rates used were 25:50, 50:50 and 75:25. Sulphuric acid was grade PA (~98% purity) and depending on the experiment, the raffinate was made up of 100% distilled H2O, Fe3+ (as Fe2(SO4)3), chloride (as NaCl) and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2, 30% v/v). _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 267 Curing times were from 3 to 6 days. After the samples went through the agglomeration and curing process, they were washed with distilled water to solubilize the sulphate produced and maintain the metals in solution. Then, they were acidulated with H2SO4 until reaching a pH=2 to maintain the metals solubilized. The liquid samples were extracted, filtered and sent to Atomic Absorption Spectroscopy to be analysed for Cu, Fe, Al, Ca and Mg. ###### **RESULTS AND DISCUSSIONS** ###### **Sulphuric acid dosage effect** Figure 1 shows the Cu recovery (%) and unit acid consumption (kg/kg Cu) in function of the H2SO4 and H2O rates (25, 50 and 75% H2SO4, and the rest, H2O). ###### **INTRODUCTION** 

In copper leaching operations, the application of leaching solutions is primarily accomplished by the use of drip emitters. Drip emitters provide several advantages over other methods for application of leaching solutions and their usage has increased dramatically in the last decades. However, there are still several challenges regarding drip emitters that have not been completely resolved. Plugging of drip emitters is a common issue in hydrometallurgical operations that affects the uniform distribution of solution in leaching pads and, as consequence, the extraction of metal value. 

In Freeport-McMoRan leaching operations, there are several causes of plugged drip emitters but the most frequent are associated with the presence of suspended solids in the leach solutions, “crud” that migrates from the SX plants into the raffinate that is applied on the leaching pads, crystallization of sulfates on the irrigation drip lines, and deficient operational and metallurgical practices that contribute to accelerating the obstruction of the drip emitters. 

The common solutions employed to address this issue are normally reactiveoriented. Basically, drip lines are removed in some point in the leaching cycle when plugging rates are too severe and they are replaced by new ones. The consequence is an increase in labor and materials that affect the operational costs of the process. The losses of production are normally difficult to quantify and they might be very serious if the problem is not identified and addressed in time. The hope that the un-leached metal will be recovered when a new lift is built in permanent heap operations is not always a correct assumption because the chemistry of the leach solutions will be different than a fresh solution especially in operations that require high availability of leaching agents. The loss of production in areas not sufficiently leached is even worse in dynamic leaching operations in which the ore has a unique chance for being leached. 

###### **CAUSES OF DRIP EMITTERS PLUGGING** 

The causes and rates of plugged emitters vary from site to site. Field audits, in which the amount of plugged emitters is quantified, have indicated that plugging rates fluctuate between 3% and 5% after the first 150 days of operation. Severe cases of emitters plugging in some of our operations resulted in more than 25% of drip emitters plugging after 60 days of leaching operation. 

Samples of plugged drip lines, as shown in Figure 1, as well as leach solutions collected at the end of the drip lines have been characterized at the Freeport-McMoRan Technology Center by using different techniques. The results show that the most 

_Proceedings of Copper

275 

common plugging agents are:  suspended solids in the leach solutions and especially “crud” generated in the solvent extraction plants that is present in the raffinate and accumulated in the internal paths of the emitters [1]. Other agents that have been recognized include sulfates of calcium, magnesium, and aluminum that crystalize outside of the drip lines [2], and even filamentous fungi closely related to the genus _Candida_ [3] has been proposed as a plugging component in one of our operations. The contributors for crud formation in SX plants is largely reported and include, among others, fine suspended solids in the PLS, degradation of the SX organic reagent and operational SX practices [4, 7]. 

However, the direct plugging agents are only one part of the issue. Some operational practices also contribute largely to plugging drip emitters. The most important of those aspects include: operating the irrigation systems below the operational pressures to which they were designed, poor and even nonexistent drip pipelines flushing practices, usage of make-up water with excessive suspended solids especially during rainy seasons and poor operating practices in SX plants such as pumping waste solutions with high suspended solids to leach operations via raffinate tanks or ponds, i.e. plant washing streams, poor “crud” removal practices and crud excursions that allow these emulsions to advance into the raffinate. 

Working at low raffinate drip line pressures is an operational practice that is more frequent than it appears and it is related to the availability of flow, the tendency to reduce irrigation flow rates in the last part of the leaching cycle, operational difficulties on distributing flows due to the lack of automatic systems, poor design of the irrigation system and deficient pressure monitoring practices.

Following a severe plugging event that occurred in one of our leaching sites, a complete study was carried out during several months and remediation practices implemented. The outcomes included the characterization of the plugging agents and most importantly the application of better operating practices that have allowed us to reduce the plugging rates to acceptable levels. The search for additional methodologies oriented to prevent plugging events is still in development at present and will be released in the future as a second part of this work. 

The characterization phase included the analysis of samples obtained from different points of the process:  raffinate solutions from the SX and leaching areas, flushed raffinate and solids from drip piping, plugged emitters and PLS samples. In order to compare the plugging agents, samples from different sites were also analyzed at the Freeport-McMoRan Technology Center in Arizona. The char

acterization techniques included:  X-Ray Diffraction (XRD), optical microscopy, Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy (EDS), Inductively Coupled Plasma (ICPOES/MS), and the determination of total suspended solids and total dissolved solids. The most relevant findings from the characterization process are summarized below [8-9]: 

- The predominant plugging agent found in both the leaching solution obtained by flushing the drip piping and the material accumulated inside the plugged emitters is basically “crud” as shown in Figure 2;

###### **PREVENTION PRACTICES** 

Preventing severe drip plugging events has been the ultimate goal of our leaching sites and the Technology Center. Prevention techniques currently being practiced in our operations include: planned plugging aud

its, pressure/flows monitoring, periodic flushing of drip lines, installation of transparent drip lines to visually monitor the progression of clogged emitters, and better SX plant practices to prevent crud and suspended solids being pumped to the leaching heaps. 

Plugging audits have been implemented at all of our leaching sites. A crew of leaching operators is scheduled to different leaching sections (randomly selected) and the drip emitters inspected and plugged drippers counted. 

To maintain a constant irrigation pressure in the leach sections a “pressure/flow skid”, shown in Figure 7, has been recently developed and successfully tested in one of our leaching sites. The skid monitors both flow and pressure with high accuracy. The pressure is regulated automatically and the data wirelessly reported in real time, in conjunction with the flow information, to ASPEN through a HART mesh network. The skid has proven to be effective and is currently in the process of being fully implemented at one of our largest leaching sites. In addition, the rates of plugging can be inferred from the pressure and flow information which reduces the labor intensity and subjectivity of manual plugging audits. 



Figure 7 – Skid for pressure and flow monitoring 

Flushing practices have also been proven to be effective to prevent drip plugging. Flushing is accomplished manually in most of our operations but also automatically in others; however, the current tendency is to implement an automatic flushing approach. In manual flushing, the discharge piping connected to the drip emitters is flushed regularly; normally every other day for a few minutes until the operator notices that the raffinate 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

280 

solution is clear. At the sites in which automatic flushing valves have been installed, the operation is done regularly every hour for a few minutes. In both cases, perforated piping or wobblers are installed at the end of the flushing pipe to prevent the erosion of the surface by the flushed solution. 

Clear drip lines are also installed at intervals among the HDPE lines to easily detect the evolution of drip emitters clogging. One of our operations has implemented, as a routine practice, the installation of 100% of clear drip lines with UV protection for heap leaching. 

Some effluents from the SX plants may contain solids in suspension as a product of the routine operation. Such effluents include SX/EW electrolytes obtained from spills, backwash solutions from electrolyte filters, etc., which normally are collected in intermediate tanks. In our operations, after a period of decantation, those solutions were pumped to the raffinate tanks and the decanted solids removed. However, on some occasions, solutions with solids in suspension and crud have contaminated the raff solutions and finally contributed to clogging the drip emitters in the leaching heaps. Currently, the practice of sending such tainted solutions is monito

red better and even those solutions are rerouted to certain sectors of the leach pads in order to avoid further plugging issues. 

In addition to the operational practices described above, metallurgical modifications were implemented in one of our leaching operations. At the end of 2011, a decision was made to change the sulfuric acid addition strategy. Originally most of the acid was added during the curing step (prior to leaching) and the remaining was added in the raffinate during the leaching cycle which resulted in high pH in the PLS due to the high acid consuming gangue of the ore. The new strategy basically consists of maintaining the same total acid addition but the proportion added during the leaching cycle has been raised up by increasing the concentration of acid in the raffinte. The change has resulted in the availability of free acid in the PLS from the fresh lift and subsequent extraction of residual copper from old lifts. The pH of the final PLS has dropped (pH~2.3) and free acid and iron in solution are now present. It is believed that this new acid addition strategy has also contributed to reducing the precipitation of gypsum and colloidal silica and, as a consequence, the reduction of suspended solids in the PLS and further formation of crud in the SX plant. 

The implementation of different types of filters in the leaching distribution pipe has not been successful. Screen filters, disc filters and others mostly similar than those used in agriculture irrigation systems were tested several times and plugged a few hours after having been installed. Self-cleaning filters have also been proven but with little success especially in leaching systems in which “crud” is the main plugging agent.

###### **RESULTS** 

As result of the operational and metallurgical practices, described in the previous section, the drip emitter plugging rates have been reduced. In most of our operations, plugging rates of 3-5% are being obtained. Figure 8 shows the plugging trends in two of our leaching operations at an average of 150 days under leaching. Normalized plugging rates are on the order of 0.02% plugged emitters per day under leach. 

Re-piping leaching sectors during the leaching cycle has been practically eliminated and is only occasionally practiced. Even when the plugging of drip emitters has not been reduced to larger extent, the leaching operating costs of previously affected sites have returned to normal values and the metallurgical outcomes are in alignment with our expected results. 

Current practices are still based on dealing with the plugging agents rather than preventing their formation. Consequently, new improvement opportunities are currently being investigated to prevent the formation of “crud” and reduce the presence of suspended solids in the leach solutions which have been identified as the main plugging agents in our leaching operations. Total suspended solids (TSS) and tu

rbidity are also being tracked in PLS and raff streams as routine practices.

###### **CONCLUSIONS** 

Crud produced in SX plants which migrates into leaching through raffinate streams as well as suspended solids in leaching solutions mainly from make-up water, have been identified as the major contributors of drip emitters plugging in FreeportMcMoRan Copper & Gold leaching operations. Other plugging agents that have been identified include fungus and solids coming from secondary operations of SX plants such as diatomaceous earth used as filtration media of the organic reagent. 

A combination of operating practices and metallurgical improvements in our operations have resulted in the reduction of drip emitter plugging. Operating leaching drip systems at the right pressure levels, periodic flushing of drip pipes, application of scheduled leaching maintenance practices, and better control of operation of the Leaching/SX plants are counted as the main operating practices that have contributed to reduce the rates of plugged drip emitters. 

Filters commonly used in irrigation systems have been tested without success to reduce plugging rates due to their rapid clogging with plugging agents and extensive required maintenance. 

Preventing the presence of main plugging agents such as crud and suspended solids in leaching solutions as well as the implementation of proven best practices among leaching sites is currently our focus at Freeport-McMoRan Copper & Gold.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Interest in exploiting low-grade and low quality copper ore deposits is increasing due to the growing copper demand and declining ore grades. Outotec has been active in developing hydrometallurgical copper processing technologies and is now launching a novel and sustainable technology suitable for treatment of wide variety of copper containing feed materials, especially for primary copper sulfides with gold and silver content. 

The technology is based on atmospheric reactor leaching after which copper, silver and gold are purified with solvent extraction. Copper is recovered as LME A grade cathode in electrowinning. Gold and silver can be recovered from purified streams with reduction, cementation or precipitation. 

Process has been tested in bench-pilot scale with high extractions in both leaching and metals recovery circuits. Process technology has been engineered and standard, readily available and proven equipment can be utilized. Materials of construction are well defined and tested in industrial scale.

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

World primary copper production is currently 18 million tons annually and a major

part is produced utilizing sulfidic raw materials [1]. Smelting and electrorefining are the main technology and chalcopyrite the dominant copper mineral. About 20 % of the total copper production is based on oxidic resources where copper is produced by heap leaching, solvent extraction and electrowinning [1]. Good quality ore bodies are becoming scarce and oxidic ores are depleting. Impurities in feed materials are increasing and oxidic copper operations will be converted into sulfide mineral processing in the future. 

Outotec has been following up these trends closely and technology development has been directed to meet the future challenges in copper production industry. Hydrometallurgical chloride based processing has been identified to be a very potential option to directly treat copper bearing sulfide feed materials, especially chalcopyrite. 

This paper presents the key features of Outotec’s latest innovation regarding the hydrometallurgical copper processing. The main driver for the development has been the need for hydrometallurgical refining method with following characteristics: 

- Process needs to be suitable to process wide variety of feed materials in terms of copper grade, impurity concentrations and mineralogy. 

- Precious metals recovery (gold and silver) is an integral part of the process. 

- Processing technology has to be based on proven technical solutions, unit processes and equipment. 

- Process needs to be robust, inherently safe and deliver excellent environmental performance. 

- Metallurgical performance should be high in terms of metal recovery and finished product quality. 

- Technology should be suitable for retrofits e.g. for existing heap leach – SX – EW operation, which are converting to sulfides processing. 

###### **PROCESS DESCRIPTION** 

Outotec’s chloride based process for copper refining is suitable for varied copper concentrates. It has been designed especially for primary sulfides such as chalcopyrite and bornite but it is also suitable for more easily leachable secondary sulfides such as chalcocite, covellite and digenite. Copper concentrate is leached in atmospheric conditions and chalcopyrite passivation is avoided by chlorides in the leach solution. Dreisinger [2] has reviewed proposed processes in literature for chalcopyrite leaching and they generally utilize either pressure leaching with or without a small amount of chlorides, ultrafine grinding or high chloride concentration. Materials selection and equipment design are in central role in every industrial project in order to build successful operation. This applies also on chloride hydrometallurgical technologies. Outotec has been working with chloride technologies for decades and has accumulated large amount of information and knowledge about material selection and equipment engineering. This work includes the operation of a demonstration plant for about two years in Outotec Research Center in Pori, Finland. During this operation industrial scale equipment (reactors, agitators, tanks, thickeners, filter, pumps, heat exchangers, instruments, etc.) were operated in real process conditions. Based on this experience a material specification documentation has been created for hydrometallurgical chloride processing technologies in general and also specifically for copper processing. Suitable and cost effective materials for the equipment can be selected from various polymers, plastics and composites. ###### **EXPERIMENTAL** 

The main steps of the process were demonstrated in a bench scale pilot at Outotec Research Center. The experimental settings consisted of copper and silver leaching, copper solvent extraction, copper electrowinning and silver solvent extraction. 

###### **Materials** 

A copper concentrate was used as the feed material. The concentrate contained 29.6 % Cu, 30.6 % Fe, 33.4 % S, 2.18 % Zn and 0.38 % Pb. Practically all copper was in chalcopyrite. Other main minerals were pyrite, sphalerite, pyrrhotite and galena. The concentrate used in the pilot had particle size of p80 71 µm

and p50 31 µm. 

###### **Equipment** 

The leaching area consisted of a pulping reactor and 4-5 leaching reactors. The effective volume of the pulping reactor was 1 L and its pH and temperature were not controlled. The effective volume of the first leaching reactor was 3 L and the rest leaching reactors were 5 L each. The concentrate was continuously fed to the pulping reactor with a vibrating feeder in one hour batches. Oxygen was fed under a mixer in all the leaching reactors. Temperature was 95<sup>o</sup> C and pH targets were 1.7 and later 2.2. pH was controlled in the first reactor with acidic raffinate from solvent extraction and any excess raffinate was fed to the second leaching reactor. pH in other reactors was controlled with concentrated sulfuric acid or calcium hydroxide slurry. Reactors also contained a reflux condenser and water feed to compensate the evaporated amount. After leaching the slurry was filtered and filtrate was fed to copper solvent extraction. 

Glass mixer-settlers were used in solvent extraction with 0.21 L mixers and 1L settlers. The settlers had a band heater and the temperature in mixers varied

###### **ABSTRACT** 

As replacement production from global refined copper rises, the need for producers to find cost effective ways to develop copper porphyry deposits is becoming increasingly important. For example, brownfield projects in South America with depleting heap leach production but with an underlying sulphide deposit represent an opportunity to integrate concentrate leaching with existing solvent extraction and electrowinning infrastructure to establish value added on-site metal production as an alternative to conventional concentrate sales. This option can accelerate the delivery of metal to market while avoiding permitting and cost issues related to long slurry pipelines. Over the last 20 years, Teck Resources Limited (“Teck”) has been at the forefront of developing copper pressure leaching technology, known as the CESL Process, which has been tested at an industrial scale and has the potential to achieve cost competitive cathode production while effectively handling impurities in concentrates which render them difficult to market. This paper highlights the successful development history of Teck’s copper pressure leaching technology while providing standard operating parameters and resulting metallurgical performance from a range of primary copper sulphide concentrates tested. A conceptual level case study is presented to assess the integration of a commercial pressure leach circuit with existing SX/EW infrastructure. The technical, economic, environmental and social value-added benefits of thi

s alternative will be compared to conventional concentrate marketing to smelters.

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Teck has developed extensive hydrometallurgical and pyrometallurgical expertise at its mining and smelting-refining operations in the production and processing of a variety of base- and precious-metal concentrates to recover a range of metals including copper, nickel, cobalt, zinc, lead, germanium, indium, silver and gold. Over the past 20 years Teck has invested in the development of Cu, Cu-Ni, Cu-Au, Cu-Mo and Cu-Zn hydrometallurgical processes collectively known as the CESL Processes which are patented and proprietary to Teck.  These technologies have been rigorously tested and developed and are being evaluated for various commercialization opportunities. Teck’s CESL hydromet group, located in Richmond, BC is focused on developing hydrometallurgical solutions which create value for Teck’s mining operations, undeveloped mining projects or partners’ operations and projects. 

This paper focuses on highlighting the successful development of Teck’s CESL Copper Process including its consistent metallurgical and operating performance achieved through several comprehensive technical programs and projects. A strong case for its use as a capital efficient alternative to conventional concentrate sales is in the integration of concentrate leaching technology with existing solvent extraction and electrowinning infrastructure for on-site metal production. Several key value creating benefits realized through this application is highlighted. 

###### **BACKGROUND** 

Global copper mine supply is largely sourced from primary sulphide mineralization (~80%) which is mined and processed to copper concentrates using conventional flotation technology [12]. Despite sizeable capital investments and lengthy permitting challenges, high-pressure slurry pipelines have proven to be an economically viable means for long distance, cross country transportation of concentrate from remote mine site locations to port facilities where material is dewatered and shipped to downstream processing markets, the majority of which are offshore [1,6]. In spite of evermore stringent environmental standards on pyrometallurigcal process emissions and management of waste materials, smelting and refining technology remains the industry standard for treating traditional copper concentrates as it is an energy efficient and low cost process [12]. 

Supergene mineralization makes up the balance (~20%) of global copper mine supply and it is processed and refined through hydrometallurgical heap leaching-solvent extraction-electrowining technology to produce saleable cathodes. The case for adopting hydrometallurgical leaching technology for primary sulphides, particularly minerals such as chalcopyrite, has been in development for over 40 years [10]. To date, several hydrometallurgical leaching technologies have gained acceptance in niche

situations such as those where concentrates are not amenable to modern smelting and refining technology due to complex mineralogy or the presence of deleterious elements such as arsenic. That said, in order for hydrometallurgical leaching of traditional copper 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

299 

concentrates to be considered a viable alternative to smelting and refining, future applications of innovative leaching technologies not only need to be cost competitive in order to pay back their required capital investment, they should also be beneficial from a community and sustainable development perspective which in many cases they have shown significant potential for generating environmental and social value-added benefits. 

Underinvestment in previous years coupled with strong copper demand from large emerging market economies such as China has resulted in the recent expansion in capital projects [1]. Unfortunately a real industry challenge has been rising development costs which have seen an average escalation of ~20% (from 2004 to 2012) largely due to a number of contributing factors including substantial infrastructure requirements, shortage of skilled labour, higher raw material input costs, increased environmental and community costs associated with new projects [1]. As a result, the need for producers to find capital efficient solutions for the development of new copper porphyry deposits is becoming increasingly important to the success of the industry. Integrating concentrate leaching technology with existing solvent extraction and electrowinning infrastructure for on-site cathode production offers a cost competitive alternative to conventional concentrate sales with additional value-added benefits to be realized. Several existing copper mining operations in South America have depleting heap leach reserves with large underlying sulphide deposits [1]. Projects such as these represent a potentially attractive opportunity to implement Teck’s CESL Copper Process. 

The CESL Copper Process is as a medium temperature pressure leach for sulphide concentrates in the presence of chloride catalytic ions (12 g/L). In most cases a light regrind of the mill concentrate is necessary to reduce particle size. Grinding the concentrate increases the surface area of the particles which improves the oxidation and recovery of the copper minerals in an autoclave. Using high purity oxygen sparging, copper minerals are oxidized in an autoclave at 150 °C and 200 psi. The oxidized minerals are leached into solution in an autoclave or from the pressure oxidation solids with acidic raffinate at atmospheric conditions depending on the pyrite content in the concentrate. Sulphur in the concentrate is primarily oxidized to elemental sulphur instead of sulphate. The presence of chloride in the autoclave helps to increase the rate of reaction and reduce sulphur oxidation. The low sulphur oxidation achieved in the process decreases operating and capital co

sts, and thus allows for economic recovery of metals [5]. Excess sulphate (acid) is removed from the process through neutralization and gypsum production. Following pressure oxidation, the slurry from the autoclave is discharged into a standard pressure letdown system. A thickener followed by filtration separates the pregnant leach solution (PLS) from the leach residue. PLS is sent to the copper solvent extraction circuit for selective copper recovery using a commercial organic extractant. The extractant is loaded with copper and then washed to remove entrained chloride and impurities. After washing the organic, the copper on the extractant is stripped into a pure copper electrolyte, providing the feed to copper electrowinning. LME Grade A copper cathodes (99.999% Cu) are produced under conventional electrowinning conditions. _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 300 An evaporator is used to maintain the plant water balance. Any water additions to the plant that are in excess of the flash steam from pressure oxidation, the evaporation from heated tanks, or the entrained solution in the solids, must be removed by the evaporator as condensate to ensure a stable plant balance. These water additions include grinding water, reagent makeup water, and wash solutions. Figure 1 provides a simplified diagram of the CESL Copper Process. Oxygen

Through the use of the CESL Gold Process, economic recovery (≥ 90%) of precious metals has been demonstrated on numerous concentrates [10]. ###### **Copper Recovery** The pressure leaching of sulphide concentrates produces copper concentrations in _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 304 the PLS (Pregnant Leach Solution) that are higher (~40 - 50 g/L Cu) than typical heap leach operations. The integration of pressure leaching into a heap leach operation with depleted reserves allows for the utilization of existing solvent extraction and electrowinning circuits by increasing reagent concentration to allow for increased delta copper requirements. The integration is highly flexible in terms of what commercial extractant is used, as various industry leading reagents have been thoroughly demonstrated on continuous piloting by Teck’s hydromet group [9]. Through extensive testing of various concentrates, configuration of the solvent extraction circuit can be varied from one to four separate stages (each operating with two counter current mixer/settlers) of extraction dependent on the concentrate grade, mineralogy, and whether there are existing mixer-settler trains at the brownfield site to integrate the pressure leaching circuit. Each configuration contains a wash stage to scrub off any chloride that may be entrained in the organic solution and small amounts of iron that are chemically loaded on the organic. The organic is stripped in a two stage

counter current process. 

Copper electrolyte produced from solvent extraction contains minimal impurities such as iron at less than 300 ppm, allows for high current efficiency and lower operating costs to be achieved in the cellhouse. Due to the high purity of the advanced electrolyte, cathodes produced are higher than LME Grade A specifications, forecast to achieve 99.999% purity for a wide range of copper concentrate quality.

###### **CONCEPTUAL CASE STUDY** 

This section presents a conceptual level case study to assess the integration of a commercial CESL concentrate leach plant with existing solvent extraction and electrowinning (SX/EW) infrastructure. A financial assessment is provided comparing on-site cathode production, and shipping by truck versus building a 150km concentrate pipeline with dewatering, storage and handling facilities at a nearby existing port to receive concentrate and then ship to traditional downstream smelting and refining markets in Asia. 

For this conceptual case study, it is assumed that supergene mineralization for a heap leaching-solvent extraction-electrowining operation with up to 150,000 tpa cathode production is nearing the end of its resource life and will soon transition to a sulphide concentrator project. Located in a major South American copper producing district, the open pit sulphide operation is expected to produce up to 150,000 tpa of contained copper in concentrate at an average grade of 30% for greater than 30 years.  The mine site cash costs (mine/mill/SG&A) are assumed to average $1.25/lb Cu while the sustaining capital for the mine is estimated at $75M/year. These mine site operating figures will be the same for either of the investment options being evaluated. 

The capital cost for development of the mine/mill is not taken into consideration, as the evaluation focuses on the trade-off between on-site cathode production and concentrate sales; the required mine/mill investment would be the same in either case. The analysis thus considers the capital and operating costs of either: 

- (1) Concentrate pipeline, dewatering and associated port facilities; or 

(2) Concentrate leach, solvent-extraction and electrowinning

- Establishing several new highly skilled jobs in-country through the construction of a concentrate leach plant while sustaining several skilled jobs by maintaining the existing SX/EW operations for the duration of the project. 

- Increased local employment will strengthen the local economy and add to the government tax revenue to help build additional capacity in country. 

- Enhanced worker health and safety conditions through the application of a new mine-to-metal hydrometallurgical solution with no hazardous gaseous emissions or fugitive dusts as seen in some pyrometallurgical facilities. 

- Delivery of value added copper cathode to market sooner while improving overall product stewardship and environmental performance through the processing of concentrates including those with elevated heavy-metals (such as Sb, As, Cd, Hg) and management of waste materials at a single industrial site. 

- Reduced demand on fresh water usage through the flexible use of seawater, brine or gray water as process water in the copper leaching plant.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Sherritt Technologies recently completed a test program to evaluate the application of pressure oxidation technology to the treatment of copper sulphide concentrate generated from ore produced at Codelco’s Radomiro Tomic mine, located near Calama, Chile.  The testwork included an eight-day pilot plant campaign, comprising continuous, integrated operation of pressure leaching, counter-current decantation washing, leach liquor neutralization, solvent extraction, raffinate neutralization and electrowinning circuits.  The main copper-bearing minerals in Radomiro Tomic concentrate are chalcopyrite and bornite, and the pilot plant feed contained 38% Cu, 22% Fe and 28% S.  Copper extraction in pressure leaching was 98.5 to 99%, recovery of copper in the wash circuit was >99.5% and there was no measurable precipitation of copper in the neutralization circuits. ###### **INTRODUCTION** 

The Corporaciуn Nacional del Cobre de Chile (Codelco) owns and operates the Radomiro Tomic mine and processing plant, located near Calama, Chile.  Current production is about 300 000 t/y Cu from copper oxide ores using heap leach-solvent extraction-electrowinning technology [1]. In high temperature pressure leaching of copper concentrate, sulphide sulphur in the concentrate is almost completely oxidized to sulphate sulphur with oxygen, by the following reactions. 







Ferrous (Fe<sup>2+</sup> ) iron is oxidized to ferric (Fe<sup>3+</sup> ) iron (Reaction 4), and most of the

ferric iron precipitates as hematite (Reaction 5).

###### **ABSTRACT** 

The flowrate of leaching solution across a porous medium mainly affected by mainly affected gravitational forces will depend on a number of factors related to the physical and chemical properties of the porous material. These factors are often evaluated and reported under saturated conditions but in practical heap or dump leaching systems the saturation appears to be highly variable. Therefore, v

ariables associated with the porous materials such as permeability, hydraulic conductivity, soil-water characteristic curve and suction must take into account unsaturated soil conditions. This research work aims at correlating the experimental liquid retention capacity measured in column leach at laboratory scale with results derived from simulations using classic soil mechanics tools. The simulations were performed with the software SVFlux® and emphasis was made in assessing the impact of soil-water characteristic curve (SWCC) on the liquid retention capacity in transient and steady state conditions. Results indicated that there is a non-linear kinetic behavior of the retention capacity, nevertheless, the steady state liquid retention capacity value referred to the overall volume of solids stored in the column stayed relatively constant when changing the column internal diameter.

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

The industrial hydrometallurgy of copper is nowadays facing one of the most challenging times in its history. Copper oxides, known to work well in heap or dump leaching operations, are less frequently found in mine sites and the copper extraction is becoming strongly related to secondary and primary copper sulphide minerals which have promoted the implementation of concentrators rather than hydrometallurgical plants. From an economical perspective, the productivity of copper mine sites estimated by the output per hour worked is highly variable among the mine sites in the world; however, in Chile the trends points out a constant decline over the last few years [1]. One way to increase such productivity involves increasing the output levels. In other words, increase the rate at which copper is extracted. In order to accomplish an increase of copper production rate, there are a number of challenges to be faced. 

Authors agree the main issues behind increasing the copper production via hydrometallurgy are inherently linked to physical aspects of heaps and dumps [2,3]. The leaching process obeys a stoichiometry defined by the ore composition. Increasing the leaching agent concentration may lead to trigger undesirable reactions between the leaching agent and the gangue material in the heap or dump [4]. Then, one option would be to increase the dripping flowrate of leaching agent per unit of surface area [5]. This aspect has been scarcely addressed in the scientific literature and usually it is limited to measurements of permeability of the porous media or numerical simulations [6,7]. In the case of heap or dumps, the permeability is often estimated under saturated conditions which are not the actual industrial operation conditions [8,9]. In these cases, the estimation of permeability in unsaturated porous media conditions would be most appropriate [10, 13]. Only a few research works address the study of heap or dump leaching operation from this perspective either via performing column leach test

s or carrying out numerical simulations [14]. This aspect has been extensively studied in the field of mechanics of unsaturated soils [15-17]. A brief review of this topic will be presented in the following section (for a complete review of this topic, please see [15]). 

###### **Unsaturated soil phenomena** 

Unsaturated soil phenomena take place when a porous structure, such as that formed during ore agglomeration, is partially filled with water and leaving the remaining voids in the structure filled with air. Such variable wetting will define how the aqueous phase will interact with the solid [15]. Three major variables can be identified as key to understand how the fluid dynamics of an aqueous phase will behave in porous unsaturated media: (i) soil porosity, (ii) saturation parameters, and (iii) soil-watercharacteristic curve (SWCC) and hydraulic conductivity [15,16].

###### **(ii) Saturation parameters** 

Saturation parameters are used in unsaturated soil phenomena as significant figures  from which unsaturated parameters are usually determined or referred to. ###### **ABSTRACT** 

During copper electrorefining, precious metals as well as valuable metals such as selenium or tellurium accumulate in the anode slime. Anode slime leaching at Aurubis, carried out with sulphuric acid under oxidative conditions, aims mainly at the extraction of copper and nickel. Precious metals and selenium are intended to stay in the residue for further treatment by oxidative smelting. Depending on the concentrates, the resulting anode slimes have different compositions and leaching behaviours. Regarding anode slime treatment, atmospheric leaching and pressure leaching can be performed. While pressure leaching usually leads to very low copper contents in the residue, it is also more challenging in terms of mai

ntenance and safety. On the other hand, additives can be used to enhance the extraction rates during atmospheric leaching. Here we report the leaching rates of several elements such as Cu and Ni depending on different process parameters, e.g. temperature, sulphuric acid concentration and oxygen partial pressure.

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

The production of copper involves the smelting of copper ores, concentrates, or recycling materials to produce copper anodes [1]. Impurities in the copper containing educts are extensively reduced by using the appropriate smelting conditions. However, the copper anodes still contain 1-2 % impurities and will be refined by electrolysis. During copper electrorefining, the anodes are dissolved, at which copper enters the sulfuric acid based electrolyte. Driven by the potential difference between anode and cathode, the copper ions move towards the cathode and are deposited as metallic copper. Elements present in the anode with a lower redox potential than the Cu/Cu<sup>2+</sup> couple (i.e., nickel, iron, arsenic) are oxidized and remain in solution, whereas elements with a higher redox potential (i.e., the precious metals) remain unaffected and sink to the bottom of the electrolysis cell [2]. Nevertheless, further reactions of the dissolved elements lead to the formation of insoluble compounds (i.e., PbSO4, Bi/Sb arsenates) which also settle to the bottom of the cell [3]. The sum of insoluble compounds formed during the refinery electrolysis is called anode slime. 

Anode slime is an important intermediate, since it contains the valuable metals such as precious metals, selenium, and tellurium. In addition, it still contains a considerable amount of copper. On the other hand, anode slime can be regarded as an outlet for impurities such as arsenic, antimony, and bismuth. 

Anode slime can be treated by pyrometallurgical methods, hydrometallurgical methods, or a combination of both of them to recover the valuable metals, and to discharge impurities [4-8]. For example, at the pyrometallurgical route, roasting procedures are often used to recover selenium [9,10]. Hydrometallurgical methods include leaching with acidic (i.e., HCl [11], H2SO4 [4]) or basic (i.e., NH3 [12], NaOH [13], KOH [14]) media to extract the desired element. A lot of research has been done in the past to identify the best leaching conditions for a certain anode slime. Parameters, such as temperature, leaching medium, time, concentration, and the application of additives have been investigated. Since 1960 pressure leaching instead of atmospheric leaching has become more important, due to better copper extraction rates and shortened processing times [6,15]. 

In the next chapter we report the influence of process parameters on anode slime leaching at Aurubis Hamburg. 

###### **ANODE SLIME LEACHING TESTS AT AURUBIS HAMBURG** 

Anode slime leaching at Aurubis Hamburg is performed in sulfuric acid (4

00 g/l) at 75 °C while passing oxygen into the solution. Under these conditions, the extraction rates of copper and nickel are about 90 and 50 %, respectively, selenium is leached by about 20 %, and silver is not leached at all. The copper content in the residue after leaching is about 3-5 %. To improve the extraction rates for copper and nickel, pressure leaching tests were performed with an autoclave in laboratory scale. The operating volume of the autoclave is four liters. Inside, a quartz container is placed to protect the stainless steel inner body of the autoclave from corrosion. An indirect heating with water as the transfer medium allows for temperatures up to 200 °C. Different gases (i.e. oxygen, nitrogen, argon) can be applied. Parameters, such

###### **SUMMARY** 

Pressure leaching of anode slime of Aurubis Hamburg was performed at laboratory scale to investigate the influence of different process parameters, such as temperature, acid concentration, and oxygen partial pressure on the extraction rate of copper, nickel, selenium, and silver. Most significant is the temperature. At temperatures ≥ 150 °C the extraction rates of copper and nickel are ≥ 99 %. Likewise, the leaching rates of selenium and silver increase significantly if the temperature is raised from 120 °C to 150 °C or even 200 °C. The variation of the sulfuric acid concentration in the range of 300 to 500 g/l has only a minor effect. The same is true for the oxygen partial pressure. Increasing the oxygen partial pressure from 5 to 8 bar shows no improvement in the leaching rates. On the contrary, successful leaching of Cu and Ni is also observed, when no oxygen is supplied during the leaching process. The same extraction rates as for leaching with oxygen were obtained. Even if the oxygen is completely substituted by an inert gas, extraction rates of 99 % for copper, and of 40 % for nickel were observed, however at prolonged leaching time. Additives, such as SeO2, PbO2, or MnO2 showed no improvement with respect to the extraction rates of nickel, selenium, and silver (copper was always ≥ 99 %).

###### **ABSTRACT** 

The Arctic Platinum Project, or APP, located in northern Finland includes a number of shallow Cu-Ni-PGM (platinum group metal) deposits.  The processing route currently under investigation for extraction of the metal values involves bulk sulphide flotation followed by hydrometallurgical treatment of the concentrate using the Platsol™ process.  The major processing steps include: crushing, milling and flotation of a bulk concentrate, chloride assisted total pressure oxidation of the concentrate for extraction of base and precious metals, reduction and precipitation of

PGEs from the autoclave solution, partial neutralization followed by copper SX-EW for production of copper cathode and nickel and cobalt recovery by mixed hydroxide precipitation from the Cu SX raffinate.  The processes have been extensively tested at SGS Minerals Services’ laboratories in Lakefield, Canada at both lab and pilot plant scale.  The overall process flowsheet, chemistry and bench and pilot plant test data will be presented covering both the flotation and hydrometallurgical processes.

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Platinum group metals (PGMs; platinum, palladium, rhodium, ruthenium, iridium and osmium) are traditionally recovered from their ores by production of a high-grade concentrate by flotation and/or gravity concentration, followed by smelting of the concentrate.  Concentrates are smelted to remove non-sulphide minerals and converted to remove iron and sulphur.  The resulting high PGM grade matte is processed hydrometallurgically to leach the base metals, leaving a residue with a very high (2040%) PGM concentration for final refining to individual PGMs.  Due to the complexity of this process and its high capital cost, it can only be applied economically to high grade PGM ores.  Lower grade PGM concentrates might be saleable to commercial copper or nickel smelters, but may not yield attractive payment terms for the PGMs. 

The Portimo and Narkaus mafic intrusions in northern Finland hosts several shallow low grade base and PGM deposits and Gold Fields is working to develop the Arctic Platinum Project (APP) there.  Earlier studies have failed to yield an economically viable project based on traditional processing. 

In the late 1990’s and early 2000’s the Platsol™ process was developed at SGS in Lakefield, Ontario (at the time Lakefield Research Limited) for the NorthMet deposit (near Duluth Minnesota, USA) owned by PolyMet Mining.  The process developed was a high temperature chloride-assisted pressure oxidation process capable of simultaneously dissolving the base metals (Cu, Ni, Co, Zn), gold and the PGMs. 

This paper discusses recent testwork involving the Platsol™ process for the development of a flowsheet for APP. 

###### **ARTIC PLATINUM PROJECT - FINLAND** 

The Arctic Platinum Project is located approximately 60 kilometers south of the city of Rovaniemi in northern Finland. APP is assessing a number of shallow Cu, Ni, PGM deposits located within the Portimo and Narkaus mafic layered intrusions.  Starting in January 2000, the initial exploration and project development focus was on the Konttijarvi (KJV) and Ahmavaara (AHM) deposits, collectively referred to as the Suhanko Project.  Gold Fields completed a mill – float – smelter feasibility study for the Suhanko Project in the third quarter of fiscal 2005 and, based on the results of the study, decided to postpone the development of a 10 Mtpa surface mining complex. 

In 2009, Gold Fields investigated Platsol™ hydrometall

urgical processing, as an alternative to off-site contract smelting, for the recovery of copper, nickel, gold and PGM from Suhanko flotation concentrates. The initial metallurgical tests in 2009 returned positive results.  Further engineering work was conducted to provide indicative operating and capital cost estimates for hydrometallurgical processing on a commercial scale at Suhanko. 

Gold Fields proceeded to integrated Platsol™ pilot plant testwork in 2011. A total of 100 tonnes of sample were collected from purpose drilled core holes comprising 50tonne samples from each of Konttijarvi (KJV) and Ahmavaara (AHM). Samples were processed to concentrate at the pilot flotation plant operated by GTK Outokumpu in

###### **MINERAL PROCESSING OF APP ORES** 

Production of concentrate from the APP ores involves bulk sulphide flotation. The major sulphide minerals in the orebody are chalcopyrite, pentlandite, pyrrhotite and pyrite.  The ores are dominated by silicate minerals and contain naturally floatable minerals such as amphiboles, chlorites and especially talc.  Previous testwork on spatial domains of the KJV and AHM deposits has shown that the content of talc can vary from 2% to 15% of the mineral mass for KJV and 1.3% to 18% of the mineral mass for AHM. For these same domains, the sulphide minerals also varied significantly from 1.3% to 2.5% for KJV and 1.5% to 6.1% for AHM.  Owing to the sheer volume of MgO bearing minerals that contain Ni displaced in the crystal structure, the recovery of nickel by flotation is highly variable and often quite low.  In the previous mineralogical study, the proportion of Ni contained in the sulphide minerals (i.e. in pentlandite, pyrrhotite and chalcopyrite) ranged from 39.6% to 77.2% of the Ni for KJV and 40.9% to 80.0% for AHM.  Unlike nickel, the vast majority of the copper is contained in the sulphide minerals which are recoverable by flotation. 

The main flotation reagents used include xanthate, AERO 3477 dithiophosphate, silicate gangue depressant (carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) or guar) and frother (methyl isobutyl carbinol (MIBC)).  The selection of the best xanthate has been troublesome. Use of a strong xanthate, isobutyl or amyl, is generally desired for strong collection power, but the sulphide minerals (especially copper minerals) are prone to overcollection, which produces a sticky froth that can be difficult to recover.  The persistence

of the frother and higher water recovery make attaining concentrate grade difficult.   Using lower dosage and/or a weaker xanthate such as isopropyl improves this situation, but recovery is lower. 

The Platsol<sup>TM</sup> process feed grade requirement is fairly modest, and a concentrate sulphide grade of 8-10% can be processed quite readily. Therefore, very little cleaning is required following rougher flotation. The flowsheet used during the 2011 GTK pilot plant and shown in Figure 1 [1] was based on testwork conducted at SGS Lakefield. This flowsheet was developed on the basis that the fast floating material recovered in the first rougher flotation interval advances to final concentrate.  This was expected to limit interference of the slow floating material floated in the later rougher stages during cleaner flotation.  The first rougher flotation stage (Ro 1) consisted of a single 0.15 m<sup>3</sup> Outotec style flotation cell, while the later rougher flotation stages consisted of two banks of two 0.5 m<sup>3</sup> Outotec style flotation cells (Ro 2-5).  Since the required rougher residence time was met using three of the 0.5 m<sup>3</sup> cells, the concentrate from the last cell of the bank was recirculated to Ro 2.  The concentrate from Ro 2-4 was advanced to the

###### **THE PLATSOL™ PROCESS** 

The Platsol™ process has been well described elsewhere [2-4] and will be reviewed briefly here.  Platsol™ is a single step, high temperature pressure leaching process. It was developed at SGS Lakefield in 1998 for PolyMet’s NorthMet Project. The key feature of the Platsol™ process is that it is a total pressure oxidation process with chloride added to solution to solubilize PGMs.  Base metals sulphides are completely oxidized with oxygen to generate soluble metal sulphates, iron hydrolysis products and sulphuric acid, while gold, platinum and palladium are dissolved and stabilized as chlorocomplexes by the presence of chloride in solution. The addition of a small amount of chloride ion to the solution at high autoclave temperature (> 200<sup>°</sup> C) represents an incremental change in autoclave chemistry that effectively allows recovery of all the metals of value in a single processing step.

A process flow diagram for the Platsol™ process is shown in Figure 3.  To control the water balance, feed concentrate generally be thickened and filtered then repulped in recycled copper SX raffinate and chloride laden process water.  The autoclave discharge will either be directly filtered or thickened then filtered and the washed autoclave residue will go to the hydromet tailings facility.  Platsol™ pregnant leach solution (PLS) will advance to PGM recovery after ferric iron is reduced by adding sulphur dioxide.  PGMs are recovered from solution by precipitation using sodium hydrosulphide or on copper sulphide (CuS), which may be generated by treating a PLS slip stream with NaHS.  The PGM-bearing CuS concentrate is then thickened and filtered and the PLS, now free of PGMs, is partially neutralized to pH ~2 with ground limestone. Copper is extracted from the PLS by conventional solvent extraction with an oxime extractant.  Loaded organic is scrubbed and then stripped and copper metal is electrowon from the strip liquor.  The raffinate from CuSX is split and a portion is recycled to the autoclave feed to build up the concentration of nickel, and as a source of acid (if needed) and chloride ions. The balance advances to the nickel recovery circuit where the acid generated in CuSX is first neutralized with limestone and iron and aluminum are precipitated from solution by raising the pH to 4-5.  The purified liquor advances to nickel and cobalt recovery by mixed-hydroxide precipitation or precipitation of some other intermediate product, such as mixed sulphide.

###### <u>Partial Neutralization</u> 

PGM barren solution was passed through a 0.5 µm filter and advanced to the partial neutralization circuit, where it was adjusted to pH 2 by the addition of 25wt% limestone slurry in a series of four tanks at 60°C.  Metal losses to the gypsum cake that was produced were negligible for gold, PGMs, copper, nickel, cobalt and zinc.  The essentially pure gypsum solids settled and filtered very well during all pilot campaigns, without the need for flocculant.  Limestone consumptions for the campaigns processing AHM and KJV concentrates were 151 and 56 kg/t feed concentrate, respectively, which were essentially stoichiometric additions based on the free acidity of the autoclave discharge PLS. 

###### <u>Copper Solvent Extraction & Electrowinning</u> 

The copper solvent extraction circuit was set up with six mixer-settler stages that were operated at 40ºC.  There were three stages of countercurrent extraction, one scrubbing stage and two countercurrent stages for stripping the loaded organic.  The electrowinning cell contained three Pb/Ca/Sn alloy anodes and two stainless steel cathodes.  The EW cell was controlled at 40ºC and contained 54 L of electrolyte with another 10-15 L held in a recirculation reservoir.  Solution was recirculated continuously from the reservoir to the cell and back at 15 L/min so the cell contents turned over every 4 minutes.  The extractant mixture used was 30vol% Acorga<sup>®</sup> M5640 oxime extractant from Cytec diluted with Exxon's Exxsol<sup>®</sup> D80 aliphatic diluent.  In the scrubbing stage, loaded organic was contacted with a bleed of spent electrolyte and deionized water to control chloride carryover to EW.  Stripping was accomplished with spent electrolyte and strip liquor forwarded to EW through 2 coalescers which prevented any organic contamination of the electrolyte.
