Batch Platsol™ Testwork Additional Platsol™ optimization testwork has been undertaken to improve PGM extraction and reduce the autoclave residence time. Testwork was also focused on stabilizing PGMs in solution after autoclaving to maximize overall PGM recovery to the _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 365 PGM concentrate. To this end, about 35 batch tests were conducted on the KJV concentrate produced in a flotation pilot plant at Lakefield in December 2012. This work has shown that by increasing the temperature in the autoclave to 230-240ºC and/or increasing the Cl concentration to 20 g/L the precious metal extractions from the KJV concentrate can be increased to ~95% Au, 80-85% Pt and 90-95% Pd in an autoclave residence time of only 1 hour. These recoveries are significantly higher than those achieved in the PP3 pilot campaign, particularly for Au and Pd. Moreover, it was shown that the problems with partial re-precipitation of precious metals (gold in particular) in the autoclave discharge were eliminated by ensuring a sufficiently high free acidity, at the higher chloride concentrations and by oxidizing any residual ferrous iron post autoclave. Base metal extractions in the bench work, at ~99% for Cu and ~96% for Ni, were also consistently 2-3% higher under these more aggressive conditions than in the PP3 pilot plant. ###### **CONCLUSIONS** 

A hydrometallurgical approach to treating APP concentrates following bulk flotation of Cu, Ni, Co, Au, Pt, Pd values is being developed utilizing the Platsol™ process.  The Platsol™ process solubilizes base and precious metals values in a single step involving pressure oxidative leaching with high levels of extraction,. ###### **INCORPORATING THE EFFECT OF ORE MINERALOGY AND DATA UNCERTAINTY ON THE INTERPRETATION OF FULLY FLOODED LEACHING KINETICS USING THE SHRINKING CORE MODEL**

###### **ABSTRACT** 

The classic shrinking core model has been widely used to analyse and to interpret experimental kinetics leaching data. The model has marveled not only by its simplicity when it is applied to experimental data but also by its strength towards interpreting data allowing unveiling the governing mechanisms involved in the metal extraction process. Nevertheless, two aspects have not been incorporated in the analysis: the ore mineralogy and the inherent uncertainty derived from the very use of the model. The aim of this research is to incorporate the effect of mineralogy and the inherent uncertainty of the use of the model and to apply these concepts to column leach data. On one hand, the presence of one or more copper-bearing minerals in the ore having different reactivities is expected to distort the recovery vs time curve. This effect is accounted for by determining fast and slow leaching components using a modified Imaizumi and Inoue (1963) experimental data analysis. On the other hand, the evaluation of the model uncertainties derived from the measuring variables is considered by using the error by propagation analysis. These two aspects will ultimately set the boundaries for predicting the metal leaching extraction. Finally, incorporating these two aspects onto the data interpretation would procure a more realistic scenario to understand, interpret and predict leaching kinetic data.

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

###### **The shrinking core model (SCM) and the ore leaching process** 

The shrinking core model (SCM) is a simple mathematical model commonly used to describe the leaching kinetics of an individual particle. The SCM, developed by Yagi & Kunii (1955), was originally used to model fluidized reactors with solid particles reducing their diameters with the reaction conversion [1]. Later on, the model was found to be useful to understand the reaction kinetics of a wider range of heterogeneous reactions and ore leaching reactions are not the exception [2-8]. The versatility behind the model is based on the assumption that heterogeneous reactions can be described as a series of subsequent step reactions or processes where the slowest or controlling step within the overall mechanism can be identified [9,10] (Figure 1). 



**Figure 1.** Sketch of the mass transport and the reaction stages modeled as a series of steps in the SCM. 

Besides all the positive features the model exhibits, some challenges on the data interpretation have been identified such as the effect of temperature gradients rising from the reaction evolution, the impact of mineral heterogeneity or grain boundaries present in particles and the effective liberation of the targeted leachable minerals, the uncertainty of

others [11]. This research work aims to integrate the effect of liberation or degree of exposure of valuable material on the overall leaching kinetics and discuss how the uncertainty of experimental data may influence the interpretation of the leaching kinetics. In the following the two topics will be briefly introduced. 

###### **The error analysis behind a model** 

The error analysis is crucial to understand the variability of the results [12]. The error analysis will not only account for the inherent uncertainty of a system but also it will provide restrictions to the conclusions being drawn. Whenever the error is associated to a mathematical model, it is possible to determine the impact that different measured variables have onto the variability of an outcome by considering the variability inherent to the former variables. The general mathematical expression for the variance of an outcome function F which is a function of xi measured variables is given by Equation 1,

###### **Imaizumi and Inoue (1963) and its application to SCM** 

Imaizumi and Inoue (1963) [13] presented a procedure to analyse kinetic data of batch flotation laboratory tests. The procedure assumes as a departing point, a process description which allows determining one or more parameters that represents one component (in froth flotation this is the pseudo-first order kinetics). Plotting conveniently the experimental data, the trend should be close to a linear behaviour. Nevertheless, when deviations of such linear behaviour are observed may imply the existence of two or more “components”. The protocol assumes the components contribute to the process efficiency (either extraction, recovery or any other parameter that allows evaluating the process evolution) from the start. The intercept in the y-axis will indicate the mass proportion of the component in the feed. (Figure 2).

###### **ABSTRACT** 

BASF Mining Solutions have developed a new generation of copper solvent extraction reagents that are not based on the current oxime chemistry. Initial laboratory studies have shown that these new reagents offer the benefits of a dramatic increase in resistance to degradation and are nitration proof. From an operational standpoint, the new reagents show acceptable copper net transfer capabilities from typical leach solutions together with a step change improvement in copper: iron selectivity in comparison to the existing highly modified aldoxime formulations. This paper details some of the fundamental laboratory studies completed to date as well as some preliminary data from a continuous pilot plant evaluation at a commercial solvent extraction operation.

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Copper solvent extraction (SX) from an acidic aqueous solution is typically accomplished using a hydroxyoxime extractant [1-3]. There are three hydroxyoximes from which all standard formulations are derived; 5-nonyl salicylaldoxime (NSAO), 5- dodecyl salicylaldoxime (DSAO), and 2-hydroxy-5-nonyl acetophenone oxime (HNAO). In the case of NSAO it is necessary to use modifiers in order to increase the copper stripped from the extractant [4]. Blends of the DSAO, NSAO, and HNAO are used to cover a wide spectrum of conditions [5]. Use of modified aldoximes and reagent blends over the last 30 years

has influenced the way copper producers and equipment manufacturers have approached the operation of copper plants. Typical pregnant leach solutions (PLS) in copper mining systems do not have a substantially adverse effect on the extraction reagents, and thus the existing reagents work well under most existing conditions. As conditions become increasingly aggressive (i.e. higher PLS temperatures in primary sulfide leach), current reagents become less capable of functioning according to expectations. One example is the effect of increasing temperature on reagents. While the effect on kinetics is positive, the effect on degradation is quite noticeable. A transition from the oxide layer to the supergene area leads to a secondary sulfide zone containing _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 383 enriched copper species such as covelite (CuS) and chalcocite (Cu2S). The secondary sulfide zone represents approximately 25% of the total copper. The rest of the ore consists of primary sulfide minerals, often chalcopyrite which contains the remaining 65% of the total copper. Initially, oxide ores were considered waste because they could not be concentrated and treated in a smelter. However, oxide ores are easily leached in weak sulfuric acid solutions producing aqueous solutions amenable to the SX-EW process. SX/EW was developed to treat these “waste” stockpiles. This led to a substantial portion of the global copper production being converted to a SX process, with the balance of primary sulfides being concentrated and sent for smelting. ###### **EXPERIMENTAL** 

###### **Reagent Kinetics and Selectivity** 

Kinetics testing was used for the comparison of reagents and understanding the rate at which they extract copper. The reproducibility of these tests allowed for comparison of different reagents without needing to rerun a control. The tests also determined copper iron extraction selectivity through iron analysis. This test was performed at 25ºC and 40ºC to show the effect of temperature on the reagent. 

The test vessel used was a 1-L PYREX® jacketed glass beaker fitted with a set of 4 stainless steel baffles (3.75 inches tall by 0.375 inch wide by 0.125 inch thick set 0.125 inches away from the beaker walls), clean and free of soap or detergent residue. A water circulator was used to maintain the jacketed glass beaker at 25ºC and 40ºC. The polypropylene impeller used was 1.75 inches in diameter with 6 slots, 0.125 inches deep and 0.125 inches wide, the top of the hub being 1 cm above the top of the impeller, and the shaft constructed of 316L stainless steel, 23 cm long. Mixer speed was adjusted to 1750  25 rpm. When sampling the emulsion it was important that no additional mixing occur. A large bore sampling tube was used. A 10 ml volumetric pipette with the tip cut off or a 10 ml serological pipette with the sample drawn through the large end were satisfactory sample taking devices. 

All reagents were sourced through BASF or purchased through Aldrich. Organic solutions were made from neat formulated reagent. They were prepared by dilution of the as received products into a 500 ml solution to exactly 10 v/v % of the appropriate reagent in Shellsol D70. Extraction and strip solutions were made according to the following specifications; standard extraction aqueous phase contained 6  0.1 g/l Cu+2, 3  0.1 g/l Fe+3 (both as sulfates) at a pH of 2.0  0.1, while the standard strip a

queous phase contained 35  0.7 g/l Cu (as the sulfate) and 160  2 g/l H2SO4. All aqueous solutions were prepared from reagent grade chemicals dissolved in D.I. water. All solution temperatures were equilibrated before use. Before and after each test all equipment was rinsed several times with DI water followed by methanol or acetone and completely dried before each use. Failure to adequately rinse and dry the equipment could yield erroneous results. 

Kinetics procedure was performed at 25ºC and 40ºC, allowing the solutions to reach the desired temperature before being contacted with the aqueous solutions. Procedure requires vigorous contact of 400 ml of the organic phase with 400 ml of strip

###### **DISCUSSION** 

Extraction formulations for these new products were based on the blending of two compounds, designated RGT-1 and RGT-2. They work synergistically to deliver the required extraction and strip kinetics while maintaining a high resistance to degradation and copper/iron selectivity. Blending of the two reagents, one a very strong extractant (RGT-1) the other a relatively weak extractant (RGT-2), works similarly to the nonmodified blends currently used by the copper industry. 

###### **Degradation** 

Extractant degradation is constantly occurring. Degradant concentrations increase if the rate of degradation is greater than the loss by entrainment and crud removal. These concentrations generally reach a steady state in the system. For high temperature systems, the higher concentration of degradation products leads to a higher entrainment and crud formation which, in turn, helps to reach this steady state, albeit at the cost of higher reagent consumption. As temperature increases, degradation of hydroxy oximes increases. This is due to an increase in the acid catalyzed hydrolysis of the oxime moiety. An illustration of the degradation rate of the neat reagents and of a modified reagent is found in Figure 2. These tests were performed individually and the data is displa

The reagents, approximately 10% solutions, were stirred individually with an electrolyte solution to simulate the most stringent conditions normally encountered at mine sites. All reagents had similar degradation behavior, with an initial high loss of reagent followed by a decrease in the loss rate over time. The shape of the curve leads to the assumption that once a substantial amount of degradation has occurred, there is a

In fact, RGT-2 stopped degrading after an initial loss of 7% of the total reagent over 100 days. RGT-1 data would suggest that the degradation over time reaches a plateau at approximately 20-25% of the total reagent over time.

###### **Kinetics** 

Extraction and stripping kinetics at 25ºC and 40°C were performed for various ratios of RGT-1 and RGT-2 and compared to the specifications for the LIX<sup>®</sup> range of reagents (Figures 3A-D). Reagent formulations were mixed with a LIX QC aqueous solution for 5 minutes (considered the equilibrium time). Samples taken at 30s, 60s, and 90s were used to quantify the transfer of copper at these respective times. At both 25ºC and 40°C, extraction kinetics were comparable to the current LIX range of reagents. This was due to the relatively high extractive strength of this new generation of reagents which shifts the equilibrium to the copper loaded species. Consequently, formulations containing high levels of RGT-1 were harder to strip at low temperatures. However, the stripping at 60s for all formulations was over 95% of the equilibrium value at 25°C. With the exception of one formulation, the stripping kinetics were all above 97% of the equilibrium value at both 30s and 60s at 40ºC.

###### **CONCLUSION** 

Novel extraction reagents have been developed which provides a higher resistance to degradation and a higher selectivity for copper over iron while maintaining similar extraction and stripping kinetics to current hydroxy oxime reagents. The substantial increase in degradation resistance is essential to the operation of plants that have an elevated PLS temperature. Both components that make up these new formulations had a far reduced incident of degradation in comparison to aldoximes, ketoxime, and modified aldoximes. The copper selectivity of these reagents is substantially better than even the most selective modified aldoximes. By reducing the amount of iron chemically transferred to the electrolyte, the amount of bleed at plants with a high iron concentration can be decreased.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Freeport-McMoRan Copper & Gold in conjunction with Turbulent Technologies Ltd. (TT), and Tenova Bateman Technologies has tested TT mixing at the Technology Center (TC) Modoc Test Facility.  Non-uniform energy dissipation in a primary mix box causes a wide distribution of droplets sizes with fine droplets being the primary concern. Fine droplet sizes do not readily coalesce, and are often the majority source of organic entrainment in aqueous. 

TT mixing technology generates homogenous energy dissipation throughout the auxiliary mixer volume, resulting in effective coalescence of fine droplets.  Due to higher coalescence rates larger droplets are formed, resulting in more effective phase separation. 

Large pilot scale testing occurred at the TC with two trains side-by-side. One train was a control parallel-strip train run with and without hydrofoil auxiliary mixing, whereas the experimental train utilized TT auxiliary mixing technology. Both trains utilized a primary pump mixer with curved vanes at maximum speed to increase the generation of fines. Results, under the conditions tested, demonstrated that TT auxiliary mixers decreased organic entrainment in aqueous by 50-75% as compared to the control train.  TT system performance yielded lower organic losses during plant instability due to forced phase continuity changes as compared to primary mixing only.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

<mark>Agglomeration is often utilized to reduce fine particle migration as well as to distribute acid for improved copper extraction during heap leaching of copper ores.  In order to improve the benefits of agglomeration, the process must be appropriately understood,

characterized, and modeled. This paper describes some of the fundamentals associated with agglomeration, tools for characterizing</mark> agglomeration, and models that can be used to predict agglomeration. 



_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

402 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

In today’s stringent environmental regulations, heap leaching is one of the economical process options for the treatment of complex ores such as copper, uranium, nickel, silver and gold ores. Some heap leach operations experience problems associated with poor recovery due to percolation issues caused by lowgrade complex ores, tailings and clayey deposits. Poor percolation can lead to low metal extraction due to solution channelling and/or the development of impermeable (dead) zones within the heap. Agglomeration is an innovative solution for heap leaching operations with ores having high fines or clay content. Crushed ore agglomeration has two major aims. First, it is the best opportunity for the thorough application of the leaching solution prior to building the heap and initiating the leaching process itself. Second, the addition of a leaching solution facilitates agglomeration by coalescing fine particles onto larger rock particles via liquid bridges. The agglomerates lead to more uniformly permeable heaps. Agglomeration with binder has been recommended for the ores, which contain more than 10-15% of minus 74 μm fines [1-2]. 

###### **Understanding agglomeration mechanisms** 

The binding mechanisms of agglomeration can be classified into five categories: (1) solid bridges, (2) adhesion and cohesion forces, (3) surface tension and capillary pressure, (4) attraction forces between solids and (5) interlocking bonds [1-3]. In crushed ore agglomeration, adhesion and cohesion forces are dominant for binderassisted agglomeration, while surface tension and capillary forces dominate the system for non-binder/wet agglomeration. The agglomerating equipment mixes the ore and solution and packs the agglomerates in a similar manner to snow rolling into a snowball [2]. Surface tension forces and capillary action between the solution and the particles is sometimes enough for the fine material to hold on to the coarser particles. In the agglomeration drum contact between particles with solution causes the particles to adhere/coalesce through liquid bridges. The liquid acts as a binder through capillary action and surface tension, predominantly because of the attachment of fine particles on the coarse particles and also the self nucleation of fines to form agglomerates. The presence of adequate liquid film thickness leads liquid bridges and results in mechanical strength to the agglomerates [4]. 

In general there are two stages of agglomerate growth. Initially, fast growth occurs by engulfment of the particles by the wetting liquid. The whole void space of the agglomerate is filled with binder liquid. The second stage of growth takes place by the attachment of new particle l

ayers. The liquid is drained from the inside of the agglomerate to its surface. This drainage stage is the rate-limiting process for growth, due to the resistance of liquid flow outward. The liquid flow is induced by the capillary pressure difference between the pores inside the agglomerate and the lower saturation near the surface of the agglomerate. The growth stops when free particles colliding with the agglomerate no longer encounter liquid at the surface of the agglomerate. Without evaporation, the maximum size of the agglomerate is limited by wetting saturation. The wetting saturation level depends on the capillary size distribution established by the particles and the wetting behavior of the liquid [1-3]. _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 403 Crushed ore agglomerates can take two forms: fine particles adhering to coarse particles and fine particles adhering to each other. The newly nucleated agglomerates are expected to be more prevalent in ores having high clay content whereas for hard crushed ores, the dominant mechanism of agglomerate growth is layering of fine particles on bigger particles (i.e. rim agglomerates) [1,5]. A sketch and a microscopic (X-Ray microtomography) image are shown in Fig. 1 to illustrate both types of agglomerate. It is evident from the Fig.1 that rim agglomerate is prevalent in copper-I ore type whereas coalesced-agglomerate is found in copper-II ore. The residence time in the agglomeration drum and the binding agents control the growth and mechanism of agglomeration. This manuscript covers fundamental aspects, industrial issues and related experimental results. ###### **FUNDAMENTALS** ###### **Liquid retention capacity** Interfacial forces such as capillary forces are an initial binding mechanism in the agglomeration process [6]. The capillary binding force generated by liquid bridges at coordination points between particles can be strong. Liquid bridges can be developed from free liquid or by capillary condensation. Liquid bridges can precede the formation of solid bridges that may form due to precipitation. The amount of liquid is an important key in determining the state of liquid bridges. When the amount of liquid is small, liquid bridges are formed between grains at contact points. Good agglomerates can be obtained by keeping the moisture at a level that creates an optimum liquid–particle bridging state for agglomeration which is generally in the capillary state. Consequently, the amount of liquid added should not exceed that needed for the capillary state to form agglomerates. This amount of liquid is termed the “liquid retention capacity” and is the amount of moisture held in soil or ore particles after excess liquid has drained away. If significant moisture is added beyond this state, slurry will form, making agglomeration a mud forming operation, rather than an agglomeration process. The bonding of crushed ore agglomerates immediately following agglomeration is by capillary forces caused by liquids. A simple procedure has been developed to measure the liquid retention capacity of an ore. This technique uses a capillary rise method to determine the amount of liquid retained in an ore sample. The detailed procedure is discussed elsewhere [3]. The authors reported that optimum moisture levels for agglomeration are generally very near the liquid retention capacity of the ore. ###### **MO

DELING** 

One of the main challenges in the analysis, control and optimization of heap leaching operations is the precise determination of agglomerate size. Special care is needed while handling wet agglomerates. The sampling and sieving may involve interferences such as coalescence and breakage of agglomerates, which alters the size distribution. Published information regarding the control and modeling studies of crushed ore agglomeration is inadequate. The research work carried out in this study included experimental work to model batch drum agglomeration. Considering the central role of agglomerate size with regard to percolation behavior of heap, agglomerate size was used as a principal variable. Recently, some related work was carried out at the University of Utah to predict agglomerate size distribution (ASD) and also improving the understanding of agglomeration behavior of different ores [3,7]. ASD prediction was mainly achieved through population balance modeling, and empirical modeling. From the batch experimental results, the use of a random coalescence model shows great promise for the modeling of the agglomerate size distribution. The coalescence rate was primarily linked with moisture content [8]. The growth rate of different ore types was different and was dependent on moisture content and feed size distribution. It was found that longer agglomeration times (more

###### **CHARACTERIZATION** 

Techniques such as QEMSCAN, SEM and others were employed for better understanding of the nature of agglomerates and associated binding. The extensive use of traditional techniques such as optimal microscope, mechanical strength, compression testing was limited due to wide agglomerate size distributions, moist state of agglomerates and abrasion tendency on drying. Considering this, an in-situ approach and non-destructive system was sought.  Based on the liquid retention capacity test and preliminary X-Ray CT work, it was found t

hat the initial agglomerate formation process is dependent on capillary forces between liquid and ore particles. Chemical bond formation through precipitation between particles was not observed for both copper ore types. Based on apparent density measurements and CT images, it was concluded that the particle porosity was not significant. 

Fluid flow and porosity effects in agglomerated ores were evaluated by a combination of high resolution X-ray tomography (HRXMT) and lattice-Boltzmann methods (LBM).  Agglomerates were scanned at both micro and milli scales and resulting tomography images were evaluated to calculate fluid flow and porosity distributions. The results showed that agglomerates break down during leaching, which causes a decrease in porosity and permeability. An extensive review on the same topic is provided elsewhere [8]. 

###### **Measurements using HRXMT and LBM** 

After sampling the agglomerates, the sample is packed in a cylindrical plastic container about 40 mm in diameter and mounted on the HRXMT stage. Depending on the type of material and level of energy required, a complete scan at 43-micron resolution can often be achieved within 30 minutes. After CT analysis, the 3D digitalized pore structures of packed agglomerate beds were used for porosity and permeability estimation using the LBM. The packed agglomerate bed porosities were measured as 35.26%, for copper-I ore packed beds. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

407 

The flow in packed agglomerate beds depends on the geometric properties of the packed bed. In this regard, the CT analysis allows for the 3D digitalization of the porous structure which controls the local flow. The LBM uses the digitalized porous structure for fluid flow simulation and determination of the local flow regime from which the macro flow properties for these complex geometries is obtained. The images of porous structures for packed agglomerate beds reveals why the LBM method is more suitable for this kind of problem than the standard CFD mesh methods. The standard solution with a CFD solver requires the construction of a grid, the definition of the boundary conditions of the boundary nodes, and the solution of the Navier-Stokes equation at each node. The standard CFD methodology, therefore, will require an enormous amount of time for grid construction and also for computer simulation. Permeability was computed by modelling Stokes flow in both the simulated pore space of a packed bed and the actual 3D digital pore space from HRXMT analysis using LBM. Based on Lattice Boltzmann (LB) simulation, it was noticed that most of the flows occur in a small fraction of the available pore space. Also, permeability values were calculated based on mean agglomerate size for standard 8-inch column using an empirical equation.  These values were compared with the values estimated from LB simulation.  The values from both methods were found to be in the range of 10<sup>-3</sup> to 10<sup>-4</sup> cm

<sup>2</sup> .

These results provide important information regarding the chemical and structural changes that are occurring in the system during column leaching. These postmortem analyses of residual copper ore samples provide some information on column performance during leaching, particularly to evaluate how the chemical and physical changes may have altered the leaching behavior. These analyses provide direct evidence of any changes which occur during the column leaching for extended times, up to 70 days. Based on the numerous benefits cited in the literature, the application of agglomeration as a pretreatment step for different heap leach systems looks highly promising. It is worthwhile to mention that proper mineralogical evaluation of ore, efficient comminution, effective agglomeration practice, and the precise use of quality control tools must be undertaken to ensure successful heap leaching. Most copper operations make use of raffinate as a binder, whereas a few have used polymeric binders on a demonstration basis. The reasons for not using binders can be related to cost considerations as well as undesirable issues in decommissioning and recovery. Liquid addition and electrical conductivity are recommended as quality control tools. Electrical conductivity can be used to monitor the agglomerate moisture in operations to insure proper moisture is being added. It is worthwhile to note that for comparative purposes and reliability on quality control tests, the agglomerates must be of equivalent sizes. The laboratory tests appear to be good for binder and agglomeration process screening, but they do not appear capable of providing feedback in a time frame needed to control an agglomeration operation. Therefore, these tests seem to be satisfactory as part of scoping test work, whereas h

ydrodynamic tests, developed by Guzman [9] may be more practical for commercial operations. There is no standardized quantitative method for evaluating agglomerate stability when using binders in agglomeration. Having reviewed the quality and characterization tools for crushed ore agglomeration, it is understood that the fundamental understanding of the agglomeration process for crushed ores is still lacking. This is primarily due to unique behavior of each ore body, lack of process insight, limited practical quality control tools for operator’s guidance and lack of advanced characterization tools. Certainly, there is a need to find optimal conditions of operation, and to measure the variation of the agglomerate properties in real time in a confined situation such as in a heap leaching system. But to find optimal conditions, a complete characterization of agglomeration and leaching process is required. The real challenge is the in-situ study of the effect of agglomeration variables, agglomeration quality and optimization process mode. The application of non-invasive characterization technologies such as X-ray computed tomography are likely to become more important in the future. Based on the review of all different types of agglomeration-heap leach operations, Dhawan [2] reviewed the general characteristics of ideal agglomerate and factors affecting them as summarized in Fig. 6. The precise use of quality control tools such as hydrodynamic testing and electrical resistivity techniques to define dry areas of poor percolation in heaps, saturated conditions and to locate leaks in liners will contribute to more control of heap leach operations. With the development of heap leach projects for different ore types, in extreme climates, complex and different mineralogy’s, the development of models for process simulation, test-work interpretation and scale-up, and process monitoring and control will also be crucial. Based, on the numerous benefits of agglomeration in the copper industry, it looks like that crushed ore agglomeration will continue as an important pretreatment step in heap-leach technology for many years to come. _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 414 Optimum moisture compatibility Chemical High mechanical strength High porosity Low cost Quality control tools

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Leaching copper from low-grade chalcopyrite dominant run-of-mine (ROM) stockpiles can be challenging and rewarding. Freeport-McMoRan Copper & Gold (FCX) tested and implemented an Engineered Heap (EH) process for increasing copper extraction from such stockpiles by means of controlling heap design, construction and operating parameters. This includes ore control, air injection, bacterial augmentation and pulse leaching. EH process technology was first applied on a

commercial scale to ROM stockpiles by FCX at its Morenci, Arizona mine in 2006. Experience to date is presented along with updates on application of this technology to other operating mine sites.

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

The Engineered Heap (EH) concept was designed and tested at FreeportMcMoRan’s Technology Center (TC) near Safford, Arizona. Several column tests were performed to evaluate and understand the effect of aeration, bacterial activity and temperature on pyrite oxidation and copper recovery from chalcopyrite. A bioaugmentation pilot plant was modeled and tested to optimize liquid-solid-gas mixing and residence time for maximal bacterial growth. Extensive phenomenological modeling was also carried out in conjunction with the leach column work. The research concluded that if heap leaching practices could be modified or engineered to significantly raise stockpile operating temperature, then copper recovery from chalcopyrite could be substantially improved in commercial stockpiles as discussed in previous publications [1-2]. 

This paper updates the current status of EH process technology after its implementation at Morenci mine and the present work being developed for other FCX properties, Chino in New Mexico and Cerro Verde in Peru. 

###### **MORENCI ENGINEERED HEAP** 

FCX’s Morenci, Arizona mine was targeted as a preferred site for EH implementation. Morenci’s Western Copper Deposit was being developed as a feed source for the concentrator and contained substantial quantities of chalcopyrite dominant sulfides below mill cut-off grade. The Western Copper Deposit also contained significant amounts of pyrite needed for heat generation in the EH process. The Morenci Engineered Heap (MEH) system comprised (1) bio-augmentation to provide additional conditioned indigenous bacteria, (2) blowers to provide oxygen in the form of air to the levels needed for bacteria growth and for pyrite oxidation, (3) ore control to ensure deliveries of lowgrade chalcopyrite with about 2% pyrite content, (4) heap construction according to design specifications, and (5) solution management and lift height control needed to maintain stockpile interior temperatures. 

The MEH project started at the end of the second quarter of 2006 in the Upper and Lower stockpiles at the Lower Chase Creek system (LCC). However, it was not until the fourth quarter of 2007 that the full implementation of the process was achieved (bioaugmentation, solution management, forced air, etc.). Once MEH was fully implemented, the benefits of this process were clearly tangible. Internal stockpile temperatures rose above 45°C, the LCC system became an acid and iron generator as measured through pregnant leach solution (PLS), and the system presented a healthy bacteria population. Copper production surpassed the forecast by 23%, including additional copper from residual leaching of lower lifts. During the second quarter of 2009, the bio

-augmentation plant was shut down. The entire LCC system had become effectually a large bioreactor for the entire Morenci circuit, thereby rendering the bio-plant redundant. Bacteria from the LCC PLS could be pumped to other locations to augment their population as needed. The remaining EH components were kept in place to assure process continuity. _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 419 ###### **Current Status** Since the inception of the EH process, copper production of the LCC stockpiles has significantly exceeded the expected production based on Morenci’s leaching model for low-grade chalcopyrite ores under standard leaching conditions. Investment for implementation of the EH process will require infrastructure (electrical power), air blowers, and a distribution system for air. ###### **CONCLUSION** The Engineered Heap (EH) process is an established technology for leaching lowgrade chalcopyrite ores within FCX properties. Key elements for successful EH implementation comprise (1) bio-augmentation to provide additional bacteria, (2) blowers to supply air for bacterial activity and pyrite oxidation, (3) ore control to ensure deliveries of low-grade chalcopyrite with sufficient pyrite content, (4) heap construction according to design specifications and, (5) solution management and lift height control for heat conservation. By incorporating the EH concept at FCX’s mines, substantial amounts of lowgrade chalcopyrite ores, typically considered “waste” would be able to be reclassified

as “ore.” Current production for run-of-mine stockpiles using the EH process at Morenci has increased copper production by 23%. Potential exists to increase copper production at other FCX properties by 16000 tons per year.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

The mixed leaching of a Chilean copper concentrate (predominantly chalcopyrite) was studied by using sulfate-chloride aqueous solution under normal pressure at different temperatures at constant pH. The use of sea water to increase the chloride concentration was studied as well. The leaching rate in sulfate-chloride solution was faster than in sulfate solution by a factor of ten in 7 days. The use of sea water led to a dissolution of 28% of the total copper in the same period of time at 60 °C, when the chloride concentration was around 60 g/L the dissolution was near to 36% at 60 °C. The iron content in the concentrate was around 30%, and remains in the solid after 7 days of leaching. The brown, reddish and yellow color solutions resulting after experiments indicate the presence of different copper chloride complexes ions. ###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Chalcopyrite (CuFeS2) is the most important copper mineral [1, 2] with the highest concentrate production, which is traditionally treated by smelting technology [3]. This copper sulfide has a high stability in aqueous systems and it is refractory to normal hydrometallurgical processes [4]. 

The leaching of chalcopyrite has been widely investigated, seeking for parameters affecting the kinetics of the dissolution [5, 2, 6] and supporting the best theoretical mechanism to explain the dissolution [7], for both chemical and bacterial leaching [8, 9]. The dissolution rate of chalcopyrite concentrate in sulfate media is slower to the leaching of secondary copper sulfide [10]; being the passivation of the mineral surface at high solutions potentials, like a dense layer of elemental sulfur or a polysulfide CuSn, one of the widely accepted reasons although the nature of the passivation film is still controversial [7, 11]. 

The dissolution of the chalcopyrite with oxygen in acidic solutions can be represented by reaction (1). When the leaching proceeds, a ferric oxidation of chalcopyrite can be carried out by reaction (2), being dissolved by ferric ions, producing ferrous ions which are re - oxidized by oxygen in acidic solutions according to reaction (3). This last step is slow at ambient pressure [12]. 







The use of chloride ions in the leaching solution involved the action of the second redox couple Cu<sup>2+</sup> /Cu<sup>+</sup> . It is advantageous due to the aggressive nature of the leaching and to the stability of cuprous ions by the formation of chloro-complexes, being a more effective process than a regular leaching in sulfate solutions with ferric ions as the oxidant agent. Some possible reasons of these phenomena are the higher rates of electron transfer in chloride solutions, as the reduction in chalcopyrite passivation [13, 14]. 

General reactions of dissolution of chalcopyrite under a sulfate chloride media are shown by equation (4) and (5) [15]. The prevailing redox couple of copper chloride complexes are still under discussion. It is suggested that cuprous ions are stable in the form [CuCln]<sup>1-n</sup> , and cupric ions in the form [CuCln]<sup>2-n</sup> [16]. The cuprous complexes are more stable than the cupric group, being the reason for reaction (4) to occur [12]. 



_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

431 

The oxidative model presented above is not enough to explain a rate promotion by the presence of ferrous and cupric ions. A reductive/oxidative dissolution model was proposed to interpret this enhancement of chalcopyrite leaching, presented by reactions (6) (7) and (8). The first step is the reduction of chalcopyrite by ferrous ions in the presence of cupric ions, represented by reaction (6) and the final step is an oxidation of intermediate Cu2S by ferric ions [17]. 







The intermediate Cu2S

in reaction (6) is formed only at potentials below the critical potential that is function of the ferrous and cupric ions concentrations. If that potential is higher, Cu2S is not formed and reaction (1) or (2) occurs. Also, Cu2S is leached faster than CuFeS2, increasing copper extractions at low potentials in the presence of these ions [18]. 

A non-oxidative/oxidative process has been proposed for the dissolution of chalcopyrite without any oxidizing reagent by reaction (9), with the formation of soluble cupric ions and hydrogen sulfide which are metastable products, being covellite precipitated by reaction (10). The rate of reaction (9) is governed by a rapid dissolution to assure the equilibrium and a diffusion of the soluble species away from the mineral surface [19]. 





The non-oxidative process was extended to include H2S removal, in the presence of oxidant agents such as Fe<sup>+3</sup> or Cu<sup>+2</sup> and sustain the reaction (9). This is represented by reaction (11) [19]. Assuming that the rate of reaction (11) is rapid compared to the rate of diffusion of H2S from the surface, the equilibrium at the surface will be perturbed by the removal of H2S by oxidation [18]. 



As we saw on this review, there is no consensus about the nature of the rate determining step and the mechanism involved in the dissolution. This work studies the effect of parameters such as initial ions concentration in the leaching solution and temperature in the dissolution of a chalcopyrite concentrate.

###### **BUILDING  COST  EFFECTIVE  SX/EW  PLANTS** 

Wayne R. Hopkins Technical Design Associate Faradelk Ltd www.faradelk.com 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Experience in the forty years since the days of Ranchers Bluebird, Bagdad and Nchanga has shown that , even though the industry has learned more about the technology of solvent extraction/electrowinning many projects are still inclined to build unnecessarily expensive plant designs . The object of this presentation is to indicate to design teams setting out on  new SX/EW projects some areas worthy of serious consideration which taken together may significantly reduce the capital and operating costs of these projects 

.SX/EW retains its popularity as a process route to not only copper but nickel,zinc and cobalt. Although written from a copper perspective many of the items discussed would apply to the other metals also. Based on wide experience in Chile and the USA, there is also experience garnered in new locations such as Spain, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Iran as well as the traditional locations .
