###### **SOLVENT  EXTRACTION** 

###### **Alternative SX Plant Configurations** 

New improved  extractant reagents have made possible  the series parallel  plant configuration . Here the leach solution flow is divided into two. One stream contacts stripped organic in a single-mixer settler and produces a raffinate. The partially loaded organic then counter currently contacts the remainder of the leach solution in two other mixer-settlers to produce a second raffinate stream and loaded organic. Thus a flow of 2F m3/h of PLS  means each contactor is seeing Fm3/h  of aqueous in the extraction stage and the organic global flow would be of the order of 1.2F m3/h. 

The two raffinates are similar in copper content but there is a reduction of copper recovery of approximately 6-7 percent compared to a conventional 2+ 1 plant for the same organic extractant concentration. The settler areas may be 30-35 percent smaller, saving inventory of organic and plant area.. The shortfall in recovery can be compensated for by increasing the reagent concentration. The organic phase flows through all extraction and strip mixer-settlers in series. 

Series-parallel is most attractive for processing leach solutions of approximately 3 g/L of copper or less. The viability of the configuration for higher copper concentrations is related to desired recovery, reagent concentration, effective entrainment recovery and the use of after-settler devices. Such circuits have been considered to be restricted to organic extractant concentrations of under 35% but the reduction of entrainment loss using hydrocyclone systems widens their application. 

There are no

w several variations on this theme such as the “optimized” or “interlaced” series parallel with the parallel stage located between the two series stages. 

###### **Organic Surge Tank and SX Plant Configuration** 

Where aqueous entrainment of leachate impurities in loaded organic is problematic aqueous entrainment transfer must be minimized. Apart from designing the mixer settler delivering loaded organic to reduce aqueous entrainment, this entrainment contamination of electrolyte can also be reduced by several other methods. 

By correctly designing the  loaded organic tank the aqueous entrainment loss to the electrolyte can be reduced to 10-50 ppm or less. Such tanks use de-entrainment baffles or chopped pipe coalescing aids to achieve the maximum aqueous entrainment coalescence and removal possible in the surge volume. These can be incorporated into the tank or located outside the tank as in the  Pacesetter design.The tank should be designed as an aftersettler with quiescent flows to enhance aqueous coalescence. 

Another solution is to use an organic wash stage prior to stripping. This requires an additional mixer-settler. Often this additional cost is not necessary if the loaded organic tank is designed to include aqueous entrainment recovery , the E1 stage is run aqueous continuous to reduce aqueous entrainment and the mixers and settler of E1 are conservatively designed. 

Another technique to avoid the investment in a complete mixer settler as a wash stage is to provide a mixer box for organic and wash water mixing with separation in essence in the 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

445 

loaded organic tank. This concept was proposed in Chile some years ago by BASF and is now seeing some application 

###### **Mixer Box Aspect Ratio and Number** 

These topics are interestingly linked together. Experience is that successful mixing can be produced with the aspect ratio of the mixing space down to 0.6:1 . This then lowers the settler in relation to the mixer box floor. 

Also if the mixer residence time is split over two or more boxes rather than a single box, CSTR theory is followed with greater closeness to equilibrium in the total box volume. Although from a kinetics and stage efficiency standpoint the difference between two and three boxes is marginal  the use of three boxes in extraction stages in particular  rather than two of the same total residence time will further reduce the height differential between settler and mixer box floors . This reduces structural or engineered fill cost. 

Compared to the early single stage box designs , using multiple boxes can introduce hydraulic problems with the settling of heavier phase in undermixed boxes and “ aqueous lock “ can occur causing levels to rise beyond those anticipated in the first and sometimes the second mixer boxes .Knowledgeable designers can anticipate and prevent such problems 

For the faster kinetics of the strip stages a shorter residence time is usually suff

icient and typically two boxes of the same size as the three boxes used in extraction are employed 

###### **Specific  Flow and Settler Design** 

Earlier designs used 3.5m<sup>3</sup> /m<sup>2</sup> h as the design specific flow for settlers without coalescing aids. Modern practice has raised this to 4.5-6 m<sup>3</sup> / m<sup>2</sup> h for about 10-30% reagent concentration in a kerosene diluent. Modern  designs also use much higher organic layer space velocities than the 3.5 cm/s used in earlier designs. Together with the new designs of aqueous take-off to replace the traditional aqueous weir which is difficult to adjust, this allows organic depths to be much thinner with dramatic savings in organic inventory 

The adoption of much higher settling rates has been made possible by the development of after settler and hydrocyclone systems to recover entrainment losses and improved organic surge tank design . 

Additionally a more elongated settler configuration results which reduces the cost of roofing and aids distribution across the settler. 

###### **Reverse Flow Mixer Settlers** 

The total concept of mixer settler design has changed in the last 15 years. ''Conventional' 'plants are no longer in the style of the original mixer settlers at Nchanga, Bagdad etc.. Today's “conventional” plant is often a reverse flow design .Although the first copper SX plant at Ranchers Bluebird used the reverse flow concept the design was not used in any large plants until the adoption of a modernization of the design at the Grupo Mexico facility at Nacozari in Mexico. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

446 

Since reverse flow mixer settlers using conventional pump mix impellers and secondary turbines were developed and refined, both organic and aqueous entrainment from “reverse flow'' units compare with or better those from more elaborately designed mixer settlers. 

The reverse flow design has now become the standard for new SX facilities Here the dispersion from the mixer boxes is delivered by a side launder to the far end of the settler and returns to discharge at the mixer box end.  This allows all mixer boxes and piping to be located on one side of the plant and better utilizes sloping site topography.  Note that the full settler length is used as before and the flow of settling phases is not disturbed. 

The distribution of the dispersion across the full width of the settler is accomplished by either 

###### - (a) a tight <u>gap picket fence,</u> 

This  provides the required pressure drop for even distribution across the settler 

###### (b) directing vanes 

Here the dispersion emerging from the side channel passes into a set of  vertical vanes which guide it around the corner then physically force the dispersion to move in the thin channels created to discharge points across the settler . No distribution fence is used  and dispersion is distributed evenly across the settler by the vanes. Some 70 % of reverse flow plants built to date

use the pressure drop distribution system 

The reverse flow concept has exceeded all its original conceptual ideas. The plants have demonstrated: 

Very significant capital cost reductions resulting from concrete wall requirement being reduced to one front wall the length of the train. 

Simplified piping resulting from the proximity of recycle lines to the mixer boxes. 

Placing all mixer boxes on one side of the plant reduces piping, electrical cabling, fire protection requirements and simplifies location inside buildings. 

Mixer settler units can be abutted to reduce foot print and produce consequent layout savings. 

A variation on the reverse flow is the “ side entry “ design which feeds dispersion from the mixer boxes at the side of the settler. through the settler wall into directing vanes which distribute the dispersion across the settler Thus all the mixers can be on the same side of the plant . There are several plants using this format in the Congo. 

###### **Mixer-settler Materials of Construction** 

Most early large mixer-settlers were constructed of 316L stainless steel lined concrete or free standing 316L stainless steel. The presence of chlorides in leach solutions requires much more sophisticated and expensive stainless steels for this type of construction. As a result  designs were  developed for large units in HDPE lined concrete and FRP. These offer savings, in most locations, over the conventional stainless steel designs. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

447 

The mixer tanks are free standing stainless steel, FRP or lined concrete. The general problem of ensuring HDPE liners do not have holes has moved most designers to free standing FRP. However recent SX plant fires , originating from static electricity discharge has meant that all piping and tanks should be conducting . The cost of conductive FRP seems comparable to duplex stainless steels so there is now a tendency towards this material especially in Africa. Here a more robust material less prone to transport damage is favoured. 



_Transportation Challenges for FRP_ 

Transportation difficulties , particularly in Africa , can mean the movement to site of large formed FRP sections can be difficult. There is now available a system known as Dualcrete which is basically polymer concrete slabs faced with a bonded on polypropylene surface . Rectangular tanks and electrolytic cells can be shipped to site as stacked panels so reducing shipping costs and assuring undamaged delivery, The panels are assembled on site and the polypropylene inner liners welded at the joints to produce the leak free unit . “Caulking” of the joint cracks between the polymer concrete panels using the vinyl ester resin of the polymer concrete provides a corrosion resistant back up support for the polypropylene inner liner. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

448 



_Self Supporting Arched Settler Roof in FRP_ 

It is normally found economical to roof all the settlers

using translucent panelling. This reduces organic evaporation losses, cuts down heat loss and contamination by dust, and prevents wind turbulence. To reduce capital investment these roofs can be added later as part of an operating maintenance budget. The advent of the reverse flow mixer settler as the industry standard has allowed all settlers to be located inside a long building with the mixer boxes outside ( depending on local occupational health regulations for exposure to aromatic compounds ).This will prevent wind disturbance of the settling process and excessive diluent evaporation and to reduce dust contamination and heat losses.  These units have a foam or high pressure water fog fire-protection system. 

Where this is environmentally acceptable it is a cost effective approach and has been employed at Gaby, Spence, Cerro Dominador, Tintaya , Mumi and  Kansanshi with new large plants for the Democratic Republic of Congo and Spain also planning this approach 

###### **Entrainment Reduction** 

###### <u>Organic Entrainment</u> 

The object of organic entrainment reduction  is twofold 

- (i) the reduction of operating cost of organic reagent loss 

- (ii) the minimization of  organic contamination of the strip extract liquor. 

###### <u>Organic Costs or Low Entrainment ?</u> 

These are not the same thing **!** 

An important design philosophy is that what the plant operator pays for organic make up per year is what is important , not what the entrainment loss is at the settler weirboxes . 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

449 

Consequently our approach is to produce simpler easier to operate mixer settlers and recover organic to very low levels in the streams leaving the plant rather than put substantial investment into elaborate designs in an attempt to minimize entrainment loss leaving the settlers 

When aftersettlers and/or hydrocyclones are placed on the leaving raffinate and electrolyte streams , the final loss of organic will be as low as 5-8 ppm. These results are borne out by figures from operations that have used hydrocyclones to reduce organic loss for some years 

. 

In a similar way the aqueous entrainment coalescer, the “ Pacesetter” , widely used for coalescence of aqueous from organic phases in other industries will certainly reduce aqueous entrainment going forward as leachate contamination of loaded organic phase.  The combination of Pacesetter and a correctly designed loaded organic tank will  confidently reach these levels . 

Thus the organic entrainment can be minimized at source by mixer and settler design to achieve low losses from the settler per se  or the whole plant can be considered with effective organic recovery equipment to produce very low losses overall. Thus there is a tradeoff between more elaborate and expensive mixer and settler design  and recovery equipment such as aftersettlers and hydrocyclones . This second approach  accommodates human error and maloperation of the mixer settler

units. 

For more expensive copper extractants at often 30+% concentrations,the units are easily justified even though they require a 5 barg feed pressure . For the organic entrainment removal on the  electrolyte side , the EW tankhouse requirement of minimum organic content would indicate their use regardless of the feed pressure needed. Here such high levels of organic capture will greatly extend the time between backwash cycles on the electrolyte filters. 

###### <u>Aqueous Entrainment</u> 

The loaded organic going forward to the stripping stage will transfer leachate impurities via the aqueous entrainment from the first extraction stage. 

If there is a wash stage this carry over  is reduced by dilution. The operation of the wash stage is assisted  by the use of a coalescing unit.  Such devices  are the “Chuqui “ Coalescer or similar system packed with bags of shredded plastic material, or the “ Pacesetter “,packed with an open hydrophilic material similar to honeycomb which promotes coalescence of aqueous droplets. 

These collect in the bottom of the Pacesetter vessel and this aqueous is periodically pumped out.  Pacesetter units have been shown to recover more than 80% of the incoming entrainment using hydrophilic or organophilic packing materials dependent on the duty required. 

The units can also be ”crud collectors” . They are used in this way in several plants where crud falls with the coalescing aqueous to the bottom of the unit where it is tapped off with the collected aqueous. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

450 

There are now15 of these units on loaded organic aqueous recovery 

The loaded organic then passes to the Loaded Organic Tank . This has a format similar to an aftersettler . The design of the loaded organic tank as an aftersettler with coalescing aids allows the aqueous to collect on the tank floor. De-entrainment baffle sets which reach the bottom of the tank can be fitted to enhance the aqueous collection. Aqueous coalesces in the quiescent region between the baffles and collects on the tank floor. Vee notches in the de-entrainment baffles allow the aqueous to flow along the tank floor to a collection point 

As the aqueous layer thickens it starts a removal pump by a conductivity switch. Thus the aqueous going forward to the wash stage is greatly reduced and the bleed of water from the wash stage is minimized. 

A spin off benefit is that maintaining a thin layer of aqueous on the floor of the loaded organic tank can assist in dissipating electrostatic charge build up in the organic phase. 

###### **Crud and Organic Treatment** 

These subjects are separate but can be considered together. Crud is best described as a slime deposit which forms usually at the organic-aqueous interface. A biological net growth occurs at kerosene-aqueous interfaces in the presence of air entrapping any fine particles of solids in the settler solutions. The deposit effectively reduces settler area as it grows and must b

e removed. 

A simple pumping vacuum cleaner system is usually sufficient to cope with the small amounts of crud produced with modern reagents. Crud is removed with a portable pump with a suction probe on a dolley that travels across the back of the organic weir and hose, and is pumped to a surge tank. 

Crud treatment by “mechanical rupture'' to release the entrapped organic is still the most common technique. What has been innovative in recent designs is the use of horizontal bowl decanter centrifuges to separate the aqueous and organic phases and solids. The surge tank can be strongly agitated with additional organic phase to rupture the crud material and release its organic content . The contents of the tank are settled and the clean phases decanted off. Then for light crud  the decanted organic can be mixed with regeneration clay and pumped over a filter press, followed by the crud layer in the rupture tank. For heavier crud build up a horizontal tricanter centrifuge is used in campaigns to treat the crud solids from the tank and also to separate clay solids from the collected organic. This organic rupture and treatment scheme was first developed at Ranchers Bluebird in the 1970s and further refined by Codelco in Chile. 

Organic treatment is required to promote regeneration of the oxime reagent particularly in salicylaldoxime systems, which degrades over time. Much of the loss of physical characteristics can be recovered by contacting with montmorillonite clays. Such organic/solids slurries can then be separated using the crud treatment centrifuge. The plant operator has several options: 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

451 

Continuous removal of a bleed stream from the circulating organic flow which is fed continuously to the centrifuge for crud solids removal. Then periodic campaigns mixing clay with returned and diverted organic, passing the slurry over the centrifuge. 

Collection of recovered organic and diverted organic, mechanical rupture of crud and centrifuge separation plus campaigns of clay treatment of diverted organic. 

Such centrifuge systems have resulted in better than 95% organic recovery in modern plants. 

The extent of crud growth is very difficult to predict for new installations unless there is experience with a similar ore deposit  or long term testwork available. A lower cost approach would be starting the plant life with a simple filter press installation and later investing in a more expensive centrifuge if crud growth encountered shows it will be a significant problem. 

###### **Holding Tank** 

The primary purpose of the holding tank or sump is to hold the contents of one mixersettler undergoing repair. Modern SX plants use fewer mixer-settlers which need very few repairs over the plant life. This large, expensive and normally empty holding tank is therefore of little use. It can be eliminated by adopting the following mode of operation: 

To repair an extraction mixer-settler, the organic is d

rained into the organic surge and the other settlers and the aqueous dumped. 

For a strip mixer-settler the electrolyte should not be discarded. By slightly oversizing the electrolyte tanks extra electrolyte can be stored in them . This is used to displace the organic to surge storage. The entire electrolyte contents of the strip mixer-settler are then drained back to the electrolyte tanks. 

However, the above procedure is cumbersome and operators will often elect to have a holding tank for operational ease. The use of the raffinate after settler in a dual role to hold mixer settler contents provides this volume 

###### **Filter Feed and Strong Electrolyte Tanks** 

It is widely considered desirable to maintain the flow flux on filter units relatively constant to avoid “shocking” the collected organic off the medium during backwashing.For this approach, for backwash periods there must be a standby filter or provision of surge in the upstream feed tank ( usually the electrolyte aftersettler ) and the downstream electrolyte recirculation tank . Note when scavenger cells are used a filtered electrolyte tank will be needed or piping provision may be necessary to feed the scavenger cells with commercial electrolyte during filter backwash 

The second method usually reduces capital investment 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

452 

###### **Spent Electrolyte Tank** 

This can be designed into the circulation tank system. 

These reductions in electrolyte volume reduce the inventory of copper in the circuit .All these tanks can be at or near grade. Large excavations for the” tank farm” and concrete/ gunnite lining of this are not always required and have fallen out of favour 

###### **Electrolyte Filtration** 

The production of high quality cathode requires virtually complete organic scouring from the incoming electrolyte, The sequence of low entrainment  production strip mixer settler , hydrocyclones and after settler will reduce organic entrainment to very low levels . To ensure the highest level of removal the electrolyte is passed through dual media filtration with garnet and anthracite. The resultant electrolyte can be expected to consistently be below 5ppm organic and usually  at 2 ppm. 

Both pressure vessel type or atmospheric type media containers are used 

. 

###### **Fire Protection System** 

This is a subject now uppermost in the minds of SX plant designers. The history over the whole period of copper SX plant design has seen us pass through the following: 

Water sprays Atomized water sprays AFFF foams High pressure water fog and always the hope of many an operator  that no fire protection was needed! 

The fire in the uranium SX plant in Namibia for Rossing Uranium concentrated attention years ago on this potentially disastrous problem. The case at Rossing was human error, bad maintenance practice and the use by the client (because of apartheid sanctions) of an incorrect diluent kerosene with a low flash point. Recen

t fires at Roxby Downs (Olympic Dam), Morenci and the Maraquita units near Cananea plus the Kristiansand fire in Norway hold lessons for us all. 

Common factors in such conflagrations seem to be: 

Lack of understanding of the generation of electrostatic build-up in plastic piping by organic flows at high velocity. 

- Allowing organic pipelines to run part full with a vapour space fed with “breather'' air 

- during unusual plant conditions. Fires have started then inside pipelines. Reduction of flash point in aerosol filled areas 

Unawareness of crud build up covering grounding rings inside plastic pipelines. Poor response of automated foam flooding systems. 

Unthinking maintenance work 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

453 

Insurers such as Factory Mutual  typically suggest items such as 

the use of stainless steel for organic piping and tanks, the spacing of the trains further apart in multi train plants 

the isolation of the tank groups serving each train. It is good practice to employ dedicated separate loaded organic surge for each train 

The primary fire safeguard for SX/EW operations for copper is the high flash points of the kerosene involved. Many plants throughout the world operate safely and within code and have no elaborate fire fighting systems. 

The owner's safety and insurance policies will determine the level of fire protection required. However recent fires in copper SX installations have raised awareness of fire hazards particularly from static electricity discharge. Recent plants have inclined towards high pressure water spray systems for enclosed tanks where organic is present( but there is some concern over maintenance of the spray heads) supplemented by water ring mains with optional AFFF foam addition. 

Typically a modern plant would provide a AFFF system with high velocity flooding ports in the settlers and mixer tanks or a high pressure water fog system .If inside a common building, firewalls along the SX building separating every two organic containing units are envisaged.. 

###### **ELECTROWINNING** 

###### **Cathode Washing and Stripping** 

To achieve high quality cathode rating the pulled cathodes must be thoroughly washed. Small plants use dip or dip/spray washing tanks but larger operations employ automated washing machines.  The usual machines employ high-temperature,(65 -75<sup>o</sup> C ) high-pressure ( 5 barg) fixed water sprays in tunnel spray booths  to drench the cathodes advancing on a conveyor in a direction perpendicular to their blades. This technique has been widely used. Other designs have modified the system to give full face impact washing of the deposited cathodes. Several designs of washing and stripping machines are available over a range of capacities. Some of these incorporate robots in place of transfer conveyors. It is important to review the proposed number of pulling shifts and actual hours worked to optimize the cost of the machine chosen. 

_Proceedings of Copp

er 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

454 



_Simplified Stripping Machine_ 

Smaller electrowinning plants can install equipment similar to fully automated machines with manual stripping of the deposit and slower operating speeds.( or more manual handling to and from the stripping station which is still simply automated ) For a typical smaller plant ( 20 000 tpy ) cathodes are harvested and processed in a simple but effective dip/spray tank wash and manual stripping facility . One third cell load of cathodes ( every third cathode) is lifted from the cells and the cathodes are lightly hosed to reduce electrolyte drying on the cathode deposits before reaching the cathode washing and stripping system  . 

The deposited cathodes are placed in an air agitated dip/spray wash tank.  The bale is then disengaged and lifts a second load already in the wash tank.  These are lifted through rinse water curtains of fresh hot water provided by spray bars across the top of the tank. . Water conditions are 65 deg C and 5 barg pressure. The copper containing wash water is routed to the electrolyte circulation system as make up for the stoichiometric and iron bleed loss of water. Thus the cathodes receive full face impingement washing generally regarded today as essential to achieve premium cathode quality 



###### _“Toastrack” Stripping_ 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

455 

The washed cathodes are lowered into a “toastrack” stripping stand where chisel knives are used to manually strip the deposits from the blanks. 

The deposits are pulled from the faces of the blanks lightly joined at the bottom as a “taco”. The cathode sides are collected in stacks. Blanks which have sticking cathodes are diverted into a reject rack for later processing. 

Cathode deposits are  weighed, sampled,  banded for shipment  and then delivered outside the tankhouse for removal by forklift truck. The stripped blanks are then returned to the cells by the tankhouse crane. 

###### **Tankhouse Cranes** 

Plant automation in zinc electrolysis has developed technology which is now appearing in copper tankhouses. Because of the uniformity of permanent cathodes with stainless steel blades, handling is simplified allowing gang loading of whole bale loads of cathodes into the cells. 

Normal electric overhead type cranes are used, but their control systems allow very smooth movement and braking In many modern plants cabs are dispensed with and crane control is by radio control or pendant. 

Use of drip trays allows loads to cross freshly loaded cells without dripping electrolyte on contacts. These retracting drip trays are also used for ventilation hood removal and replacement in some recent automated plants. 

Crane design improvements and the use of permanent cathodes now make it possible for copper tankhouses to move towards more extensive automation. Several plants are using addressable cranes with PLC units and designs are available for fully automated systems. These are very com

plicated and sophisticated pieces of equipment and the election of such systems must take into account the possibility of corrosive damage in acid misted areas and the desire to reduce operator exposure to acid mist. 

By using remote controlled cranes in a ''pitch and catch'' mode, two part time operators.one at cathode handling and the other at cell loading,can operate the crane and dedicated crane operators are not needed. 

For smaller operations there can be significant savings by adopting a gantry type design running on floor rails. This removes all effects of crane load from the building design. 

###### **Electrolyte Heating** 

In a wax-free permanent cathode electrowinning plant the heating requirements are usually only trim heating after strong/spent electrolyte heat interchange if required, cathode washing and cleanup duties. Usually no low cost steam is available and in-plant boilers need only to heat water. These do not impose the material selection , manning requirements and water treatment needs of steam heating, Capital cost can be reduced by employing a small hot water package heater rather than a steam boiler. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

456 

###### **Current Densitv** 

Recent designs for copper electrowinning tankhouses have pushed the design envelope with the use of innovative technologies such as air sparging. The large plant at Spence was expected to produce 99.9999% copper at 380-400 A/m<sup>2</sup> for example . As the plant uses a hood mist capture system the additional air to be handled was thought not be a problem. However these hood based systems for ventilation have been difficult to design effectively and it may be prudent to lower the expectations of current density to around 300 A/m<sup>2.</sup> Here it is recognized that the use of several layers of floating balls with minimal foam addition can produce adequate tankhouse acid mist conditions when used with a “pencil” type narrow building suitable for a horizontal air curtain background ventilation system 

There is then a trade off calculation between increasing current density, busbar and rectifier cost, numbers of cells and electrodes per cell, building size which must consider whether the additional acid mist (per m2 of building plan ) will be controlled and whether cathode quality can be maintained. There is a fundamental question of whether it is worth the trouble given all the uncertainty associated with such a move. It is sometimes forgotten that the plant is there primarily to make money not copper ! 

###### **Anode Development** 

The past thirty years are littered with attempts to replace the traditional  lead alloy anodes used in copper electrowinning.The various alternatives examined can be divided into two classes: 

<u>Non-lead Systems</u> 

Various types of ''dimensionally stable anodes'' or DSAs were developed. These follow the format of the chlorine industry where a coating of platinum group metals or metal oxides cover an

expanded mesh titanium substrate. It was hoped that their high initial cost compared to lead anodes would be offset by higher prices for lead free cathode and reduced cell voltage. 

The successful development of cobalt dosing and improved lead alloy anodes have allowed electrowon copper cathodes to achieve qualities better than electrorefined copper so the incentive for changing to the DSA has largely disappeared. A variation is the ALE (Activated Lead Electrode) which carries the activated titanium particles in a lead matrix in an attempt to lower cost 

With most DSA systems the oxygen overpotential at the anode is some 10% lower than with a lead alloy anode surface. This results in a power saving but it has been difficult to balance the power saving with the higher initial first cost of DSA anodes and the ease with which they can be damaged during operation. 

<u>.Lead Alloy lmprovement</u> 

Improvements in alloy design for lead acid batteries have been transferred to copper electrowinning. Ternary alloys of lead-calcium-tin and lead-strontium-tin have demonstrated 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

457 

much longer life, reduced wear rate and less damage from deenergized circuits than the earlier antimonial lead anode. Both cast and wrought anodes have been used but until recently the favoured design has been hot rolling  followed by cold rolling of the anode blade then fixing it to a solid copper bar 

The principal difference between manufacturers was the fixing of the blade to the copper suspension bar. It was considered that antimonial lead provides a much better electrical contact with a tinned copper bar than lead- calcium-tin and the designs all welded the Pb-Ca-Sn blade to an antimonial lead sheath  over the bar. An alternative is to fix the PbCa-Sn blade into a bottom slot in the bar and coat the whole in antimonial lead. 

The usual conventional standard anode fabricated  from a rolled lead plate and welded to a cast header assembly or slotted into a copper bar and soldered can have the following disadvantages. 

The weld is dependent on manual welding (lead burning) which is subject to human error; and if not done correctly, can lead to mechanical failure. 

The corrosive attack on the weld is greater than that on the rest of the anode and as a result the solution level in the cell must be kept some distance typically 50 – 100 mm lower than the weld of the anode . This increases anode length ( and cathode blank length and cell depth ) but not plating area. The soldered joint and exposed copper is also subject to splashing and acid mist attack. 

Normally the rolled calcium anode has a calcium /tin/lead blade but the lead used covering the header bar is antimonial lead. The antimonial lead facilitates the welding of the joint. Welding calcium lead is extremely difficult and requires very skilled lead burners. 

Another area which is prone to corrosion attack is at the solution/ electrolyte level. 

New developments

are rapidly changing the supply picture.One supplier casts the Pb/Ca/Sn alloy over the bar and also forms  a cast thick blade in a water cooled hydraulically operated mould. The cast anode with bar is then robotically handled and passed into a roll pair where the blade only is hot  rolled to achieve the metallographic requirements. 

As in the conventional rolled anodes the cast lead slab is reduced by rolling from the thick casting.  The current reduction of between 30% and 40% is more than adequate to achieve substantial change in the crystal structure, size, orientation and removal of porosity. Reduction during rolling by the conventional method is often of the same magnitude. 

This enables the cast anode to be rolled with the copper bus bar in position with a minimum of 5mm lead encapsulated around the copper and eliminating all soldered or welded joints. Thus it is a seamless rolled anode and the electrolyte level can be brought much closer to the suspension bar than with the conventional type. 

A major feature is that the blade can be rolled to 6mm thickness for example from just the solution line area to the bottom edge but remain at 8-9 mm thickness above the solution for added strength at the solution line. This can result in major savings over a full 9mm blade in the traditional form or give a much stronger design than a 6mm blade anode made traditionally.

The modern individual cell box cast from vinyl ester polymer concrete  does not require a liner. Such units are well proven in Africa, Chile and the U.S. and are economically attractive because of cost savings in areas apart from the cells such as the tank-house building. 

Correctly fabricated, polymer concrete is several times stronger than conventional reinforced concrete. It is resistant to corrosion by the electrolyte and organic entrainment throughout its thickness. 

For monolithic polymer concrete cell construction there are now two basic alternatives: 

The “ traditional”  box cast over one male mould which has a thin FRP lining applied after the cell is removed from the mould. 

The Stoddart type design where a FRP tank using the same vinyl ester resin as the polymer concrete is integral with the polymer concrete cell tank.

Baoping Zhang 

Key Laboratory for Metallurgy and Resources Utilization of Ministry of Education,Wuhan University of Science and Technology, Wuhan, Hubei, China, 430081 zbp2001@sina.com 

Michael L. Free University of Utah, 135 S. 1460 E. Rm 412, Salt Lake City, Utah, USA, 84112 Michael.free@utah.edu 

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Many of the world’s copper ore reserves are associated with chalcopyrite. Hydrometallurgical extraction of copper from chalcopyrite is difficult by conventional sulfuric acid heap leaching technology. Significant research and development to improve chalcopyrite leaching have involved the use of thermophilic microorganisms and to a more minor extent chloride. In this paper, some of the technology that has been explored for chloride based extraction and recovery will be discussed and related data will be presented. 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Most of the world’s copper reserves are in form of chalcopyrite. Traditionally, copper is recovered from chalcopyrite ore after a series of processing steps. Copper production from sulfide ores typically involves some form of pyrometallurgical processing such as crushing and grinding, flotation, smelting, and converting followed by hydrometallurgical processing such as electrorefining. The traditional method has the disadvantage of several processing steps, high energy consumption, and environmental issues. Producers have always been and are interested in using more efficient technology to produce higher quality products at lower monetary and environmental costs. The elimination of pyrometallurgical processing necessitates a leaching hydrometallurgical approach to metal production. 

Hydrometallurgical extraction methods have been the most common alternative to traditional chalcopyrite processing methods, including bacterial leaching [1-4], sulfate-based extraction [5, 6], halide-based extraction [7-10] and additional processes [19-34]. Bacterial leaching often requires a significant quantity of iron sulfide such as pyrite in order to provide sufficient iron for ferrous oxidation. The leachate is sent to a solvent extraction circuit where copper is loaded by the extractant. The loaded solvent extractant is stripped in concentrated sulfuric acid and sent for copper electrowinning. Most sulfate-based chalcopyrite processing methods 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

470 

require elevated temperature and oxygen. With bacterial leaching, sulfate-based process are li

mited to concentrates or very slow kinetics and poor extractions in heap leaching scenarios dominated by chalcopyrite. For many sulfide minerals, reaction rates are problematic. In particular, chalcopyrite leaches at an unacceptably slow rate in acidic ferric sulfate media due to the formation of a passive sulfur layer [11-13]. 

A number of techniques have been explored to mitigate the effects of the passive film. The addition of conductive carbon particles to ferric sulfate leaching solutions has been shown to increases the rate of chalcopyrite oxidation by a factor of 4 to 7 due most likely to improved electron transport through the carbon and possibly improved sulfur nucleation [12], The addition of silver ions has also been demonstrated to improve chalcopyrite leaching rates in ferric sulfate media [7], The problems associated with reduced kinetics due to passive film formation can also be successfully circumvented using fine grinding or mechanical activation [11, 13, 14], Mechanical activation or fine-grinding can also be extended to other sulfide minerals [11, 15-16]. 

Alternative chemistries such as halides offer the opportunity for higher extractions and reduced energy requirements in copper recovery. Dissolution of copper in the cuprous form eliminates half of the need for electrons during electrowinning [17], which can save energy relative to the traditional reduction of copper from the cupric form during sulfate based electrowinning. Furthermore, chalcopyrite leaching in halide media is more rapid than in sulfate media [18]. One promising alternative method of recovering copper from chalcopyrite involves the use of halide solutions containing chloride and/or bromide ions and an oxidant such as cupric ions to leach the copper from the chalcopyrite, followed by precipitation of the iron in the form of goethite using oxygen and water.  The overall extraction reaction is expressed as: 



The associated electrowinning reactions are: 



The dissolved copper is then recovered from solution by electrowinning from the cuprous ion state, which requires only half of the energy needed for traditional electrowinning from the cupric ion (Cu<sup>2+</sup> ) state, since the cuprous ion (Cu<sup>+</sup> ) needs only one electron.  The sulfur contained in chalcopyrite is converted predominantly to elemental sulfur, rather than sulfuric acid.  The electrowinning reactions, which utilize cuprous oxidation rather than water hydrolysis utilize approximately half of the voltage, thereby reducing the power and energy requirement by 50 %.  This 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

471 

reduction, combined with the use of only one electron per copper atom results in an overall potential energy reduction of 75 % compared to conventional technology. Thus, this alternative copper recovery technology that is based upon halide leaching holds significant promise from energy and environmental perspectives.  In addition, halide extraction also facilitat

es gold extraction. 

A number of processes have been developed for the extraction of metal from chalcopyrite-based sulfide ores. Only a few processes are representative of most of the available processes. Including Arbiter Process [19], Broken Hill Associated Smelters (BHAS) Process [20], Cymet Process [21], Bromide Process [22], Canmet Process [23], CENIM-LNETI Process [24], Copper Leach, Electrolysis, and Regeneration (CLEAR) Process [25], Cuprex Metal Extraction Process (CMEP) [20], Dextec Process [26], Ecochem Process [27], Electroslurry Process [28], Elkem Process [29], Intec Process [30], Minemet Recherche Process [31], Nenatech Process [32], Nitric Acid Process [33], USBM Process [34]. All of the processes occur between 25 and 140<sup>o</sup> C with the majority occurring between 80 and 105<sup>o</sup> C.  Most of the processes utilize halide, sulfate, or ammonia/ammonium chemistries, although nitric acid has also been used. More recently, there has been substantial momentum in the direction of high pressure oxidation in autoclaves.  However, these elevated temperature and pressure scenarios are not amenable to large scale heap leaching scenarios for mid and low grade ores.  This study focused on conditions that may be feasible in heap leaching operations. 

In this study, chalcopyrite concentrate was leached in order to identify optimal conditions with chloride based solutions containing NaCl, FeCl3, CuCl2, HCl.  This study also compares the leaching results using ZnCl2, AlCl3, CaCl2, MgCl2 and KBr as replacements for NaCl in chalcopyrite concentrate leaching. Finally, chalcopyrite ore was leached under the optimal conditions for 45 days.

The deposit is situated in the central part of the Udokan mountain range. The highest elevation point of the deposit is at 1,800-2,100 m level. The lowest elevation point is at 1,200-1,300 m level. Udokan copper deposit include sulphide and oxide copper-bearing minerals which overlay one another practically on the whole territory of the deposit. Main ore types in the region are bornite-chalcocite (67.5%), copper pyrite (6.5%) and secondary malachite-brochantite ores (26%). Ore grade fluctuates from tenths of percent to 36%. Silver is an associated component. The ore includes sandstones (8590%), sandstones (7-10%) and argillites (3-5%) which all have different composition. It is known that for full dissolution of copper sulphide raw materials and exclusion of atomic sulphur formation autoclave leaching should be performed at temperature not lower than 180<sup>о</sup> С; partial oxygen pressure in all cases should not be less than 0.3 MPa. 

###### **EXPERIMENTAL METHODOLOGY** 

The testworks were performed in a titanic autoclave manufactured by Premex with capacity 1.2 dm<sup>3</sup> . To prevent formation of pregnant solutions in the process of experiment it was decided to increase dilution rate of the slurry loaded into the autoclave and liquid/solid phase ratio became 3. Before autoclave leaching commencement copper oxide was dissolved in diluted sulphuric acid solutions. Stirrer rotation speed was taken as 600 revolutions per minute which corresponds to intensive aeration of suspension (with (the sulphite number) amounting to 1 mol of Na2SO3/dm<sup>3</sup> x atm x hr. The oxygen was supplied always during the liquid phase through the immersed pipe. Test procedure was the following. Initial master sample of material (atmospheric leach cake) was mixed with water and loaded into the autoclave. Amount of water to be added was calculated basing on coefficient of autoclave filling 0.6 and taking into account the necessity to add a certain amount of sulphuric acid solution later on. Prior the acid was diluted with water with 1:5 ratio. 

Decision to stop leaching was taken basing on the information on oxygen consumption rate displayed on the screen of the computer on continuous basis. When oxygen absorption stopped the process of its supply from the cylinder was stopped

too. Later the autoclave was cooled to the temperature 70-75<sup>о</sup> С and the waste gas was released. 

Wet cake produced in the process of leaching was divided into two parts. One part was sent for direct cyanization and the other was subjected to lime boiling. It was boiled for several hours with limestone. Then the product was washed and also sent for cyanide treatment. Therefore it was possible to estimate the efficiency of lime boiling in each experiment basing on silver content in the final cake. The results were estimated taking into account two parameters: silver recovery and average rate of potassium cyanide consumption. 

On the initial stage of the testworks lime boiling was conducted at the temperature 90-95<sup>о</sup> С during 2 hours with reactive lime consumption rate 100 kg/t of the  solid. Later on another series of experiments was conducted aimed at definition of this operation duration. The temperature and lime consumption rate in all the expe

After completion of the experiment sorbent agent was isolated from the slurry on the sieve, the slurry was filtrated, its solid phase was washed and assayed for estimation of silver content. During cyanide treatment samples were taken several times for CN content measurement. ###### **Studies of silver recovery processes** 

###### <u>Cyanide treatment diagrams</u> 

Relatively high indexes as regards to silver can be achieved during the experiments which provided copper recovery amounting to 95%. During all the experiments the total volume of copper recovery into sulphate solution prevails over silver recovery volume into cyanide solution. This difference fluctuates within the wide range - from 20 to 50%. 

Cyanide consumption is related to copper recovery into solution, to be exact with its remaining amount in the cake. Fig.5 presents connection of Ag recovery and KCN consumption with Cu content in the cake after autoclave leaching. The specified diagrams confirm earlier assumption that considerable amount of silver is associated with copper sulphides (chalcocite and covellite). Defined own silver minerals such as jalpaite are also related to sulphides. Due to these reasons all the activities targeted at increase of sulphides decomposition rate will be favorable for the process of silver recovery. Cyanide consumption is directly related to copper content in the cake of autoclave oxidation leaching and it is quite understandable. It is known that copper sulphides are intensive absorbers of CN.

###### **CONCLUSION** 

During investigation of the impact of autoclave oxidation leaching parameters on metals recovery from sulphide copper concentrate of Udokan copper deposit it was stated that at the temperature higher than 200<sup>о</sup> С and partial pressure 0.7 MPa the maximal possible recovery values can be achieved: 99-99.5%  of copper and after the following cyanide treatment 90-96% of silver. Pressure oxidation process can be simulated if large-sc

ale test is performed which forms favorable predispositions for the following development of the process in pilot and industrial scale. 

Cyanide consumption rate depends directly upon remaining concentration of copper in the cake of autoclave oxidation leaching. If autoclave oxidation leaching runs under optimal parameters KCN consumption on the following cyanide treatment stage can be decreased till 10 kg/t. Lime boiling operation of the cake of autoclave oxidation leaching is a mandatory process operation and it is impossible to achieve acceptable indexes of silver recovery into the cyanide solution without it. Duration of this stage should be not less than 8 hours.

###### **IMPROVEMENTS IN THE VAT LEACHING OPERATION AT MANTOS BLANCOS DIVISION OF ANGLOAMERICAN COPPER** 

Juan Nuсez, Jessica Cueto, Saddy Peroncini, Mantos Blancos Division Gabriel Zarate, Anglo American Chile Pedro de Valdivia 291, Santiago, Chile 

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Mantos Blancos Division of AngloAmerican Copper started the treatment of oxide ore in March 1961 at a production capacity of 13,300 tpy of copper, which was later expanded to 30,000 tpy in 1967. The process included vat leaching, cuprous chloride precipitation, pelletizing and smelting. In November 1995, this process was replaced by vat leaching, solvent extraction and electrowinning at a production capacity of 44,000 tpy of copper which was later expanded to 60,000 tpy. 

The vat leach cycle was modified with the introduction of the SX-EW plant when copper grade was well above 1 %Cusol (sulphuric acid soluble copper). The total lea

ch cycle was 98 hours, 70 hours of which were dedicated to the leaching itself. 

As the copper ore grade has decreased significantly with time, a number of modifications have been implemented in the operation to deal with this lower copper grade ore, among them leach cycle, particle size, acid addition in curing stage and specific flow rates. 

The modifications implemented in the vat leach operation and the results obtained are discussed in this paper. 

494 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Mantos Blancos is located 45 km NE from Antofagasta in the Atacama Desert. Mantos Blancos has two processing plants for treating oxide and sulfide ore separately. Sulfide ore is processed by milling and flotation to produce copper concentrate as a final product. Oxide ore is acid leached to produce copper cathodes in a solvent extraction and electrowinning (SX-EW) plant. The main copper mineral in Mantos Blancos oxide ore is atacamite with a minor amount of chrysocolla. 

Mantos Blancos oxide plant was commissioned in 1960 with a capacity of 6,000 t/d using vat leaching to dissolve the copper. Continuous improvements allowed by the end of 1991 to increase to 9,500 t/d in ten vats of 4,000 t each in a counter-current leach circuit. The ore was crushed to less than 6 mm and loaded into the vats. Then, it was leached in an up-flow mode at a rate of 375 l/h/m<sup>2</sup> . The rich solution tenor was 35-40 g/l Cu and 30 -35 g/l chloride, and was the overflow of the latter loaded vat. The barren solution from the downstream process, at a tenor of 7-10 g/l Cu, was fed to the first loaded vat and the overflow was passed successively through the vats until it reached the fresh ore loaded vat. 

The Mantos Blancos downstream process included a cuprous chloride precipitation stage with SO2, followed by reduction with limestone and coke at high temperature to produce copper ingots. As part of the project to replace this process by an SX-EW one, it was necessary to evaluate heap leaching as an alternative to the existing vat leaching or the modification of the existing vat leach circuit to produce a copper solution suitable for solvent extraction. 

In November 1995, the old process was replaced by vat leaching, solvent extraction and electrowinning at a production capacity of 44,000 tpy of copper which was later expanded to 60,000 tpy of copper. 

The vat leach cycle was modified with the introduction of the SX-EW plant when the copper head grade was well above 1% Cusol (sulfuric acid soluble copper). It used the solution application ratio as indicator, which was 3 m<sup>3</sup> /t ore at that time. The total leach cycle was 98 hours, 70 hours of which were dedicated to the leaching itself. 

This indicator is independent of the head grade, which has decreased significantly in the past years, from more than 1 %Cusol down to 0.5 %Cusol and reaching occasionally values as low as 0.3 %Cusol. Therefore, an indicator based on m<sup>3</sup> /kg Cu dissolved instead of m<sup>3</su

p> /t ore was implemented after conducting a test work program using the same commercial vats. The use of this new indicator allowed to reduce the leach cycle from 70 hours down to 56 hours, among other achievements.

As shown in the previous tables, the recoveries obtained in heap leaching were significantly higher than those obtained in vat leaching, but the net acid consumptions were also higher. In order to decide which alternative to select, a basic engineering study was prepared for each case including the required SX-EW plant. The best economical indicators were for the vat leaching alternative, which was therefore selected. 

One of the main disadvantages of the vat leaching process is the amount of solids in the PLS. As the leach is carried out in the up-flow mode, during the first two hours of the process, suspended solids can reach up to 10 g/l. As the effect of solids in the solvent extraction plant is well known, an exhaustive study of several clarifier alternatives available in the industry was carried out to guarantee a maximum of 20 ppm of suspended solids in the feed to SX. Equipment from three suppliers was tested at pilot plant scale, achieving the required results in all cases. 

###### **PLANT MODIFICATIONS** 

In order to adapt the existing vats for production of the PLS required for the SX plant, major modifications to the area piping were required. 

The crushed ore is mixed with acid in two drums and loaded with a tripper loader bridge into twelve vats now. The loading is done in layers of 50 cm to avoid segregation. Intermediate solution is fed in such way to bring the solution level approximately 50 cm lower than the ore level. 

Once the vat is fully loaded, the rich solution overflows to the clarifiers; leaching time with intermediate solution was 35 hours. Then raffinate solution from the SX plant was fed to the vats for another 35 hours; the overflow solution of this stage is collected in intermediate tanks and pumped to the first leach cycle. Finally the vat is unloaded with cranes and the tails are disposed on dumps. The false bottom of the vat is cleaned and repaired when necessary, before the next batch of ore is loaded. 

In order to avoid any contamination of the organic

phase with asphalt, it was also necessary to change the vat lining from asphalt to HDPE. A minimum amount of asphalt in the organic phase resulted in severe problems in the SX plant with the phase disengagement time increasing dramatically. Two EIMCO reactor clarifiers were installed after the vats and prior the SX plant to control the suspended solids. The modified plant was commissioned by the end of 1995 and reached the nominal capacity in a very short period of time. ###### **INTRODUCTION** 

The metallurgical complex of Mexicana de Cobre (MDC) is located 21 Km from Nacozari de Garcнa in Sonora, Mйxico. The complex includes a copper smelting plant, an electrolytic refinery, a copper rod plant, a precious metals plant and a plant for treatment of dust and aqueous effluents. The smelting operation consists of a flash furnace and a Teniente converter where copper concentrates produced at MDC´s and Cananea’s concentrator plants (both companies property of Grupo Mexico) are smelted. The copper anodes produced at the smelting plant are processed at the electrolytic refinery and the final cathode product is sent to the rod plant. 

As it is known during the electrorefining process the copper anodes are oxidized and the dissolved copper is deposited on the cathodes, while some other species present in the anodes (impurities and metal values) precipitate and form anodic slimes that build up at the bottom of the electrolytic cell [1]. Once the electrorefining process concludes, the anodic slimes are collected and sent as slurry to another stage of the process where they are decopperized. The recovery of copper is carried out at high pressure and high temperature in a reactor fed with sulfuric acid and oxygen. It is a requirement that during this recovery stage less than 1% of copper remains in the slimes, before the decopperized slimes are sent to the precious metals plant for dorй recovery. Table 1 shows the typical composition of the slimes after decopperizing.

From the results of the acid chloride and alkaline leaching tests, the advantages of both processes were considered and a third option was evaluated, which included a two stage leaching. The first stage consisted of using the acid chloride system (100 g/L, Table 3

) with only a minor change in the sulfuric acid concentration that was decreased to 200 g/L. According to the results except for tellurium, all the other species were fairly dissolved particularly arsenic, bismuth and antimony, leaving an even richer silver residue. ###### **RELEVANCE OF HYDRO-GEOMECHANICAL-GEOCHEMICAL PROCESSES IN THE DESIGN AND MANAGEMENT OF COPPER HEAP LEACH PADS** 

Mayu Tincopa, Albert Nardi, Gabriela Roman-Ross, Jorge Molinero, David Arcos and Orlando Silva _Amphos 21 Consulting Espaсa_ Eduardo Ruiz _Amphos 21 Perъ_ 

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Heap leach pads constitute a common practice in the mining industry. In the design and management it is not common to take into account criteria based on coupled hydro-geomechanical-geochemical processes, and these are of paramount importance for two main reasons: (1) they could play an important role on the physical stability of the pad and; (2) they are keys for the metallurgical efficiency, especially in the mid-long term. 

As an example of the relevance of such a complex coupled phenomena it could be mentioned that geotechnical stability of the heap is related to the distribution of liquid pressures which, at the same time, is related to the permeability through the Darcy’s law. In its turn, permeability will be affected by porosity changes, which depends on the consolidation state and the dissolution/precipitation of minerals. Obviously, hydrometallurgical performance of the heap ore is also strongly linked with the abovementioned coupled processes. 

In this work, we present a numerical model to solve the hydro-geomechanicalgeochemical coupled processes, developed with COMSOL-PHREEQC, a java interface developed for combining COMSOL Multiphysics – a well-known commercial FEM platform – with PHREEQC, the open-software geochemical simulator developed at USGS and used worldwide. The resulting numerical tool is able to solve simultaneously unsaturated liquid flow, soil effective stress and geochemical dissolution and precipitation. 

Geochemical changes affecting porosity and permeability are coupled explicitly in the hydraulic and geomechanical calculations. 

In this paper we provide a demonstrative simulation of a synthetic copper heap leach pad case in order to show the relevance of the coupling, as well as the capabilities of the

Conclusions** - Development of a numerical interface (iCP) that allows simulating metal recovery hydrometallurgical processes through the modelling of coupled HMC phenomena. - The iCP interface allows:

- Predicting and optimizing metal recovery processes; irrigation rates, irrigation-rest cycles, layer geometry, etc. 

   - Evaluating the hydro-chemical-mechanical changes that affect the leaching heaps layer stability. 

   - Calculating more precise and realistic leach heaps safety factors. 

- iCP flexibility and expansion capacity: 

   - Only reactive transportation (HC); reactive transportation with mechanics and thermal effects (HTMC). 

   - Different geometries: 1D, 2D, 3D; regular, irregular, etc.
